JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.title: INTRODUCTION TO SCIENCE
JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.note:
MEANING OF SCIENCE

Science is the systematic study of living things, non-living things, and natural phenomena through observation, experimentation and investigation.

Science helps us to understand the world around us and explains how things work.

Examples of scientific activities include observing plants as they grow, investigating why objects fall to the ground, studying the human body, and examining how water changes into vapour.

BRANCHES OF SCIENCE

Science has several branches, but the three major branches commonly introduced at the junior secondary school level are Biology, Chemistry and Physics.

BIOLOGY

Biology is the branch of science that deals with the study of living things.

It involves the study of plants, animals, human beings and microorganisms.

Examples of topics in Biology include:

  • Plants and animals.
  • The human body.
  • Nutrition.
  • Reproduction in living things.
  • The environment.

CHEMISTRY

Chemistry is the branch of science that deals with the study of matter, its composition, properties and changes.

Examples of topics in Chemistry include:

  • Matter and its properties.
  • Elements and compounds.
  • Mixtures and their separation.
  • Acids and bases.
  • Chemical changes.

PHYSICS

Physics is the branch of science that deals with matter, energy, forces, motion, light, heat, sound and electricity.

Examples of topics in Physics include:

  • Force and motion.
  • Light and shadows.
  • Heat energy.
  • Sound.
  • Electricity and magnetism.

OTHER AREAS OF SCIENCE

Other areas of science include:

  • Agricultural Science: The study of farming, crops, animals and agricultural practices.
  • Environmental Science: The study of the environment and the relationship between living things and their surroundings.
  • Earth Science: The study of the Earth, rocks, soil and natural processes.
  • Astronomy: The study of the Sun, Moon, stars, planets and other objects in space.

IMPORTANCE OF SCIENCE

Science is important in our daily lives for the following reasons:

  • It helps us understand natural events and phenomena.
  • It improves healthcare through the development of medicines, vaccines and medical equipment.
  • It improves agriculture by helping farmers increase crop and animal production.
  • It supports communication through phones, computers, radio and television.
  • It helps provide electricity and other forms of energy.
  • It improves transportation through the development of cars, aeroplanes and ships.
  • It helps us protect the environment and manage natural resources.
  • It encourages critical thinking, creativity and problem-solving.

THE SCIENTIFIC METHOD

The scientific method is a systematic process used by scientists to investigate questions, solve problems and discover new knowledge.

The major steps include:

OBSERVATION

Observation involves using the senses or scientific instruments to gather information about something.

Example: Observing that a plant grows faster in sunlight than in a dark place.

IDENTIFICATION OF A PROBLEM OR QUESTION

This involves identifying what you want to investigate.

Example: Does sunlight affect the growth of a plant?

FORMULATION OF A HYPOTHESIS

A hypothesis is a possible explanation or prediction that can be tested.

Example: A plant exposed to sufficient sunlight will grow better than a plant kept in darkness.

EXPERIMENTATION

Experimentation involves carrying out a test to find out whether the hypothesis is supported by evidence.

Example: Keeping two similar plants under different light conditions while providing them with equal amounts of water.

COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS OF DATA

This involves recording observations and comparing the results obtained during the experiment.

Example: Measuring and recording the heights of the two plants over several days.

CONCLUSION

A conclusion is drawn from the results of the investigation. The results may support the hypothesis or show that it needs to be changed.

CHARACTERISTICS OF SCIENCE

Science has the following characteristics:

  • It is based on observation and evidence.
  • It involves testing ideas through investigation.
  • It encourages careful measurement and recording.
  • Its findings can be checked by other investigators.
  • Scientific explanations can be revised when new evidence becomes available.
  • It helps people solve practical problems.

SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY

Science and technology are closely related but have different meanings.

Science is the systematic study of the natural world to gain knowledge and understanding.

Technology is the application of scientific knowledge, skills and methods to develop tools, machines and processes that solve problems.

Examples:

  • Science helps us understand electricity.
  • Technology uses this knowledge to develop electrical appliances.
  • Science helps us understand diseases.
  • Technology uses scientific knowledge to develop medical equipment and treatments.

SCIENTIFIC EQUIPMENT AND THEIR USES

Scientific equipment refers to tools and instruments used for observation, measurement and experimentation.

Examples include:

  • Microscope: Used to observe very small objects that cannot be seen clearly with the naked eye.
  • Thermometer: Used to measure temperature.
  • Measuring cylinder: Used to measure the volume of liquids.
  • Beam balance: Used to compare the masses of objects.
  • Magnifying glass: Used to enlarge the appearance of small objects.
  • Stopwatch: Used to measure time.
  • Ruler: Used to measure length.

SAFETY RULES IN THE SCIENCE LABORATORY

A science laboratory is a room or place where scientific experiments and investigations are carried out.

Students must observe the following safety rules:

  • Obey the teacher's instructions at all times.
  • Do not eat or drink in the laboratory.
  • Do not taste or directly smell chemicals.
  • Handle glassware and laboratory equipment carefully.
  • Do not run or play in the laboratory.
  • Report accidents, spills and broken equipment immediately.
  • Wear protective equipment when instructed.
  • Do not touch or use chemicals without permission.
  • Wash your hands after practical activities.
  • Keep the laboratory clean and tidy.

CAREERS IN SCIENCE

Science provides opportunities for many careers in society.

Examples include:

  • Doctor: Diagnoses and treats diseases.
  • Nurse: Provides healthcare and supports patients.
  • Pharmacist: Prepares, supplies and advises on medicines.
  • Engineer: Designs, builds and maintains structures, machines and systems.
  • Laboratory Scientist: Performs scientific tests and analyses samples.
  • Agriculturist: Applies scientific knowledge to farming and agricultural production.
  • Environmental Scientist: Studies environmental problems and develops ways to address them.
  • Science Teacher: Teaches scientific knowledge and practical skills.
  • Meteorologist: Studies weather and atmospheric conditions.

CLASS EXERCISE

  1. Define science.
  2. Mention three major branches of science and explain what each branch studies.
  3. State five importance of science in everyday life.
  4. List and explain four steps involved in the scientific method.
  5. Mention five scientific instruments and state one use of each.

  3. Mention five careers in science and explain the work of any three.
  4. What is a hypothesis? Give one example of a hypothesis about plant growth.
  5. Explain four ways science contributes to the development of Nigeria.

JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.title: LIVING AND NON LIVING THINGS
JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.note:
MEANING OF LIVING AND NON-LIVING THINGS

Living things are organisms that possess life and carry out basic life processes such as nutrition, respiration, movement, growth, sensitivity, excretion and reproduction.

Examples include humans, goats, birds, trees, grasses and microorganisms.

Non-living things are things that do not possess life and cannot carry out all the basic life processes of living organisms.

Examples include stones, water, air, chairs, books, tables and cars.

CHARACTERISTICS OF LIVING THINGS

The characteristics of living things are commonly represented by the term MRS GREN.

  • Movement: The ability of an organism to change position or move parts of its body.
  • Respiration: The process by which cells release energy from food.
  • Sensitivity: The ability to detect and respond to changes in the environment.
  • Growth: A permanent increase in the size and dry mass of an organism.
  • Reproduction: The process by which organisms produce new organisms of their own kind.
  • Excretion: The removal of metabolic waste products from the body.
  • Nutrition: The process by which organisms obtain or manufacture food.

CLASSIFICATION OF LIVING THINGS

Living things can be grouped into plants, animals and microorganisms.

PLANTS

Plants are living organisms that generally manufacture their own food through photosynthesis.

Examples include maize, mango trees, grasses, beans and ferns.

Characteristics of plants:

  • Most plants contain chlorophyll.
  • Most plants make their food through photosynthesis.
  • They usually remain fixed in one place.
  • They grow, respire and reproduce.

ANIMALS

Animals are living organisms that obtain food from plants or other organisms.

Examples include humans, goats, lions, fish, birds and butterflies.

Characteristics of animals:

  • They depend on other organisms for food.
  • Most animals can move from one place to another.
  • They respond to changes in their surroundings.
  • They respire, grow and reproduce.

MICROORGANISMS

Microorganisms are organisms that are generally too small to be seen clearly with the naked eye.

Examples include bacteria, yeast and some microscopic algae.

Some microorganisms are useful in food production and decomposition, while others can cause diseases in humans, animals and plants.

JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.title: LIVING AND NON LIVING THINGS II
JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.note:
Non-living things can be grouped into natural non-living things and man-made non-living things.

NATURAL NON-LIVING THINGS

These are non-living things that occur naturally in the environment.

Examples include:

  • Water
  • Air
  • Rocks
  • Sand
  • Minerals

MAN-MADE NON-LIVING THINGS

These are objects made by humans using natural or processed materials.

Examples include:

  • Tables
  • Chairs
  • Cars
  • Books
  • Buildings
  • Pencils

DIFFERENCES BETWEEN LIVING AND NON-LIVING THINGS

Living things:

  • Possess life.
  • Carry out biological life processes.
  • Grow biologically.
  • Respire to release energy from food.
  • Respond biologically to stimuli.
  • Can reproduce, although not every individual organism reproduces.
  • Eventually die.

Non-living things:

  • Do not possess life.
  • Do not carry out all the basic life processes.
  • Do not grow biologically.
  • Do not respire to release energy from food.
  • Do not respond biologically to stimuli.
  • Do not reproduce biologically.
  • Can be damaged or destroyed.

THINGS THAT WERE ONCE LIVING

Some materials come from living things but are no longer alive.

Examples include:

  • Dry wood obtained from trees.
  • Leather obtained from animal skin.
  • Paper made mainly from wood pulp.
  • Cotton obtained from cotton plants.
  • Wool obtained from sheep.

These materials are not living things simply because they came from organisms.

THINGS THAT APPEAR TO BE LIVING BUT ARE NOT LIVING

Some non-living things may appear to be living because they move, grow or spread.

Examples include:

  • Cars: They move when powered by fuel or electricity, but they do not possess life.
  • Fire: It can spread and increase in size, but it is not a living organism.
  • Crystals: They can increase in size as new material accumulates, but they do not grow biologically.
  • Robots: They can move and respond to programmed instructions, but they are not living organisms.

IMPORTANCE OF STUDYING LIVING AND NON-LIVING THINGS

Studying living and non-living things helps us to:

  • Understand our environment.
  • Identify organisms and their needs.
  • Protect plants and animals.
  • Appreciate the importance of air, water and soil.
  • Maintain a clean and healthy environment.
  • Conserve natural resources.

  4. Explain why cars and fire are classified as non-living things.

JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.title: HUMAN DEVELOPMENT
JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.note:
MEANING OF HUMAN DEVELOPMENT

Human development is the process of physical, mental, emotional and social changes that occur in a human being from conception through childhood, adolescence and adulthood to old age.

Human development involves changes in the body, thinking, feelings, behaviour and ability to interact with other people.

MEANING OF GROWTH AND DEVELOPMENT

Growth is the permanent increase in the size, height, weight or mass of the body.

Development is the gradual improvement in the abilities and skills of a person as they grow older.

Examples of growth include an increase in height and weight.

Examples of development include learning to walk, talk, read, write and solve problems.

STAGES OF HUMAN DEVELOPMENT

Human development takes place in different stages.

PRENATAL STAGE

The prenatal stage is the period of development before a baby is born. It begins at conception and continues until birth.

During this stage:

  • The baby develops inside the mother's uterus.
  • The organs and body systems begin to form and develop.
  • The baby grows in size and weight.
  • The mother needs proper nutrition, medical care and rest.

INFANCY

Infancy is the stage from birth to about one year of age.

Characteristics of infancy include:

  • Rapid growth in height and weight.
  • Development of basic movements.
  • Learning to sit, crawl and eventually stand.
  • Beginning to recognise familiar people.
  • Depending on adults for food, protection and care.

CHILDHOOD

Childhood is the stage between infancy and adolescence. It involves important physical, mental, emotional and social changes.

Characteristics of childhood include:

  • Increase in height and weight.
  • Development of language and communication skills.
  • Learning to read, write and count.
  • Improvement in movement and coordination.
  • Learning to interact and play with others.
  • Developing independence and problem-solving skills.

ADOLESCENCE

Adolescence is the period of transition from childhood to adulthood. It commonly begins around 10 to 19 years of age, although the timing of development differs from one person to another.

During adolescence:

  • The body experiences a growth spurt.
  • Reproductive organs mature.
  • Secondary sexual characteristics develop.
  • Emotional changes may occur.
  • Thinking and decision-making abilities continue to develop.
  • Relationships with family members and friends may change.

CLASS EXERCISE

Instruction: Answer all the questions.

  1. Define human development.
  2. Differentiate between growth and development.
  3. Mention the stages of human development covered in this note.
  4. State four characteristics of infancy.
  5. Explain three changes that occur during adolescence.

ASSIGNMENT

  2. State five characteristics of childhood.
  3. Mention four important changes that occur during adolescence.
  4. Give three differences between growth and development.
  5. Draw a simple chart showing the stages of human development from conception to adolescence.

CONCLUSION

Human development is a continuous process involving changes in the body, mind, emotions and social relationships. Understanding the different stages helps us appreciate the changes that occur as people grow from before birth through childhood and adolescence.

TOPIC: HUMAN DEVELOPMENT (CONTINUED)

STAGES OF HUMAN DEVELOPMENT (CONTINUED)

ADULTHOOD

Adulthood is the stage when a person has reached physical maturity, although some aspects of mental, emotional and social development continue throughout life.

Characteristics of adulthood include:

  • Physical maturity.
  • Increased independence and responsibility.
  • Ability to make important decisions.
  • Development of occupational and family responsibilities.
  • Continued learning and emotional development.

OLD AGE

Old age is the later stage of human life. The age at which a person is considered old varies across individuals and societies.

Characteristics may include:

  • Changes in skin and hair.
  • Reduced muscle strength in some people.
  • Changes in vision and hearing.
  • Greater need for healthcare and support for some individuals.
  • Continued sharing of knowledge and experience with younger generations.

Ageing occurs differently in different people. Many older adults remain active, independent and healthy.

FACTORS THAT AFFECT HUMAN DEVELOPMENT

Human development is influenced by several factors.

HEREDITY

Heredity refers to the characteristics passed from parents to their children through genes.

Examples include inherited tendencies affecting height, natural hair texture and some aspects of body structure.

NUTRITION

Good nutrition provides the nutrients needed for healthy growth and development.

A balanced diet contains carbohydrates, proteins, fats and oils, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water in appropriate amounts.

Poor nutrition may affect physical growth, learning and general health.

ENVIRONMENT

The environment includes the physical and social conditions in which a person lives.

A clean environment, safe housing, access to education and supportive relationships can promote healthy development.

HEALTHCARE

Regular medical care, immunisation, proper hygiene and early treatment of illnesses help support healthy development.

EXERCISE AND REST

Physical activity helps develop strong muscles and bones. Adequate sleep and rest support physical recovery, learning and emotional well-being.

EDUCATION AND SOCIAL INTERACTION

Education develops knowledge and skills, while positive interaction with family members, teachers and friends supports communication, confidence and social development.

IMPORTANCE OF UNDERSTANDING HUMAN DEVELOPMENT

Understanding human development helps us to:

  • Recognise normal changes that occur at different ages.
  • Understand the nutritional needs of growing children.
  • Promote healthy habits and personal hygiene.
  • Prepare young people for the changes of adolescence.
  • Encourage respect for people at different stages of life.
  • Provide appropriate care and support for children and older adults.

HEALTHY PRACTICES THAT PROMOTE HUMAN DEVELOPMENT

The following practices help promote healthy development:

  • Eating a balanced diet.
  • Exercising regularly.
  • Getting enough sleep and rest.
  • Maintaining personal hygiene.
  • Attending recommended medical check-ups.
  • Maintaining healthy relationships.
  • Avoiding harmful substances.
  • Seeking help from trusted adults or healthcare professionals when necessary.

JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.title: FAMILY HEALTH
JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.note:
MEANING OF FAMILY HEALTH

Family health refers to the physical, mental and social well-being of all members of a family. It involves maintaining good health, preventing diseases, keeping the home clean and providing proper care for every family member.

A healthy family is one in which members work together to maintain good hygiene, eat balanced diets, support one another and seek medical attention when necessary.

MEANING OF A FAMILY

A family is a group of people related by blood, marriage, adoption or other recognised family relationships who share responsibilities, care and support.

Members of a family may include parents, children, grandparents, uncles, aunts and other relatives.

IMPORTANCE OF FAMILY HEALTH

Family health is important for the following reasons:

  • It helps family members remain healthy and active.
  • It reduces the spread of communicable diseases.
  • It promotes peace, love and cooperation in the home.
  • It helps children grow and develop properly.
  • It reduces unnecessary medical expenses.
  • It improves the quality of life of family members.
  • It promotes emotional stability and happiness.
  • It encourages responsible health habits among children.

FACTORS THAT AFFECT FAMILY HEALTH

Several factors can influence the health of a family.

GOOD NUTRITION

Eating a balanced diet provides the body with nutrients needed for growth, energy and protection against illness.

PERSONAL HYGIENE

Personal hygiene involves keeping the body clean to prevent infections and maintain good health.

Examples include bathing regularly, brushing the teeth, washing hands with soap and wearing clean clothes.

ENVIRONMENTAL SANITATION

A clean environment helps prevent diseases and encourages healthy living.

Proper waste disposal, clean toilets, safe water and good drainage are important for family health.

SAFE WATER

Families need clean and safe water for drinking, cooking, bathing and washing. Unsafe water may spread diseases such as cholera and typhoid fever.

ADEQUATE SHELTER

A good house should provide protection from rain, excessive heat, cold and dangerous animals. It should also have adequate ventilation and sufficient space.

HEALTHCARE SERVICES

Access to hospitals, clinics, immunisation, health education and medical advice helps families prevent and manage illnesses.

EMOTIONAL AND SOCIAL SUPPORT

Love, respect, communication and cooperation among family members promote mental and emotional well-being.

  2. What is a family?

  4. Mention five factors that affect family health.

JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.title: FAMILY HEALTH II
JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.note:
MEANING OF MAINTENANCE OF FAMILY HEALTH

Maintenance of family health refers to the activities and practices that family members carry out to protect their health, prevent diseases and maintain a clean and safe home.

Every member of the family has a role to play in maintaining good health.

PROPER NUTRITION IN THE FAMILY

Proper nutrition means eating the right types and amounts of food needed for healthy living.

A balanced diet contains carbohydrates, proteins, fats and oils, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water.

Examples of nutritious foods include rice, beans, eggs, fish, vegetables, fruits, milk and whole grains.

Importance of proper nutrition:

  • It provides energy for daily activities.
  • It supports growth and development.
  • It helps repair damaged body tissues.
  • It supports the immune system.
  • It reduces the risk of malnutrition.

PERSONAL HYGIENE IN THE FAMILY

Personal hygiene refers to practices that keep the body clean and help prevent diseases.

Ways to maintain personal hygiene include:

  • Bathing regularly with clean water and soap.
  • Brushing the teeth at least twice daily.
  • Washing hands with soap after using the toilet and before preparing or eating food.
  • Wearing clean clothes.
  • Keeping fingernails short and clean.
  • Covering the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing.
  • Avoiding the sharing of personal items such as toothbrushes and razors.

ENVIRONMENTAL SANITATION IN THE HOME

Environmental sanitation involves keeping the home and its surroundings clean and safe.

Ways to maintain environmental sanitation include:

  • Sweeping and cleaning the house regularly.
  • Disposing of refuse properly.
  • Keeping toilets and bathrooms clean.
  • Preventing stagnant water around the home.
  • Clearing blocked drainage channels.
  • Keeping food covered to prevent contamination.
  • Controlling rats, flies, mosquitoes and other disease-carrying pests.

SAFE STORAGE AND PREPARATION OF FOOD

Food should be handled properly to prevent contamination and food poisoning.

Important practices include:

  • Washing hands before handling food.
  • Washing fruits and vegetables with safe water.
  • Cooking food thoroughly.
  • Separating raw food from cooked food.
  • Storing perishable foods at safe temperatures.
  • Keeping cooking utensils clean.
  • Avoiding food that has spoiled.

PREVENTION OF DISEASES IN THE FAMILY

Families can prevent diseases by:

  • Ensuring that children receive recommended immunisations.
  • Using safe drinking water.
  • Practising good personal hygiene.
  • Keeping the environment clean.
  • Seeking medical care when symptoms of illness appear.
  • Taking medicines only as directed by a qualified healthcare professional.
  • Avoiding close contact with others when contagious illnesses require precautions.
  • Using mosquito nets and other recommended measures to prevent mosquito-borne diseases.

IMPORTANCE OF REST, EXERCISE AND SLEEP

Rest, exercise and adequate sleep are necessary for healthy living.

  • Rest helps the body recover from daily activities.
  • Exercise strengthens muscles and bones and supports heart health.
  • Adequate sleep supports concentration, growth and emotional well-being.

Children and adolescents need sufficient sleep to support their development.

JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.title: FAMILY HEALTH III
JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.note:
MEANING OF FAMILY HEALTH SERVICES

Family health services are healthcare activities and support provided to individuals and families to promote health, prevent diseases and treat illnesses.

These services may be provided by hospitals, health centres, clinics, public health workers and other qualified healthcare professionals.

TYPES OF FAMILY HEALTH SERVICES

IMMUNISATION SERVICES

Immunisation helps protect people against certain infectious diseases by preparing the body's immune system to fight specific infections.

Children should receive vaccines according to the recommended national immunisation schedule.

MATERNAL AND CHILD HEALTH SERVICES

These services support the health of pregnant women, mothers, newborn babies and young children.

They include antenatal care, skilled assistance during childbirth, postnatal care, child growth monitoring and recommended immunisation.

FAMILY PLANNING SERVICES

Family planning services provide information and healthcare support to adults who wish to make informed decisions about whether and when to have children and the spacing of pregnancies.

Such services should be provided by qualified healthcare professionals.

NUTRITIONAL SERVICES

Nutritional services provide advice and support on healthy eating, growth monitoring and the prevention or management of malnutrition.

MEDICAL TREATMENT SERVICES

These services involve the diagnosis, treatment and management of illnesses and injuries by qualified healthcare professionals.

Families should seek medical attention when a member is seriously ill or has symptoms that require professional assessment.

HEALTH EDUCATION

Health education provides information about disease prevention, personal hygiene, nutrition, sanitation and healthy lifestyles.

It helps family members make informed decisions about their health.

RESPONSIBILITIES OF FAMILY MEMBERS IN MAINTAINING HEALTH

Every member of a family has responsibilities for maintaining good health.

RESPONSIBILITIES OF PARENTS OR GUARDIANS

Parents or guardians should:

  • Provide nutritious food and safe drinking water.
  • Ensure that the home is clean and safe.
  • Arrange appropriate healthcare when necessary.
  • Ensure that children receive recommended immunisations.
  • Teach children good personal hygiene.
  • Provide emotional support and guidance.
  • Encourage healthy habits and responsible behaviour.

RESPONSIBILITIES OF CHILDREN

Children should:

  • Keep their bodies and clothes clean.
  • Help maintain cleanliness in the home.
  • Eat nutritious foods.
  • Wash their hands regularly.
  • Obey reasonable safety instructions.
  • Report illness or injuries to a responsible adult.
  • Respect and support other family members.

RESPONSIBILITIES OF THE COMMUNITY

The community also contributes to family health by:

  • Providing access to clean water and sanitation facilities.
  • Supporting health education programmes.
  • Maintaining clean public spaces.
  • Promoting immunisation and disease-prevention campaigns.
  • Supporting access to healthcare services.

COMMON FAMILY HEALTH PROBLEMS

Some common health problems that may affect families include:

  • Malaria.
  • Diarrhoeal diseases.
  • Respiratory infections.
  • Malnutrition.
  • Injuries and accidents in the home.
  • Poor dental health.
  • Stress and other mental health challenges.

Many of these problems can be reduced through good hygiene, proper nutrition, safe surroundings, preventive healthcare and timely medical attention.

SAFETY MEASURES IN THE HOME

Families should observe safety measures to prevent accidents and injuries.

  • Keep medicines and harmful chemicals away from children.
  • Store sharp objects safely.
  • Keep electrical appliances and sockets in good condition.
  • Avoid playing with fire or matches.
  • Keep floors and stairways free of objects that may cause falls.
  • Ensure adequate ventilation.
  • Seek help from a responsible adult when an accident occurs.

  3. List five common health problems that may affect a family and state one preventive measure for each.
  4. Explain four ways to prevent accidents in the home.
  5. Write a short paragraph on how you can contribute to maintaining good health in your family.

JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.title: REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM I
JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.note:
MEANING OF REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH

Reproductive health refers to the physical, mental and social well-being of individuals in matters relating to the reproductive system and its functions.

It involves having accurate information about the reproductive system, maintaining reproductive hygiene, preventing infections and obtaining appropriate healthcare when necessary.

MEANING OF REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH SERVICES

Reproductive health services are healthcare services and educational programmes that help individuals maintain the health of their reproductive systems, prevent reproductive health problems and obtain appropriate medical care.

These services are provided by hospitals, health centres, clinics and qualified healthcare professionals.

IMPORTANCE OF REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH SERVICES

Reproductive health services are important because they:

  • Provide accurate information about reproductive health.
  • Promote personal hygiene and healthy habits.
  • Help prevent and identify reproductive tract infections.
  • Provide care during pregnancy and childbirth.
  • Support the health of mothers and babies.
  • Help individuals understand physical changes during puberty.
  • Provide guidance on preventing sexually transmitted infections (STIs).
  • Encourage people to seek medical attention when necessary.

TYPES OF REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH SERVICES

REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH EDUCATION

Reproductive health education provides information about the reproductive system, puberty, personal hygiene, responsible behaviour and the prevention of infections.

It helps young people understand the changes that occur during adolescence and make informed decisions about their health.

PUBERTY EDUCATION AND GUIDANCE

Puberty is the stage when a child's body begins to develop towards physical and reproductive maturity.

Puberty education helps young people understand changes such as growth spurts, the development of body hair, voice changes, menstruation and other changes associated with sexual maturation.

It also teaches personal hygiene, self-respect and respect for others.

MATERNAL HEALTH SERVICES

Maternal health services support women before, during and after pregnancy.

Examples include:

  • Antenatal care during pregnancy.
  • Medical assistance during childbirth.
  • Postnatal care after childbirth.
  • Health education on maternal nutrition.
  • Monitoring the health of the mother and baby.

These services help reduce risks associated with pregnancy and childbirth.

FAMILY PLANNING SERVICES

Family planning services provide information and healthcare support to adults who wish to make informed decisions about whether and when to have children and the spacing of pregnancies.

These services may include counselling and information about contraceptive methods provided by qualified healthcare professionals.

PREVENTION AND TREATMENT OF SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTIONS

Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are infections that can spread through sexual contact.

Reproductive health services provide education, testing, treatment and counselling for STIs.

Examples of STIs include gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes and HIV, although HIV can also be transmitted through other routes.

Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment can help prevent complications and further transmission.

JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.title: REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM II
JSS 1|First term|Integrated Science.note:
PERSONAL REPRODUCTIVE HYGIENE

Personal reproductive hygiene refers to practices that keep the reproductive organs clean and help prevent irritation and infections.

Good reproductive hygiene practices include:

  • Washing the external genital area gently with clean water.
  • Wearing clean, breathable underwear.
  • Changing underwear regularly.
  • Avoiding harsh chemicals and scented products around sensitive genital areas.
  • Not sharing underwear or personal hygiene items.
  • Seeking medical advice when unusual pain, itching, sores or discharge occurs.
  • Avoiding the use of unprescribed medicines to treat reproductive symptoms.

For girls who menstruate, menstrual hygiene includes changing sanitary materials regularly, washing hands before and after changing them, and disposing of used materials safely.

MENSTRUAL HEALTH SERVICES

Menstruation is the monthly shedding of the lining of the uterus through the vagina when pregnancy has not occurred.

Menstrual health services provide information, support and healthcare for people who menstruate.

These services may include:

  • Education about the menstrual cycle.
  • Guidance on using and changing sanitary materials.
  • Advice on menstrual hygiene.
  • Access to clean water and suitable toilets.
  • Medical assessment of severe menstrual pain or unusually heavy bleeding.

Menstruation is a normal biological process and should not be a source of shame.

ADOLESCENT REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH SERVICES

Adolescent reproductive health services are healthcare and educational services designed to meet the needs of young people during adolescence.

They include:

  • Information about puberty and body changes.
  • Guidance on personal hygiene.
  • Counselling on healthy relationships and personal boundaries.
  • Education on preventing STIs.
  • Support for emotional and mental well-being.
  • Access to confidential and appropriate healthcare, subject to applicable laws and safeguarding requirements.

These services help adolescents understand their bodies and make responsible health decisions.

PREVENTION OF REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH PROBLEMS

Reproductive health problems can be reduced through the following practices:

  • Maintaining good personal hygiene.
  • Obtaining accurate information from qualified health professionals.
  • Seeking medical attention when symptoms occur.
  • Avoiding self-medication.
  • Receiving recommended vaccinations, such as the HPV vaccine where available and appropriate.
  • Taking prescribed medicines correctly.
  • Seeking professional testing and treatment for suspected infections.
  • Respecting personal boundaries and avoiding coercion or abuse.

ROLE OF HEALTHCARE PROFESSIONALS

Healthcare professionals play important roles in reproductive health services.

DOCTORS

Doctors examine patients, diagnose illnesses and recommend appropriate treatment.

NURSES AND MIDWIVES

Nurses and midwives provide health education, maternal care, support during childbirth and follow-up care.

COUNSELLORS AND HEALTH EDUCATORS

They provide accurate information, guidance and emotional support on reproductive health matters.

PUBLIC HEALTH WORKERS

Public health workers organise health education programmes, promote disease prevention and help communities access health services.

IMPORTANCE OF REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH EDUCATION FOR YOUNG PEOPLE

Reproductive health education is important because it:

  • Helps young people understand puberty.
  • Promotes good hygiene habits.
  • Corrects myths and misconceptions about reproductive health.
  • Encourages respect for personal boundaries.
  • Helps prevent infections and health complications.
  • Encourages responsible decision-making.
  • Teaches young people when and where to seek professional help.

JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.title: NATIONAL VALUES
JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.note:
Meaning of National Values

National values are the beliefs, principles, and standards of behaviour that are accepted and encouraged by the people of a country. They guide citizens on how to behave towards one another and contribute to the development of their nation.

National values promote peace, unity, honesty, discipline, respect, and responsible citizenship.

In Nigeria, national values help people from different ethnic groups, religions, and cultural backgrounds live together peacefully.

Examples of National Values
The major national values include the following:

  1. Honesty: Telling the truth and refusing to cheat, steal, or deceive others.
  2. Integrity: Doing what is right and keeping to good moral principles even when nobody is watching.
  3. Discipline: Controlling one's behaviour and obeying rules and regulations.
  4. Tolerance: Respecting people whose opinions, religions, cultures, or beliefs are different from ours.
  5. Cooperation: Working together with others to achieve a common goal.
  6. Patriotism: Showing love, loyalty, and commitment to one's country.
  7. Respect: Showing regard for other people, constituted authority, and the laws of the country.
  8. Hard work: Making efforts to achieve goals through dedication and commitment.
  9. Justice: Treating people fairly and ensuring that everyone receives what they are entitled to under the law.
  10. Unity: Living and working together peacefully despite differences.
  11. Responsibility: Performing one's duties and accepting the consequences of one's actions.
  12. Selflessness: Considering the needs and welfare of others rather than thinking only about oneself.

Importance of National Values

National values are important for the following reasons:

  1. They promote peace and unity among citizens.
  2. They encourage honesty and accountability.
  3. They help to reduce corruption and other social problems.
  4. They promote respect for human rights.
  5. They encourage citizens to obey the law.
  6. They promote peaceful coexistence among different ethnic and religious groups.
  7. They encourage hard work and productivity.
  8. They support national development.
  9. They help young people develop good character.
  10. They promote responsible citizenship and good leadership.

Ways of Promoting National Values

National values can be promoted through the following activities:

Teaching good moral behaviour at home and in school.

Providing civic education in schools.

Parents serving as good examples to their children.

Leaders demonstrating honesty, fairness, and accountability.

Obeying the laws of the country.

Respecting people from different cultural and religious backgrounds.

Rewarding good behaviour and correcting misconduct fairly.

Organising public awareness programmes.

Participating in community development activities.

Respecting national symbols, such as the Nigerian flag and national anthem.

Consequences of the Lack of National Values
When citizens fail to practise national values, the following problems may occur:

Corruption and dishonesty.

Disobedience to laws and regulations.

Conflict and disunity among citizens.

Disrespect for constituted authority.

Examination malpractice and other forms of cheating.

Destruction of public property.

Discrimination and intolerance.

Slow economic and national development.

Increased crime and insecurity.

Loss of trust among members of society.

Roles of Students in Promoting National Values
Students can promote national values in the following ways:

Being honest during examinations and other school activities.

Respecting teachers, parents, and fellow students.

Obeying school rules and regulations.

Avoiding bullying and discrimination.

Keeping the school environment clean.

Cooperating with classmates during group activities.

Respecting the Nigerian flag and national anthem.

Taking care of school property.

Showing tolerance towards people from different backgrounds.

Being punctual and responsible.

Conclusion
National values are important principles that guide the behaviour of citizens and promote peace, unity, and development. Every Nigerian, including students, should practise honesty, integrity, discipline, tolerance, patriotism, and respect to build a better society.

JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.title: IMPORTANCE OF NATIONAL VALUES
JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.note:
Meaning of National Values
National values are the beliefs, principles, and standards of behaviour that guide citizens in their relationships with one another and their country.

Examples of national values include honesty, discipline, integrity, tolerance, patriotism, respect, cooperation, justice, and hard work.

Importance of National Values
National values are important for the following reasons:

Promotion of Peace: National values encourage citizens to live peacefully and resolve disagreements without violence.

Unity Among Citizens: They help people from different ethnic groups, religions, and cultural backgrounds to live and work together.

Promotion of Honesty: National values encourage citizens to tell the truth and avoid cheating, stealing, and deception.

Reduction of Corruption: Values such as integrity and accountability discourage the misuse of public funds and positions.

Respect for the Law: National values encourage citizens to obey the laws and regulations of their country.

National Development: Values such as hard work, discipline, and responsibility encourage citizens to contribute to the progress of the nation.

Respect for Human Rights: They teach citizens to respect the rights, freedoms, and dignity of others.

Good Leadership: National values encourage leaders to be responsible, fair, honest, and accountable to the people.

Tolerance: They help citizens accept and respect people whose opinions, beliefs, and cultures differ from theirs.

Responsible Citizenship: National values encourage citizens to perform their duties and contribute to community development.

Reduction of Crime: Values such as honesty, self-discipline, and respect for the law discourage criminal behaviour.

Good Character Formation: National values help children and young people develop good morals and responsible habits.

Patriotism: They encourage citizens to love their country, respect national symbols, and contribute to national progress.

Cooperation: National values encourage people to work together to achieve common goals.

Social Stability: They promote trust, fairness, and mutual respect, helping society function peacefully.

Ways Students Can Practise National Values
Students can practise national values in the following ways:

Obeying school rules and regulations.

Being honest during examinations.

Respecting teachers, parents, and fellow students.

Avoiding bullying and discrimination.

Cooperating with classmates during group work.

Keeping the school environment clean.

Being punctual and responsible.

Respecting people from different backgrounds.

Conclusion
National values are essential for building a peaceful, united, and progressive nation. Every citizen should practise values such as honesty, discipline, tolerance, patriotism, and respect to promote national development.

JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.title: NATIONAL VALUES[HONESTY]
JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.note:
Meaning of Honesty
Honesty is the quality of being truthful, sincere, and trustworthy in our words and actions. It means telling the truth, doing what is right, and refusing to cheat, steal, or deceive others.

An honest person can be trusted because they speak the truth and act with integrity, even when nobody is watching.

Examples of honesty include returning a lost item to its owner, admitting a mistake, and refusing to cheat during an examination.

Characteristics of an Honest Person
An honest person has the following characteristics:

Tells the truth at all times.

Does not steal or cheat.

Keeps promises and agreements.

Admits mistakes and accepts responsibility.

Returns lost property to its rightful owner.

Does not give false information.

Keeps accurate records.

Can be trusted by others.

Importance of Honesty
Honesty is important for the following reasons:

It builds trust among people.

It promotes peace and unity in society.

It helps to reduce corruption and dishonesty.

It encourages fairness and justice.

It builds a good reputation for individuals.

It promotes good relationships among friends and family members.

It encourages responsible behaviour.

It contributes to national development.

It helps students succeed through hard work rather than cheating.

It promotes accountability among leaders and public servants.

Ways of Demonstrating Honesty
Honesty can be demonstrated in the following ways:

Telling the truth, even when it is difficult.

Refusing to cheat during examinations.

Returning borrowed items in good condition.

Reporting lost property to the appropriate person.

Admitting mistakes instead of blaming others.

Avoiding bribery and corruption.

Keeping promises.

Giving correct information.

Refusing to take what belongs to another person.

Being sincere in our dealings with others.

Consequences of Dishonesty
Dishonesty can lead to the following problems:

Loss of trust and respect.

Damaged relationships.

Punishment at home, in school, or at work.

Loss of good reputation.

Increased corruption and crime.

Unfair treatment of others.

Conflict and misunderstanding.

Poor academic or professional development.

Ways of Promoting Honesty
Honesty can be promoted through the following measures:

Parents teaching children to tell the truth.

Teachers rewarding honest behaviour.

Leaders serving as good examples.

Punishing dishonest acts fairly and according to established rules.

Teaching moral and civic values in schools.

Encouraging people to admit their mistakes.

Promoting transparency and accountability in public institutions.

Conclusion
Honesty is an important national value that promotes trust, fairness, peace, and responsible behaviour. Every student should practise honesty at home, in school, and in the community to become a responsible citizen.

JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.title: NATIONAL VALUES[COOPERATION]
JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.note:
Cooperation is the act of working together with other people to achieve a common goal. It involves helping one another, sharing ideas, and combining efforts to complete a task successfully.

Cooperation is an important national value because it promotes peace, unity, understanding, and development in society.

Examples of cooperation include students working together on a class project, family members sharing household duties, and community members working together to clean their surroundings.

Types of Cooperation
There are different types of cooperation, which include:

Family cooperation: Family members work together to perform household duties and solve family problems.

School cooperation: Students and teachers work together to achieve educational goals.

Community cooperation: Members of a community join efforts to improve their environment and provide community facilities.

National cooperation: Citizens and government work together to promote peace, unity, and national development.

International cooperation: Two or more countries work together to solve common problems and achieve shared goals.

Importance of Cooperation
Cooperation is important for the following reasons:

It promotes peace and unity among people.

It makes work easier and faster.

It encourages friendship and good relationships.

It helps people solve problems together.

It promotes mutual understanding and respect.

It encourages the sharing of ideas, knowledge, and skills.

It reduces unnecessary conflict and misunderstanding.

It promotes community and national development.

It encourages people to help those in need.

It builds a sense of belonging and responsibility.

Ways of Demonstrating Cooperation
Cooperation can be demonstrated in the following ways:

Working together to complete a task.

Sharing ideas and useful information.

Helping classmates with school activities.

Participating in community sanitation exercises.

Respecting the opinions of others.

Sharing responsibilities fairly.

Listening to other people's suggestions.

Supporting family members in household duties.

Participating in peaceful group discussions.

Helping people during emergencies when it is safe to do so.

Qualities Needed for Cooperation
The following qualities are necessary for effective cooperation:

Tolerance: Respecting people's differences and opinions.

Patience: Giving others enough time to contribute.

Honesty: Being truthful when working with others.

Respect: Valuing the ideas and contributions of others.

Selflessness: Considering the needs of the group.

Communication: Sharing information clearly and listening to others.

Commitment: Taking group responsibilities seriously.

Trust: Believing that others will perform their duties responsibly.

Problems That Can Prevent Cooperation
Cooperation may be difficult when the following problems occur:

Selfishness among group members.

Lack of trust.

Poor communication.

Intolerance of other people's opinions.

Dishonesty and betrayal.

Discrimination based on religion, ethnicity, or social background.

Unwillingness to share responsibilities.

Frequent disagreements and quarrels.

Ways of Promoting Cooperation
Cooperation can be encouraged through the following measures:

Teaching children the importance of teamwork.

Respecting the opinions of others.

Encouraging peaceful discussions.

Sharing responsibilities fairly.

Building trust among group members.

Avoiding discrimination and selfishness.

Promoting honesty and tolerance.

Participating in community development activities.

Resolving disagreements peacefully.

Recognising and appreciating the contributions of others.

Conclusion
Cooperation is an important national value that helps people work together to achieve common goals. It promotes peace, unity, friendship, and development. Students should practise cooperation at home, in school, and in their communities.

JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.title: NATIONAL VALUES[FACTORS THAT INFLUENCE COOPERATION]
JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.note:
Meaning of Cooperation
Cooperation is the act of working together with other people to achieve a common goal. It involves helping one another, sharing ideas, and combining efforts to achieve success.

Cooperation is important in the family, school, community, and nation because it promotes peace, unity, and development.

Factors That Influence Cooperation
The following factors can influence cooperation positively or negatively:

Common Goals: People are more willing to cooperate when they have the same goal or objective. For example, students work together to complete a group assignment.

Trust: When people trust one another, they can work together easily. Lack of trust may lead to suspicion and disagreement.

Good Communication: Clear communication helps people understand one another and avoid misunderstanding.

Tolerance: Respecting other people's opinions, beliefs, and differences encourages cooperation.

Honesty: Honest people can be trusted to perform their duties and keep their promises.

Leadership: Good leadership encourages teamwork, fairness, and unity. Poor leadership may cause conflict among group members.

Respect: When people respect one another, they are more willing to listen to ideas and work together.

Willingness to Help: People who are ready to assist others encourage teamwork and cooperation.

Fair Distribution of Duties: Cooperation improves when responsibilities are shared fairly among group members.

Rewards and Benefits: People may cooperate more readily when they understand the benefits of working together and receive fair recognition for their efforts.

Cultural and Religious Differences: Differences in culture or religion may either enrich cooperation or create difficulties when people refuse to respect one another.

Conflict and Disagreement: Frequent quarrels and unresolved disagreements can weaken cooperation among individuals or groups.

Selflessness: People who consider the needs of others and the common good are more likely to cooperate.

Availability of Resources: Adequate materials, equipment, and funds can make teamwork easier and more effective.

Discipline and Commitment: People who follow agreed rules and take their responsibilities seriously help cooperation succeed.

Conclusion
Cooperation is influenced by factors such as trust, communication, common goals, tolerance, leadership, and honesty. Cooperation becomes stronger when people respect one another, share responsibilities fairly, and work towards a common objective.

JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.title: NATIONAL VALUES[SELF RELIANCE]
JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.note:
Meaning of Self-Reliance
Self-reliance is the ability of an individual to depend on their own abilities, skills, knowledge, and resources to meet their needs and solve problems without always depending on others.

A self-reliant person is hardworking, responsible, creative, and willing to make efforts to achieve personal goals.

For example, a student who studies independently, learns a useful skill, and takes responsibility for completing assignments demonstrates self-reliance.

Characteristics of a Self-Reliant Person
A self-reliant person has the following qualities:

Hardworking and responsible.

Independent in making decisions.

Creative and innovative.

Confident in their abilities.

Determined to achieve goals.

Able to solve problems.

Willing to learn new skills.

Honest and disciplined.

Able to manage resources wisely.

Persistent when facing difficulties.

Importance of Self-Reliance
Self-reliance is important for the following reasons:

It encourages independence and responsibility.

It reduces unnecessary dependence on others.

It helps people develop useful skills.

It promotes creativity and innovation.

It encourages hard work and discipline.

It helps people solve problems independently.

It can create employment and business opportunities.

It helps to reduce poverty and unemployment.

It builds confidence and self-esteem.

It contributes to national development.

Ways of Developing Self-Reliance
Self-reliance can be developed through the following activities:

Acquiring practical and vocational skills.

Learning to perform tasks independently.

Developing good reading and study habits.

Setting realistic personal goals.

Saving money and avoiding waste.

Learning from mistakes and experiences.

Being hardworking and disciplined.

Developing problem-solving skills.

Participating in school and community activities.

Taking responsibility for one's actions.

Examples of Self-Reliance Among Students
Students can demonstrate self-reliance in the following ways:

Completing assignments independently.

Studying without always waiting for a teacher to remind them.

Keeping their books and school materials organised.

Learning skills such as sewing, drawing, baking, or computer use.

Managing their pocket money wisely.

Solving simple problems before asking for assistance.

Taking responsibility for their duties at home and in school.

Problems That Hinder Self-Reliance
The following factors can hinder self-reliance:

Laziness and lack of motivation.

Excessive dependence on other people.

Lack of education and practical skills.

Poverty and inadequate resources.

Fear of failure.

Lack of confidence.

Poor planning and time management.

Unwillingness to learn new things.

Lack of employment and training opportunities.

Ways of Promoting Self-Reliance in Nigeria
Self-reliance can be promoted in Nigeria through the following measures:

Providing quality education and vocational training.

Encouraging entrepreneurship and small businesses.

Providing access to financial support for eligible business owners.

Promoting agriculture and local production.

Teaching young people practical skills.

Encouraging citizens to use locally available resources.

Providing reliable electricity, roads, and other infrastructure.

Supporting creativity and innovation.

Encouraging hard work and responsible behaviour.

Conclusion
Self-reliance is an important quality that enables people to depend on their abilities and resources to meet their needs. It encourages independence, responsibility, creativity, and hard work. Students should develop useful skills and learn to take responsibility for their education and daily activities.

JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.title: IMPORTANCE OF SELF RELIANCE
JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.note:
Importance of Self-Reliance
Self-reliance is important for the following reasons:

Promotes Independence: It enables individuals to perform tasks and make decisions without always depending on others.

Reduces Unemployment: People who acquire useful skills can create jobs for themselves instead of waiting only for government or private employment.

Reduces Poverty: Self-reliant individuals can earn income through farming, trading, crafts, and other productive activities.

Encourages Hard Work: It teaches people to work diligently to achieve their goals.

Builds Self-Confidence: It helps individuals believe in their abilities and face challenges with courage.

Promotes Creativity: Self-reliance encourages people to develop new ideas and find solutions to problems.

Develops Useful Skills: It motivates people to learn practical skills that can help them earn a living.

Promotes Responsibility: Self-reliant individuals learn to take responsibility for their decisions and actions.

Encourages Saving: It teaches people to manage their money and other resources wisely.

Promotes National Development: Self-reliant citizens contribute to the economy through production, business activities, and the provision of services.

Reduces Overdependence on Others: It enables people to meet some of their needs without constantly seeking assistance.

Improves Problem-Solving Skills: It encourages individuals to think carefully and find solutions to everyday challenges.

Promotes Entrepreneurship: It encourages people to establish small businesses and become productive members of society.

Improves Living Standards: Through hard work and useful skills, individuals may improve their income and quality of life.

Encourages Resourcefulness: It teaches people to make good use of available materials and resources instead of wasting them.

Examples of Self-Reliance Among Students
Students can practise self-reliance in the following ways:

Completing assignments independently.

Studying regularly without constant reminders.

Learning practical skills such as sewing, baking, drawing, or computer operation.

Keeping school materials organised.

Managing pocket money wisely.

Taking responsibility for personal duties at home and in school.

Trying to solve simple problems before seeking assistance.

Conclusion
Self-reliance is important because it promotes independence, hard work, creativity, responsibility, and economic development. Everyone, especially young people, should develop useful skills and learn to use available resources wisely.

JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.title: NATIONAL TALENT
JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.note:
Meaning of National Talent
National talent refers to the natural abilities, special skills, and gifts possessed by citizens of a country that can be developed and used to promote personal growth and national development.

These talents may be found in areas such as sports, music, dancing, acting, farming, science, technology, writing, art, and craftsmanship.

Every individual has the potential to develop one or more talents through education, practice, training, and hard work.

Examples of National Talent
Examples of talents that can contribute to national development include:

Sports: Football, athletics, basketball, and swimming.

Music: Singing, playing musical instruments, and composing songs.

Arts and crafts: Painting, drawing, sculpting, and designing.

Science and technology: Inventing machines, developing software, and solving scientific problems.

Agriculture: Developing better farming methods and producing food.

Writing: Writing books, poems, stories, and educational materials.

Entrepreneurship: Creating new business ideas and products.

Entertainment: Acting, dancing, filmmaking, and comedy.

Leadership: Organising people and helping groups achieve common goals.

Importance of National Talent
National talent is important for the following reasons:

It promotes national development.

It creates employment opportunities.

It helps citizens discover and develop their abilities.

It generates income for individuals and the country.

It promotes the country's culture and traditions.

It encourages creativity and innovation.

It can bring international recognition to the country.

It reduces unemployment when talents are developed into useful skills.

It encourages young people to work hard and achieve their goals.

It promotes national pride and unity.

Ways of Discovering and Developing National Talent
National talents can be discovered and developed through the following methods:

Providing quality education and practical training.

Organising sports competitions and talent shows.

Encouraging students to participate in extracurricular activities.

Establishing training centres and skill acquisition programmes.

Providing equipment and facilities for talented individuals.

Encouraging parents and teachers to identify children's abilities.

Offering scholarships and other forms of support to talented people.

Organising art, music, science, and technology competitions.

Providing opportunities for young people to practise their skills.

Rewarding outstanding achievements.

Roles of Government in Developing National Talent
The government can help develop national talent by:

Establishing sports centres, libraries, and cultural centres.

Providing educational and vocational training facilities.

Organising national competitions and exhibitions.

Supporting talented individuals with scholarships and grants.

Promoting science, technology, arts, and sports.

Providing employment and development opportunities.

Protecting the rights of creative individuals.

Encouraging investment in industries that use local talents.

Problems Facing the Development of National Talent
The following problems may hinder the development of national talent:

Lack of training facilities and equipment.

Inadequate funding.

Poverty and lack of opportunities.

Poor encouragement from parents and society.

Lack of qualified trainers and teachers.

Discrimination and favouritism.

Poor access to education and modern technology.

Failure to recognise and reward talented individuals.

Ways Students Can Develop Their Talents
Students can develop their talents by:

Identifying their areas of interest and ability.

Practising regularly.

Listening to advice from teachers and coaches.

Participating in school competitions and clubs.

Reading books and learning new skills.

Being disciplined and hardworking.

Avoiding laziness and discouragement.

Using their talents positively to help others.

Conclusion
National talent is an important resource for the development of a country. When citizens discover, develop, and use their talents properly, they can create employment, promote innovation, preserve culture, and contribute to national progress. Therefore, parents, schools, and the government should encourage talented individuals to develop their abilities.

JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.title: CONSEQUENCES OF WASTING TALENT
JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.note:
Meaning of Wasting Talent
Wasting talent means failing to develop or use one's natural abilities and skills in a useful way. This may happen when a person is lazy, lacks interest, refuses to practise, or does not take advantage of opportunities to improve their abilities.

For example, a student who is good at drawing but refuses to practise or develop the skill may waste that talent.

Consequences of Wasting Talent
Wasting talent has several negative consequences, including the following:

Unemployment: A person who fails to develop useful skills may find it difficult to obtain employment or create a job.

Poverty: Wasting talents that could provide income may make it difficult for a person to improve their standard of living.

Loss of Opportunities: A person may miss opportunities for scholarships, competitions, training, and employment by failing to develop their abilities.

Low Self-Confidence: Failure to practise and improve one's skills may reduce confidence in one's abilities.

Slow National Development: When citizens fail to use their talents productively, the country may lose valuable contributions to science, technology, sports, agriculture, and other fields.

Dependence on Others: A person who does not develop useful skills may depend unnecessarily on other people for financial or material support.

Lack of Innovation: Wasting creative and intellectual abilities may prevent the development of new ideas, inventions, and solutions to problems.

Regret and Disappointment: A person may later regret failing to use opportunities to develop their talents.

Loss of Income: Talents that could be used to earn money may remain unproductive when they are neglected.

Poor Personal Development: Wasting talent can prevent a person from gaining experience, knowledge, and useful skills.

Loss of National Recognition: Talented individuals who fail to develop their abilities may miss opportunities to represent their schools, communities, or country.

Increased Social Problems: When many people fail to develop productive skills, it may contribute to unemployment and other social and economic difficulties.

Ways of Preventing the Wastage of Talent
Talent wastage can be prevented through the following measures:

Discovering one's abilities and interests early.

Practising regularly to improve skills.

Being hardworking, disciplined, and committed.

Seeking advice from teachers, parents, and qualified coaches.

Participating in school clubs, competitions, and other activities.

Taking advantage of educational and training opportunities.

Avoiding laziness and harmful peer pressure.

Setting clear goals and working towards them.

Providing facilities and support for talented individuals.

Encouraging young people to use their talents positively.

Conclusion
Talent is a valuable gift that should be discovered, developed, and used wisely. Wasting talent can lead to missed opportunities, unemployment, poverty, and slow national development. Every student should identify their abilities and work hard to improve them for personal success and the progress of society.

JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.title: NATIONAL VALUES[FACTORS THAT PROMOTE COOPERATION]
JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.note:
Meaning of Cooperation
Cooperation is the act of working together with other people to achieve a common goal. It involves helping one another, sharing ideas, and working as a team.

Factors That Promote Cooperation
The following are factors that promote cooperation in the family, school, and society.

Good Communication: Sharing information and ideas clearly helps people to understand one another and work together peacefully.
Mutual Respect: Respecting the opinions, feelings, and rights of others encourages people to cooperate.
Tolerance: Accepting the differences in people's opinions, cultures, and beliefs promotes peaceful relationships.
Trust: When people trust one another, they can work together without fear or suspicion.
Love and Understanding: Showing love and understanding helps people to care for one another and work together.
Common Goals: People cooperate more easily when they have the same goals or objectives to achieve.
Good Leadership: A good leader encourages teamwork, settles disagreements, and guides people towards achieving their goals.
Honesty: Being truthful helps to build trust and strengthen relationships among people.
Willingness to Help: People promote cooperation when they are ready to assist others whenever necessary.
Peaceful Settlement of Disputes: Resolving disagreements peacefully helps to prevent conflict and maintain unity.
Importance of Promoting Cooperation
It promotes peace and unity.
It makes work easier and faster.
It encourages teamwork.
It helps people achieve common goals.
It promotes love and friendship.
It encourages community and national development.
Conclusion
Cooperation is necessary for peaceful living and development. Factors such as trust, honesty, tolerance, good communication, and mutual respect help people to work together successfully in the family, school, and society.

JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.title: NATIONAL TALENT[CONSEQUENCES OF WASTING TALENT]
JSS 1|First term|Citizenship and Heritag.note:
Meaning of Talent
Talent is a natural ability or special skill that a person possesses in a particular area, such as singing, dancing, sports, drawing, teaching, or solving problems.

Wasting talent means failing to develop or use one's natural abilities and skills in a useful way.

Consequences of Wasting Talent
The following are the consequences of wasting talent:

Unemployment: People who fail to develop their talents may miss opportunities to get jobs or earn a living.
Poverty: Wasting talent may prevent a person from using their abilities to earn money and meet their needs.
Lack of Self-Development: A person who wastes their talent may fail to improve their skills and abilities.
Loss of Opportunities: Wasting talent can cause a person to miss opportunities for education, training, awards, and career advancement.
Low Self-Confidence: A person may lose confidence in themselves when they fail to develop their abilities.
Slow National Development: When citizens waste their talents, the country may lose valuable skills and ideas needed for development.
Dependence on Others: People who fail to use their talents productively may depend too much on others for their needs.
Regret: A person may feel disappointed later in life for failing to develop and use their talents.
Loss of National Recognition: The country may miss opportunities to gain honour and recognition when talented citizens fail to develop their abilities.
Increase in Idleness: Wasting talent may lead to unproductive activities instead of using one's abilities positively.
Ways of Preventing the Waste of Talent
By identifying one's talents early.
By practising regularly to improve one's skills.
By attending training programmes and workshops.
By listening to advice from parents, teachers, and coaches.
By making good use of available opportunities.
By avoiding laziness and negative influences.
By working hard and remaining determined.
Conclusion
Talent is a valuable gift that should be developed and used positively. Every student should discover their talents, practise regularly, and use their abilities to benefit themselves, their families, and the nation.

JSS 1|First term|Business Studies.title: INTRODUCTION TO BUSINESS STUDIES
JSS 1|First term|Business Studies.note:
Meaning of Business Studies
Business Studies is the subject that teaches us how to buy, sell, produce and manage goods and services.
It helps us to understand how people work, earn money and run businesses.
Examples of business activities:
- A trader selling rice in the market.
- A barber cutting people's hair.
- A teacher teaching students in a school.
- A tailor sewing clothes for customers.
Meaning of Business
A business is an activity in which people produce, buy or sell goods and services to earn money.
Examples: A supermarket, a bakery, a hair salon and a provision shop.
Goods and Services
Goods are things we can see and touch that satisfy our needs.
Examples: Books, shoes, rice, bags and phones.
Services are activities people do for others to satisfy their needs.
Examples: Teaching, hairdressing, driving and repairing phones.
Importance of Business Studies
Business Studies is important because it:
- Teaches us how to buy and sell goods.
- Helps us to understand how businesses work.
- Teaches us how to manage money.
- Helps us to develop business skills.
- Prepares us for future jobs.
- Encourages people to become self-employed.
- Teaches us how to keep simple business records.
Areas of Business Studies
The major areas of Business Studies include:
Commerce: The buying and selling of goods and services.
Bookkeeping: The recording of money received and money spent.
Office Practice: Learning how an office works and how office duties are performed.
Keyboarding: Learning how to type using a keyboard.
Entrepreneurship: Learning how to start and manage a business.
People Who Engage in Business
Trader: A person who buys and sells goods.
Producer: A person or organisation that makes goods or provides services.
Consumer: A person who buys or uses goods and services.
Entrepreneur: A person who starts and manages a business, usually to make a profit.
Difference Between Needs and Wants
Needs are things we must have to live.
Examples: Food, water, clothing and shelter.
Wants are things we would like to have but can live without.
Examples: Expensive jewellery, video games and luxury watches.
Qualities of a Good Businessperson
A good businessperson should be:
- Honest.
- Hardworking.
- Punctual.
- Polite to customers.
- Careful with money.
- Responsible.
- Good at keeping records.

An office is a place where people work to perform duties such as writing, keeping records, receiving visitors and handling business activities.
Examples of offices:
- School office
- Hospital office
- Bank office
- Government office
- Company office
Uses of an Office
An office is used for:
- Keeping important documents.
- Receiving visitors and customers.
- Making and receiving phone calls.
- Writing letters and other documents.
- Keeping records of money and business activities.
- Giving information to people.
- Organising business activities.
Items Found in an Office
Some common items found in an office are:
- Table: Used for writing and keeping documents.
- Chair: Used for sitting.
- Computer: Used for typing and storing information.
- Printer: Used for printing documents.
- Telephone: Used for making and receiving calls.
- Filing cabinet: Used for keeping documents safely.
- Stapler: Used for fastening sheets of paper together.
- Pen: Used for writing.
Types of Office
Small office: An office with few workers and limited equipment.
Large office: An office with many workers and more equipment.
Private office: An office used by an individual or a private organisation.
Public office: An office used by a government department or public organisation.
People Who Work in an Office
Secretary: Types letters, prepares documents and handles office records.
Receptionist: Welcomes visitors and directs them to the right person.
Office clerk: Keeps records and arranges documents.
Manager: Supervises workers and makes important decisions.
Office assistant: Helps with simple office duties.

- Honest.

JSS 1|First term|Business Studies.title: RIGHT ATTITUDE TO WORK
JSS 1|First term|Business Studies.note:
Meaning of Right Attitude to Work
Right attitude to work means having good behaviour and a positive mindset towards the work we do.
It means doing our work properly, being serious and doing our best at all times.
Examples: A teacher coming to school early, a cleaner keeping the environment clean and a student doing assignments on time.
Examples of Right Attitude to Work
Punctuality: Coming to work at the correct time.
Honesty: Always telling the truth and refusing to steal.
Hard work: Making an effort to do our work well.
Dedication: Giving our time and attention to our work.
Cooperation: Working peacefully with other people.
Obedience: Following lawful instructions from people in authority.
Neatness: Keeping ourselves and our workplace clean.
Responsibility: Doing our duties properly without being forced.
Respect: Treating other people politely.
Patience: Being able to work calmly without giving up easily.
Importance of Right Attitude to Work
Right attitude to work is important because it:
- Helps us to do our work properly.
- Increases productivity.
- Makes people trust and respect us.
- Helps us to achieve our goals.
- Promotes peace among workers.
- Helps us to get promoted at work.
- Reduces mistakes and waste.
- Helps a business to succeed.
Wrong Attitude to Work
Wrong attitude to work means behaving badly or carelessly towards our duties.
Examples include:
- Laziness.
- Dishonesty.
- Lateness.
- Disobedience.
- Carelessness.
- Fighting with other workers.
- Refusing to do assigned duties.
- Wasting working hours.
Wrong attitude to work can lead to poor performance, loss of trust and dismissal from a job.
