JSS 3|First term|English.title: GRAMMER[ PHRASES AND CLAUSES]
JSS 3|First term|English.note:
MEANING OF A PHRASE

A phrase is a group of words that makes sense as part of a sentence but does not contain a complete subject-and-verb structure expressing a complete thought.

Examples:

  • in the classroom

  • under the table

  • a beautiful girl

  • after the lesson

  • very quickly

Sentences:

  • The boy is in the classroom.

  • The cat is under the table.

  • We saw a beautiful girl.

The bold words are phrases.

TYPES OF PHRASES

Noun Phrase

A noun phrase is a group of words that acts as a noun in a sentence.

Examples:

  • the tall boy

  • a beautiful house

  • my English teacher

Sentences:

  • The tall boy won the race.

  • My English teacher is kind.

Verb Phrase

A verb phrase consists of a main verb and any helping verbs that go with it.

Examples:

  • is reading

  • have eaten

  • will be coming

  • was sleeping

Sentences:

  • The girl is reading.

  • They have eaten their food.

Adjective Phrase

An adjective phrase is a group of words that describes a noun or pronoun.

Examples:

  • full of joy

  • very beautiful

  • extremely intelligent

Sentences:

  • The girl is full of joy.

  • She is extremely intelligent.

Adverbial Phrase

An adverbial phrase is a group of words that tells us how, when, where or why an action happens.

Examples:

  • in the morning

  • with great care

  • at the bus stop

  • very quickly

Sentences:

  • We arrived in the morning.

  • The nurse worked with great care.

Prepositional Phrase

A prepositional phrase begins with a preposition and includes the words that follow it.

Examples:

  • under the bed

  • beside the school

  • behind the door

  • on the table

Sentences:

  • The shoes are under the bed.

  • The girl stood beside the school.

MEANING OF A CLAUSE

A clause is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb.

Examples:

  • She is sleeping.

  • The boy laughed.

  • Because I was tired.

In these examples, each group contains a subject and a verb. However, not every clause expresses a complete thought.

TYPES OF CLAUSES

Main Clause

A main clause is a clause that expresses a complete thought and can stand alone as a sentence.

Examples:

  • I went to school.

  • The baby is crying.

  • My father bought a car.

Each example makes complete sense on its own.

Subordinate Clause

A subordinate clause is a clause that does not express a complete thought on its own. It depends on a main clause to complete its meaning.

Examples:

  • because I was sick

  • when the teacher arrived

  • although she was tired

  • if you study hard

Sentences:

  • I stayed at home because I was sick.

  • We stood up when the teacher arrived.

  • Although she was tired, she completed her work.

The bold parts are subordinate clauses because they depend on the main clauses to complete their meanings.

Noun Clause

A noun clause is a subordinate clause that performs the function of a noun in a sentence.

Examples:

  • What he said was true.

  • I know that she is honest.

  • Where he lives is unknown.

Adjective Clause

An adjective clause describes a noun or pronoun.

It often begins with words such as who, which or that.

Examples:

  • The boy who won the race is my friend.

  • The book that I bought is interesting.

  • The woman who teaches us is kind.

Adverbial Clause

An adverbial clause tells us how, when, where, why or under what condition an action happens.

Examples:

  • I slept because I was tired. (Reason)

  • When the bell rang, the students left. (Time)

  • You will pass if you study hard. (Condition)

  • She spoke as if she were angry. (Manner)

DIFFERENCES BETWEEN PHRASES AND CLAUSES

Phrase

Clause

A phrase does not contain a complete subject-and-verb structure.

A clause contains a subject and a verb.

It does not express a complete thought on its own.

It may or may not express a complete thought.

Example: under the chair

Example: the boy is sleeping

Example: after the lesson

Example: after the lesson ended

Remember: A main clause can stand alone, but a subordinate clause depends on another clause.

CLASSWORK

Answer the following questions.

  1. What is a phrase?

  2. What is a clause?

  3. Identify the phrase in this sentence: The boy sat under the tree.

  4. Identify the subordinate clause in this sentence: I went home because I was tired.

  5. State whether each group of words is a phrase or a clause:

    • in the kitchen

    • the girl is singing

    • after the examination

    • when the rain started

    • a very beautiful dress

ASSIGNMENT

  1. Define a phrase and give five examples.

  2. Define a clause and give three examples.

  3. Explain three types of phrases and give two examples of each.

  4. State the difference between a main clause and a subordinate clause.

  5. Identify the type of clause in each sentence:

    • The man who came yesterday is my uncle.

    • I know that he is innocent.

    • We stayed indoors because it was raining.

  6. Identify the phrase in each sentence:

    • The cat slept under the table.

    • The very tall boy won the competition.

    • She completed her work with great care.

  7. Write three sentences containing subordinate clauses.

  8. Write two sentences containing noun clauses.

  9. Write two sentences containing adjective clauses.

  10. Write two sentences containing adverbial clauses.

JSS 3|First term|English.title: GRAMMER[SIMPLE, COMPOUND, COMPLEX SENTENCE]
JSS 3|First term|English.note:
MEANING OF A SENTENCE

A sentence is a group of words that expresses a complete thought.

Examples:

  • The boy is reading.

  • My mother cooks every day.

  • We went to school yesterday.

There are different types of sentences. In this lesson, we will study simple, compound and complex sentences.

SIMPLE SENTENCE

A simple sentence contains one independent clause. It expresses a complete thought.

An independent clause is a group of words that can stand alone as a complete sentence.

Examples:

  • John plays football.

  • The baby is sleeping.

  • My teacher teaches English.

  • The children are happy.

  • I went to the market.

Each sentence expresses one complete thought.

More examples:

  • Mary washed her clothes.

  • The dog barked loudly.

  • My father bought a new car.

Remember: A simple sentence can have a long subject or several verbs and still be simple, as long as it contains only one independent clause.

Example: John and Peter played football and washed their clothes.

COMPOUND SENTENCE

A compound sentence is a sentence that contains two or more independent clauses joined together.

The clauses are often joined by coordinating conjunctions such as:

FANBOYS

  • F – For

  • A – And

  • N – Nor

  • B – But

  • O – Or

  • Y – Yet

  • S – So

Examples:

  • I was hungry, so I ate some food.

  • John studied hard, and he passed the examination.

  • She was tired, but she continued working.

  • You can stay here, or you can follow us.

  • He did not come, nor did he send a message.

Each clause can stand alone as a complete sentence.

For example:

  • I was hungry.

  • I ate some food.

When they are joined with so, they form a compound sentence:

I was hungry, so I ate some food.

COMPLEX SENTENCE

A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one subordinate clause.

A subordinate clause does not express a complete thought on its own. It depends on the main clause to complete its meaning.

Common words used to introduce subordinate clauses include:

because, although, when, while, if, since, after, before, unless and until.

Examples:

  • I stayed at home because I was sick.

  • When the teacher arrived, the students became quiet.

  • She passed the examination although it was difficult.

  • We will play football if it does not rain.

  • After he finished his work, he went to bed.

In the first example:

  • Independent clause: I stayed at home.

  • Subordinate clause: because I was sick.

The subordinate clause gives the reason why the person stayed at home.

MORE EXAMPLES OF COMPLEX SENTENCES

Example 1: Although Mary was tired, she completed her homework.

  • Independent clause: She completed her homework.

  • Subordinate clause: Although Mary was tired.

Example 2: The boy cried because he lost his book.

  • Independent clause: The boy cried.

  • Subordinate clause: because he lost his book.

Example 3: When the rain stopped, we went outside.

  • Independent clause: We went outside.

  • Subordinate clause: When the rain stopped.

DIFFERENCES BETWEEN SIMPLE, COMPOUND AND COMPLEX SENTENCES

Simple sentence

Compound sentence

Complex sentence

Contains one independent clause.

Contains two or more independent clauses.

Contains one independent clause and at least one subordinate clause.

Expresses a complete thought.

Joins complete thoughts.

Joins a complete thought with a dependent thought.

Example: I was hungry.

I was hungry, so I ate.

I ate because I was hungry.

HOW TO IDENTIFY EACH SENTENCE

Simple sentence: Look for one independent clause.

Example: The girl danced beautifully.

Compound sentence: Look for two independent clauses joined together.

Example: The girl danced, and the boy sang.

Complex sentence: Look for an independent clause and a subordinate clause.

Example: The girl danced because she was happy.

CLASSWORK

Identify each sentence as simple, compound or complex.

  1. The teacher entered the classroom.

  2. I wanted to play, but it started raining.

  3. Because she was ill, she did not attend school.

  4. My brother washed the car and cleaned the room.

  5. We stayed indoors because the weather was bad.

ASSIGNMENT

  1. Define a simple sentence.

  2. Define a compound sentence and list the seven coordinating conjunctions represented by FANBOYS.

  3. Define a complex sentence.

  4. Write five examples of simple sentences.

  5. Write five examples of compound sentences.

  6. Write five examples of complex sentences.

  7. Identify the independent and subordinate clauses in this sentence: Although he was poor, he was honest.

  8. Join these sentences to form compound sentences:

    • I was tired. I continued working.

    • She studied hard. She passed her examination.

  9. Join these sentences to form complex sentences:

    • He was sick. He went to school.

    • The rain stopped. We went outside.

  10. Identify each sentence as simple, compound or complex:

  • The baby cried loudly.

  • I called him, but he did not answer.

  • When the bell rang, the students left the classroom.

JSS 3|First term|English.title: VOCABULARY DEVELOPMENT
JSS 3|First term|English.note:
MEANING OF VOCABULARY DEVELOPMENT

Vocabulary development is the process of learning new words, understanding their meanings and learning how to use them correctly when speaking and writing.

Vocabulary helps us to communicate clearly and understand what we read.

Examples:

  • Happy – feeling joy.

  • Courageous – showing bravery.

  • Enormous – very big.

  • Ancient – very old.

  • Intelligent – clever.

IMPORTANCE OF VOCABULARY DEVELOPMENT

Vocabulary development is important because it helps us to:

  • Speak English correctly.

  • Write good essays and letters.

  • Understand passages and stories.

  • Improve our spelling.

  • Express our thoughts clearly.

  • Perform better in examinations.

WAYS OF DEVELOPING VOCABULARY

Reading books: Reading novels, newspapers, textbooks and stories helps us learn new words.

Using a dictionary: A dictionary helps us find the meanings, spellings and pronunciations of words.

Listening carefully: Listening to teachers, news broadcasts and English programmes helps us learn new expressions.

Learning synonyms and antonyms: This helps us understand words with similar and opposite meanings.

Using new words in sentences: This helps us remember words and understand how to use them correctly.

SYNONYMS

A synonym is a word that has the same or nearly the same meaning as another word.

HOMONYMS

Homonyms are words that have the same spelling or pronunciation but different meanings.

Examples:

JSS 3|First term|English.title: COMPREHENSION
JSS 3|First term|English.note:
MEANING OF COMPREHENSION

Comprehension is the ability to read a passage, understand its meaning and answer questions based on what has been read.

In English Language, comprehension helps students understand stories, identify main ideas, learn new words and draw conclusions from a passage.

IMPORTANCE OF COMPREHENSION

Comprehension helps us to:

  • Understand what we read.

  • Identify the main idea of a passage.

  • Find important information.

  • Learn the meanings of unfamiliar words.

  • Answer questions correctly.

  • Improve our reading and writing skills.

HOW TO ANSWER COMPREHENSION QUESTIONS

Read the passage carefully. Read the passage at least twice if necessary.

Understand the main idea. Identify what the passage is mainly about.

Read the questions carefully. Make sure you understand what each question requires.

Look for answers in the passage. Most answers can be found directly in the passage.

Use your own words when necessary. When a question asks you to explain something, express the answer clearly without changing its meaning.

Write complete answers. Avoid giving answers that are too short or unclear.

Check your spelling and grammar. Ensure that your answers are written in correct English.

TYPES OF COMPREHENSION QUESTIONS

Literal Questions

These questions ask for information directly stated in the passage.

Example: Where did the boy go?

Inferential Questions

These questions require you to use information from the passage to work out an answer that is not directly stated.

Example: Why do you think the boy was afraid?

Vocabulary Questions

These questions ask for the meanings of words as they are used in the passage.

Example: What does the word enormous mean as used in the passage?

Main Idea Questions

These questions ask what the passage is mainly about.

Example: What is the passage mainly about?

Personal Response Questions

These questions ask you to give an opinion based on the passage.

Example: What would you have done if you were in the boy's position?

COMPREHENSION PASSAGE

THE IMPORTANCE OF EDUCATION

Education is one of the most important tools for the development of an individual and society. It helps people to acquire knowledge, develop useful skills and make good decisions. An educated person is better prepared to face the challenges of life.

In many communities, children attend school to learn different subjects such as English Language, Mathematics, Basic Science and Social Studies. These subjects help them understand the world around them and prepare them for future careers. Education also teaches children important values such as honesty, discipline, respect and cooperation.

However, some children are unable to attend school because of poverty, lack of educational facilities or the need to assist their parents with household activities. This situation can limit their opportunities and make it difficult for them to achieve their dreams.

Parents, teachers and the government all have important roles to play in providing quality education. Parents should encourage their children to study, while teachers should make learning interesting and meaningful. The government should provide adequate classrooms, qualified teachers, books and other learning materials.

Education should not be seen only as a means of obtaining certificates. It should also prepare individuals to solve problems, contribute to society and become responsible citizens. When people are properly educated, they can help improve their communities and promote national development.

COMPREHENSION QUESTIONS

Answer the following questions in complete sentences.

  1. What is education?

  2. Mention three benefits of education according to the passage.

  3. List four subjects children may study in school.

  4. Mention two reasons why some children cannot attend school.

  5. What roles should parents play in their children's education?

  6. State two things the government should provide to improve education.

  7. Why should education not be seen only as a means of obtaining certificates?

  8. What does the word “adequate” mean as used in the passage?

  9. Give another word that can replace “acquire” in the first paragraph.

  10. Suggest a suitable title for the passage.

SUMMARY OF THE LESSON

Comprehension is the ability to read and understand a passage. To answer comprehension questions correctly, students should read carefully, understand the main ideas, identify relevant information and write clear answers in correct English.

ASSIGNMENT

  1. Define comprehension.

  2. State five ways to answer comprehension questions correctly.

  3. Explain the difference between literal and inferential questions.

  4. Read the passage again and write a summary of it in five sentences.

  5. Write a short passage of about 150 words on “The Importance of Keeping Our Environment Clean” and set five comprehension questions on it.

JSS 3|First term|English.title: ESSAY WRITING[ FORMAL LETTER]
JSS 3|First term|English.note:
MEANING OF A FORMAL LETTER

A formal letter is a letter written to a person or an organisation for an official purpose. It is usually written in a polite and respectful manner.

Formal letters are written to people such as school principals, teachers, government officials, company managers and newspaper editors.

Examples of formal letters:

  • A letter of complaint.

  • A letter of application for a job.

  • A letter to the principal requesting permission.

  • A letter to the local government chairman.

  • A letter to the editor of a newspaper.

FEATURES OF A FORMAL LETTER

A formal letter has the following parts:

Writer's Address: This is the address of the person writing the letter. It is written at the top right-hand corner.

Date: The date is written below the writer's address.

Receiver's Address: This is the address of the person receiving the letter. It is written on the left-hand side below the date.

Salutation: This is the greeting used to address the receiver. Examples include Dear Sir and Dear Madam.

Heading or Title: This states the reason for writing the letter. It is usually written clearly and may be underlined.

Introduction: This explains the purpose of the letter.

Body: This contains the main information. Each major point should be explained in a separate paragraph.

Conclusion: This summarises the writer's request or expectations.

Complimentary Close: This is the polite ending of the letter. Examples include Yours faithfully and Yours sincerely, depending on the recipient and the style required.

Signature and Name: The writer signs and writes their full name below the complimentary close.

FORMAT OF A FORMAL LETTER

12 School Road, Yaba, Lagos. 18 October, 2026. The Principal, Bright Path Academy, Yaba, Lagos. Dear Sir, APPLICATION FOR PERMISSION TO ORGANISE A SCHOOL EVENT I am writing to request permission to organise a school event for the students. The purpose of the event is to encourage teamwork, creativity and friendship among students. The programme will include educational games, quizzes and other activities. I promise that the event will be properly organised and that all school rules will be obeyed. I will also ensure that the school environment is kept clean. I hope my request will receive your kind consideration. Yours faithfully, [Signature] John Adewale

RULES FOR WRITING A FORMAL LETTER

  • Use polite and respectful language.

  • Write the addresses in the correct positions.

  • State your purpose clearly.

  • Divide the body into paragraphs.

  • Avoid slang and informal expressions.

  • Do not use unnecessary abbreviations.

  • Use the correct complimentary close.

  • Check your spelling, punctuation and grammar.

  • Follow the word limit given in the examination question.

FORMAL LETTER AND INFORMAL LETTER

Formal letter

Informal letter

Written for official purposes.

Written to friends and relatives.

Uses polite, official language.

Uses friendly and relaxed language.

Usually begins with Dear Sir or Dear Madam.

May begin with Dear John or Dear Mum.

Often ends with Yours faithfully.

Often ends with Your friend or Yours lovingly.

Has a formal tone.

Has a personal tone.

EXAMINATION QUESTION

Your school has been experiencing a shortage of textbooks in the library. Write a letter to the principal of your school explaining three problems caused by the shortage and suggesting three ways of solving the problem.

GUIDE TO ANSWERING THE QUESTION

Your letter should contain:

Introduction: State why you are writing.

First paragraph: Explain the problems caused by the shortage of textbooks.

Second paragraph: Suggest ways the school can obtain more textbooks.

Conclusion: Politely ask the principal to take action.

Remember to include your address, date, receiver's address, salutation, heading, complimentary close and signature.

CLASSWORK

  1. Define a formal letter.

  2. Mention five occasions when a formal letter may be written.

  3. List the main parts of a formal letter.

  4. State four differences between a formal letter and an informal letter.

  5. Write a formal letter to your principal requesting permission to organise an inter-house sports competition.

ASSIGNMENT

  1. Explain the meaning of a formal letter.

  2. State five rules for writing a good formal letter.

  3. Write a letter to the chairman of your local government area complaining about the poor condition of roads in your community.

  4. Write a letter to the editor of a newspaper explaining three ways of reducing examination malpractice in secondary schools.

  5. Write a formal letter to your principal suggesting three ways of improving discipline in your school.

JSS 3|First term|English.title: ESSAY WRITING[ INFORMAL LETTER]
JSS 3|First term|English.note:
MEANING OF AN INFORMAL LETTER

An informal letter is a letter written to someone we know personally, such as a friend, parent, brother, sister or relative.

It is written in a friendly and relaxed manner. The language used is usually simple and conversational.

Examples of informal letters:

  • A letter to your friend describing your new school.

  • A letter to your mother explaining how you spent your holiday.

  • A letter to your cousin inviting them to your birthday party.

  • A letter to your brother telling him about your examination.

FEATURES OF AN INFORMAL LETTER

Writer's Address: This is the address of the person writing the letter. It is written at the top right-hand corner.

Date: The date is written below the writer's address.

Salutation: This is the greeting used to address the receiver.

Examples: Dear John, Dear Mum, Dear Aunty Grace.

Introduction: This is the opening paragraph. It may include greetings and enquiries about the receiver's health.

Body of the Letter: This contains the main message. It is usually divided into paragraphs to make the letter easy to read.

Conclusion: This is the closing paragraph. It may include good wishes, greetings to other family members or a request for a reply.

Complimentary Close: This is the friendly ending of the letter.

Examples: Your friend, Yours lovingly, Your loving son.

Name: The writer writes their first name or familiar name at the end.

FORMAT OF AN INFORMAL LETTER

12 School Road, Yaba, Lagos. 18 October, 2026. Dear John, How are you and your family? I hope everyone is doing well. I am writing to tell you about my new school and the wonderful experiences I have had since I resumed. My new school is very interesting. The teachers are friendly and explain their lessons clearly. I have also made many new friends who help me with my schoolwork. Last week, our school organised a quiz competition. My class took part and came second. I was very happy because I answered two difficult questions correctly. We also have a library where students can read different books. I wish you were here to share these experiences with me. Please write back and tell me about your school too. Remember me to your parents. I hope to hear from you soon. Your friend, Victory

RULES FOR WRITING AN INFORMAL LETTER

  • Write your address at the top right-hand corner.

  • Write the date below the address.

  • Use a friendly salutation such as Dear John.

  • Use simple and friendly language.

  • Divide the body into clear paragraphs.

  • Write according to the topic given.

  • You may use contractions such as I'm, don't, can't and we're.

  • End with a suitable complimentary close.

  • Write your first name or familiar name at the end.

DIFFERENCES BETWEEN FORMAL AND INFORMAL LETTERS

Formal letter

Informal letter

Written for official purposes.

Written to friends and relatives.

Uses polite, official language.

Uses friendly, relaxed language.

Usually addressed to officials or organisations.

Usually addressed to people we know personally.

Often ends with Yours faithfully.

May end with Your friend or Yours lovingly.

Usually has a clear official subject heading.

Usually does not require a subject heading.

EXAMINATION QUESTION

Your friend who lives in another town has written to ask about your new school. Write a letter to your friend describing your school, the subjects you enjoy and the activities you participate in.

CLASSWORK

  1. Define an informal letter.

  2. Mention five people to whom you can write an informal letter.

  3. List the main parts of an informal letter.

  4. State four differences between formal and informal letters.

  5. Write a letter to your friend describing how you spent your last holiday.

ASSIGNMENT

  1. Explain the meaning of an informal letter.

  2. State five features of an informal letter.

  3. Write a letter to your elder brother telling him about three challenges you face in school.

  4. Write a letter to your cousin inviting them to spend the next holiday with you.

  5. Write a letter to your friend describing your best teacher and explaining why you like the teacher.

JSS 3|First term|English.title: SUMMARY WRITING
JSS 3|First term|English.note:
MEANING OF SUMMARY WRITING

Summary writing is the act of reducing a long passage to a shorter form by selecting and writing only the main points.

A summary gives the important information in a passage without including unnecessary details.

Example:

Original passage:

John wakes up early every morning. He sweeps his room, takes his bath and prepares for school. He always arrives at school before the morning assembly begins. His teachers like him because he is hardworking and obedient.

Summary:

John is an early-rising, hardworking and obedient student who prepares well for school.

IMPORTANCE OF SUMMARY WRITING

Summary writing helps students to:

  • Identify the main ideas in a passage.

  • Understand what they read.

  • Write clearly and briefly.

  • Avoid unnecessary information.

  • Improve their reading and writing skills.

  • Prepare for English Language examinations.

RULES OF SUMMARY WRITING

Read the passage carefully.

Read the passage at least twice to understand its meaning.

Identify the main points.

Look for the important information in each paragraph.

Avoid unnecessary details.

Do not include examples, repetitions or explanations that are not needed.

Use your own words.

Express the main ideas in simple, correct English where possible.

Write briefly.

A summary should be shorter than the original passage.

Use complete sentences.

Write your points in clear sentences with correct grammar.

Avoid adding personal opinions.

Write only what the passage says. Do not add your own ideas.

Follow the word limit.

If the question gives a word limit, make sure your answer stays within it.

HOW TO ANSWER SUMMARY QUESTIONS

Follow these steps when answering a summary question.

  1. Read the passage carefully.

  2. Read the questions that follow the passage.

  3. Identify the information needed to answer each question.

  4. Underline or note the relevant points.

  5. Rewrite the points briefly in your own words.

  6. Check your grammar and spelling.

  7. Count your words if a word limit is given.

WHAT TO AVOID IN SUMMARY WRITING

  • Copying the entire passage.

  • Repeating the same idea.

  • Including unnecessary examples.

  • Adding information that is not in the passage.

  • Writing very long sentences.

  • Giving personal opinions.

  • Changing the original meaning.

  • Using incorrect grammar.

EXAMPLE OF SUMMARY WRITING

Passage

Many students perform poorly in examinations because they do not prepare adequately. Some spend too much time watching television or playing games instead of studying. Others fail to attend lessons regularly or complete their assignments.

Students can improve their performance by preparing a timetable and following it strictly. They should attend lessons, ask questions when they do not understand a topic and revise their notes regularly. They should also avoid distractions and seek help from their teachers whenever necessary.

Summary points

  • Some students perform poorly because they do not prepare well.

  • Watching television and playing games distract students from studying.

  • Missing lessons and failing to do assignments affect performance.

  • Students should prepare and follow a timetable.

  • Regular revision and asking questions improve understanding.

  • Students should avoid distractions and seek teachers' assistance.

Short summary

Students perform poorly because of inadequate preparation, distractions and irregular attendance. They can improve by following a timetable, revising regularly, attending lessons and seeking help from teachers.

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN SUMMARY AND COMPREHENSION

Summary writing

Comprehension

Reduces a passage to its main points.

Tests understanding of a passage.

Requires brief answers containing key information.

May require explanations, meanings and direct answers.

Avoids unnecessary details.

Answers depend on the specific questions asked.

CLASSWORK

Read the passage and answer the questions below.

Passage: Keeping the Environment Clean

A clean environment is important for healthy living. When our surroundings are dirty, germs can spread and cause diseases. Blocked drainage systems may also lead to flooding during the rainy season.

Everyone has a responsibility to keep the environment clean. People should dispose of refuse in proper waste bins instead of dumping it on roads or inside gutters. They should also clean their homes, clear drainage channels and avoid littering public places.

Government authorities should provide waste collection services and educate the public about proper sanitation. Schools should also teach students the importance of environmental cleanliness. When individuals and government work together, the environment becomes safer and healthier.

Questions

  1. State two dangers of a dirty environment.

  2. Mention three ways people can keep the environment clean.

  3. State two responsibilities of the government and schools in maintaining cleanliness.

ASSIGNMENT

Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

Passage: The Benefits of Reading

Reading is a useful habit that helps students improve their knowledge and language skills. Students who read regularly learn new words, improve their spelling and understand how to construct correct sentences. Reading also helps them develop their imagination and think more clearly.

However, some students do not enjoy reading because they spend most of their free time watching television or using their phones for entertainment. Others avoid reading because they find books difficult to understand.

Students can develop a reading habit by choosing interesting books and setting aside time to read every day. Teachers and parents should encourage children to read and provide suitable books for them. Schools can also establish libraries and organise reading competitions to motivate students.

Questions

  1. State three benefits of reading.

  2. Give two reasons some students do not enjoy reading.

  3. Mention three ways students can develop a reading habit.

  4. Write a summary of the passage in not more than 60 words

JSS 3|First term|English.title: LITERATURE
JSS 3|First term|English.note:
MEANING OF LITERATURE

Literature is the study of written or spoken works that express people's ideas, feelings, experiences, and imagination.

Literature teaches us about life, human behaviour, culture, and society through stories, poems, and plays.

Examples of literary works include Things Fall Apart by Chinua Achebe and poems written by Nigerian poets.

There are three major forms of literature.

Prose

Prose is a form of literature written in sentences and paragraphs. It is usually used to tell stories.

Examples include novels, short stories, and folktales.

Drama

Drama is a form of literature written to be acted on a stage or performed before an audience.

Examples include plays and stage performances.

Poetry

Poetry is a form of literature that expresses feelings, thoughts, and ideas through carefully chosen words and lines.

Examples include poems about love, nature, death, and patriotism.

A genre is a category or type of literary work.

The major genres of literature are:

  • Prose

  • Drama

  • Poetry

Plot: The sequence of events in a story or play.

Setting: The time and place where a story or play happens.

Character: A person or being that takes part in a story.

Theme: The main message or idea in a literary work.

Conflict: The problem or struggle faced by a character.

Dialogue: A conversation between two or more characters.

Style: The way a writer uses language to express ideas.

Main character: The most important character in a story.

Minor character: A character who plays a smaller role in the story.

Protagonist: The main character in a story, usually the one whose actions drive the plot.

Antagonist: The character or force that opposes the protagonist.

Literature is important because it:

  • Teaches moral lessons.

  • Helps us understand different cultures.

  • Improves our reading and writing skills.

  • Develops our imagination.

  • Entertains readers and audiences.

  • Teaches us about human behaviour.

  • Helps us understand the problems of society.

Prose

Drama

Poetry

Written in sentences and paragraphs.

Written mainly for performance.

Written in lines and stanzas.

Usually tells a story.

Uses characters and dialogue.

Often expresses feelings and ideas.

Examples are novels and short stories.

Examples are plays.

Examples are poems.

Read the note carefully and answer these questions.

  2. Mention the three major forms of literature.

  3. Explain the meaning of prose.

  4. What is the difference between a protagonist and an antagonist?

  5. State four elements of literature.

  2. What is poetry?

  3. Define plot, setting, and theme.

  4. State five importance of literature.

  5. Give two examples each of prose, drama, and poetry.

JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.title: DRUG AND SUBSTANCE ABUSE I
JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.note:
Meaning of Drug

A drug is a substance used to prevent, treat or cure sickness. Examples are paracetamol, antibiotics and cough syrup.

Meaning of Drug Abuse

Drug abuse is the wrong use of drugs. It happens when someone takes too much medicine or uses drugs wrongly.

Meaning of Substance Abuse

Substance abuse is the harmful use of drugs, alcohol, cigarettes or other substances that can damage the body and mind.

Examples of Abused Substances

  • Alcohol

  • Cigarettes

  • Indian hemp (cannabis)

  • Cocaine

  • Tramadol when misused

  • Harmful inhalants such as glue

Causes of Drug and Substance Abuse

Peer pressure: Friends may encourage someone to take harmful substances.

Curiosity: Some people take drugs because they want to know how they feel.

Bad company: Keeping friends who abuse drugs may encourage the habit.

Stress: Some people misuse drugs to escape their problems.

Lack of knowledge: Ignorance of the dangers of drugs can lead to abuse.

Poor parental guidance: Lack of proper guidance may expose young people to drug abuse.

Effects of Drug and Substance Abuse

  • It can damage the brain and other body organs.

  • It can lead to addiction.

  • It can cause poor academic performance.

  • It can lead to accidents.

  • It can cause mental problems.

  • It can cause family problems.

  • It can lead to sickness or death.

Classwork

Answer the following questions.

  1. What is a drug?

  2. Explain drug abuse.

  3. Mention five examples of substances that can be abused.

  4. State four causes of drug abuse.

  5. Mention five effects of drug abuse.

Assignment

  1. Explain substance abuse.

  2. State three differences between proper drug use and drug abuse.

  3. Explain four ways peer pressure can lead to drug abuse.

  4. Mention five dangers of substance abuse among students.

  5. Write a short paragraph explaining why students should avoid drug abuse.

JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.title: DRUG AND SUBSTANCE ABUSE II
JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.note:
Prevention of Drug and Substance Abuse

Drug and substance abuse can be prevented through the following ways:

Proper education: Students should learn about the dangers of drug abuse.

Avoiding bad company: Young people should avoid friends who encourage drug abuse.

Parental guidance: Parents should guide their children properly.

Following medical instructions: Drugs should be taken according to the instructions of qualified health professionals.

Saying no to peer pressure: Students should refuse harmful substances offered by friends.

Counselling: People struggling with substance abuse should seek professional help.

Engaging in useful activities: Sports, reading and learning skills can help young people avoid harmful habits.

Drug Control Agencies in Nigeria

National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA)

The NDLEA is a government agency that fights illegal drug production, trafficking and related offences in Nigeria.

Its duties include:

  • Arresting people involved in illegal drug trafficking.

  • Seizing illegal drugs.

  • Educating people about the dangers of drug abuse.

  • Helping to prevent the spread of illegal drugs.

National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC)

NAFDAC is a government agency responsible for regulating the safety and quality of food, drugs and other regulated products.

Its duties include:

  • Preventing the circulation of fake and substandard drugs.

  • Regulating the quality of medicines.

  • Inspecting regulated products.

  • Educating the public on safe drug use.

Misuse of Herbal Medicine

Herbal medicine is medicine prepared from plants or plant parts.

Herbal medicine can be harmful when it is improperly prepared or used.

Examples of misuse include:

  • Taking too much herbal medicine.

  • Using unknown herbal mixtures.

  • Mixing herbal medicine with other drugs without medical advice.

  • Using herbal remedies with unknown ingredients.

  • Replacing prescribed treatment with unverified remedies.

Dangers of Misusing Herbal Medicine

  • It may damage the liver or kidneys.

  • It may cause poisoning.

  • It may interact dangerously with other medicines.

  • It may delay proper treatment.

  • It may cause serious illness or death.

Answer the following questions.

  2. What is the full meaning of NDLEA?

  3. State three duties of the NDLEA.

  4. What is the full meaning of NAFDAC?

  5. Mention four dangers of misusing herbal medicine.

  2. State four duties of NAFDAC.

  4. Explain four ways herbal medicine can be misused.

JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.title: FAMILY TRAITS
JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.note:
Meaning of Family Traits

Family traits are the features or characteristics that children inherit from their parents.

These traits make family members look alike or behave similarly in some ways.

Examples of family traits include eye colour, skin colour, hair type, nose shape and blood group.

Types of Family Traits

Family traits can be divided into two main types.

Inherited traits

These are characteristics passed from parents to their children through genes.

Examples include:

  • Skin colour

  • Eye colour

  • Natural hair type

  • Blood group

  • Natural nose shape

  • Dimples

Acquired traits

These are characteristics or abilities a person develops during life through learning, practice or experience. They are not usually inherited genetically.

Examples include:

  • Learning how to swim

  • Learning how to read

  • Speaking a language

  • Learning how to ride a bicycle

  • Developing writing skills

Meaning of Heredity

Heredity is the passing of characteristics from parents to their children through genes.

For example, a child may inherit their father's eye colour or their mother's hair type.

Meaning of Genes

Genes are parts of DNA that carry information responsible for inherited characteristics.

Genes are passed from parents to their children.

Meaning of Variation

Variation refers to the differences that exist among individuals of the same species.

For example, children from the same parents may have different heights, skin shades or hair textures.

Examples of Family Traits

Trait

Example

Eye colour

Brown eyes

Hair type

Curly or straight hair

Skin colour

Different natural skin shades

Blood group

A, B, AB or O

Dimples

Presence or absence of dimples

Earlobes

Attached or free earlobes

Dominant and Recessive Traits

Dominant traits

A dominant trait can appear when a person has just one copy of the associated dominant gene variant.

Recessive traits

A recessive trait generally appears when a person inherits two copies of the associated recessive gene variant.

The inheritance of traits can be more complicated than this, and not every family trait follows a simple dominant-recessive pattern.

Importance of Studying Family Traits

  • It helps us understand why children resemble their parents.

  • It helps us understand differences among family members.

  • It helps us learn about heredity.

  • It helps scientists study inherited conditions.

  • It helps us understand human variation.

Classwork

Answer the following questions.

  1. What are family traits?

  2. Explain the meaning of heredity.

  3. What are genes?

  4. State four examples of inherited traits.

  5. Differentiate between inherited and acquired traits.

Assignment

  2. Explain dominant and recessive traits.

  3. Mention five characteristics children may inherit from their parents.

  4. State four importance of studying family traits.

  5. Give three examples of acquired traits and explain how each is developed.

JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.title: ENVIRONMENTAL HARARDS; SOIL EROSION
JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.note:
Meaning of Environmental Hazards

Environmental hazards are things or events that can cause harm to people, animals, plants and the environment.

Examples include flooding, soil erosion, bush burning, deforestation and pollution.

Meaning of Soil Erosion

Soil erosion is the removal of the top layer of soil by water, wind or human activities.

The topsoil is important because it contains nutrients that help plants grow.

Types of Soil Erosion

Water erosion

This occurs when running water washes away the soil.

Wind erosion

This occurs when strong wind blows away loose soil.

Sheet erosion

This occurs when water removes a thin layer of soil over a large area.

Rill erosion

This occurs when running water forms small channels on the soil.

Gully erosion

This occurs when running water creates deep and wide channels in the ground.

Causes of Soil Erosion

Heavy rainfall: Rainwater washes away loose soil.

Deforestation: Cutting down trees exposes the soil to erosion.

Overgrazing: Animals eat grasses that protect the soil.

Poor farming methods: Improper farming can leave the soil exposed.

Road construction: Removing vegetation during construction exposes the soil.

Bush burning: Burning vegetation leaves the soil without enough protection.

Strong wind: Wind can carry away dry and loose soil.

Effects of Soil Erosion

  • It removes fertile topsoil.

  • It reduces crop production.

  • It creates deep gullies.

  • It damages roads and buildings.

  • It can destroy farmland.

  • It can cause sediment to enter rivers and streams.

  • It can lead to the displacement of people.

  • It can contribute to flooding in affected areas.

Control and Prevention of Soil Erosion

Planting trees: Tree roots hold the soil together.

Planting grasses: Grass covers the soil and reduces the force of running water.

Cover cropping: Growing cover crops protects the soil from heavy rainfall.

Terracing: Making steps on slopes slows down running water.

Building drainage channels: Proper drainage directs water safely away from exposed soil.

Avoiding deforestation: Trees should not be cut down carelessly.

Mulching: Covering the soil with dry leaves or other suitable materials protects it from rainfall.

Controlled grazing: Animals should not be allowed to destroy all the vegetation in an area.

Importance of Preventing Soil Erosion

  • It protects fertile soil.

  • It improves agricultural production.

  • It protects roads and buildings.

  • It reduces the formation of gullies.

  • It helps protect rivers and streams.

  • It protects the environment.

Classwork

Answer the following questions.

  1. What is soil erosion?

  2. Mention four types of soil erosion.

  3. State five causes of soil erosion.

  4. Mention five effects of soil erosion.

  5. Explain five ways of preventing soil erosion.

Assignment

  2. Explain the difference between water erosion and wind erosion.

  3. What is gully erosion?

  4. State four effects of soil erosion on farmers.

JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.title: ENVIRNOMENTAL HAZARD; FLOODING
JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.note:
Meaning of Flooding

Flooding is the covering of normally dry land with water.

Flooding occurs when water overflows from rivers, heavy rainfall accumulates, or drainage systems cannot carry water away properly.

Types of Flooding

River flooding: This occurs when a river overflows its banks and covers nearby land.

Flash flooding: This occurs when water rises very quickly after heavy rainfall.

Coastal flooding: This occurs when seawater covers land near the coast.

Urban flooding: This occurs when streets, homes and other parts of a town or city become covered with water.

Causes of Flooding

Heavy rainfall: Too much rain can cause water to accumulate on land.

Blocked drainage: Rubbish and dirt can block drains and prevent water from flowing away.

Poor drainage systems: Inadequate drainage can cause water to collect in streets and homes.

Deforestation: Cutting down trees reduces the amount of water absorbed by vegetation and the soil.

Building on waterways: Buildings placed on natural water channels prevent water from flowing freely.

Overflowing rivers: Rivers may overflow their banks after heavy rainfall.

Improper waste disposal: Dumping refuse into drains can block the passage of water.

Effects of Flooding

  • It destroys houses and buildings.

  • It damages roads and bridges.

  • It destroys crops and farmland.

  • It can cause the death of people and animals.

  • It can destroy household property.

  • It can contaminate drinking water.

  • It can spread waterborne diseases such as cholera.

  • It can force people to leave their homes.

  • It can cause financial losses.

  • It can disrupt transportation and school activities.

Prevention and Control of Flooding

Proper waste disposal: Refuse should not be dumped into drains or waterways.

Cleaning of drains: Drains should be cleared regularly to allow water to flow freely.

Construction of good drainage systems: Proper drains help carry rainwater away safely.

Planting trees: Trees help reduce surface runoff and improve water absorption.

Avoiding waterways: People should not build houses on waterways or flood-prone areas.

Building flood barriers: Barriers can help prevent water from entering certain areas.

Proper town planning: Buildings and roads should be planned to allow water to drain properly.

Public education: People should be taught how to prevent flooding and respond to flood warnings.

Safety Measures During Flooding

  • Move to higher ground when flooding occurs.

  • Stay away from fast-moving floodwater.

  • Do not walk or drive through floodwater.

  • Switch off electricity if it is safe to do so.

  • Drink safe or treated water.

  • Follow instructions from emergency authorities.

  • Avoid touching electrical wires in flooded areas.

Classwork

Answer the following questions.

  1. What is flooding?

  2. Mention four types of flooding.

  3. State five causes of flooding.

  4. Mention five effects of flooding.

  5. Explain five ways of preventing flooding.

Assignment

  2. Explain how blocked drainage causes flooding.

  3. State four dangers of flooding to human health.

  4. Mention five safety measures to observe during flooding.

  5. Explain how proper town planning can help prevent flooding.

JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.title: BUSH BURNING
JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.note:
Bush burning is the act of setting fire to grasses, bushes and other vegetation on land.

It may occur naturally or be caused by human activities. People sometimes burn bushes to clear farmland, hunt animals or remove dry grasses.

Causes of Bush Burning

Careless use of fire: People may leave fires burning after use.

Farming activities: Some farmers burn vegetation to clear land before planting.

Hunting: Some hunters set fire to bushes to chase animals.

Cigarette smoking: A carelessly discarded cigarette can start a bush fire.

Lightning: Lightning can sometimes cause natural fires.

Deliberate acts: Some people intentionally set bushes on fire.

Effects of Bush Burning

  • It destroys plants and trees.

  • It kills wild animals and insects.

  • It destroys the habitats of animals.

  • It reduces soil fertility by destroying organic matter.

  • It exposes the soil to erosion.

  • It causes air pollution through smoke.

  • It can destroy houses, farms and other property.

  • It can cause injuries or death.

  • It contributes to the release of greenhouse gases.

Prevention of Bush Burning

  • Avoid setting fire to bushes unnecessarily.

  • Create firebreaks in areas at risk of bush fires.

  • Do not throw burning cigarettes into dry grasses.

  • Extinguish campfires completely after use.

  • Educate people about the dangers of bush burning.

  • Enforce laws against uncontrolled burning.

  • Report bush fires quickly to the appropriate authorities.

  • Use safer methods to clear farmland where possible.

Importance of Preventing Bush Burning

  • It protects plants and animals.

  • It helps maintain soil fertility.

  • It reduces air pollution.

  • It protects homes, farms and other property.

  • It helps prevent soil erosion.

  • It protects human life and the environment.

Classwork

Answer the following questions.

  1. What is bush burning?

  2. Mention four causes of bush burning.

  3. State five effects of bush burning.

  4. Mention five ways of preventing bush burning.

  5. Explain three reasons why bush burning is harmful to the environment.

Assignment

  2. Explain four ways human activities can cause bush burning.

  3. State four effects of bush burning on soil and plants.

  4. Mention five safety measures that can help prevent bush fires.

  5. Write a short paragraph explaining why bush burning should be controlled.

JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.title: DEFORESTATION
JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.note:
Meaning of Deforestation

Deforestation is the cutting down or clearing of forests and trees without replacing them.

People clear forests to obtain wood, build houses, construct roads and create farmland.

Causes of Deforestation

Farming: Trees are cut down to create land for planting crops.

Logging: Trees are cut down to obtain timber for furniture and building.

Building construction: Forests are cleared to build houses, schools and offices.

Road construction: Trees are removed to make roads and highways.

Fuelwood: Trees are cut down for firewood and charcoal.

Mining: Forests are cleared to extract minerals from the ground.

Bush burning: Fires can destroy large areas of forest.

Effects of Deforestation

  • It destroys the homes of wild animals.

  • It reduces the number of trees in the environment.

  • It exposes the soil to erosion.

  • It can reduce soil fertility.

  • It contributes to global warming because fewer trees are available to absorb carbon dioxide.

  • It can reduce rainfall in some regions and disturb the water cycle.

  • It can lead to the extinction of some plant and animal species.

  • It can cause desertification in vulnerable areas.

Prevention of Deforestation

  • Plant new trees to replace those that are cut down.

  • Avoid cutting down trees unnecessarily.

  • Practise selective logging instead of clearing entire forests.

  • Establish forest reserves and protect them.

  • Use alternative sources of energy where possible.

  • Recycle and reuse paper and wood products.

  • Enforce laws against illegal logging.

  • Educate people about the importance of forests.

Importance of Forests

  • Forests provide homes for wild animals.

  • Trees absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen during photosynthesis.

  • Forests provide timber, fruits and medicinal plants.

  • Tree roots help hold the soil together.

  • Forests help regulate the water cycle and climate.

  • Forests provide jobs and income for many people.

Classwork

Answer the following questions.

JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.title: DESERTIFICATION
JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.note:
Meaning of Deforestation

Deforestation is the cutting down or clearing of forests and trees without replacing them.

People clear forests to obtain wood, build houses, construct roads and create farmland.

Causes of Deforestation

Farming: Trees are cut down to create land for planting crops.

Logging: Trees are cut down to obtain timber for furniture and building.

Building construction: Forests are cleared to build houses, schools and offices.

Road construction: Trees are removed to make roads and highways.

Fuelwood: Trees are cut down for firewood and charcoal.

Mining: Forests are cleared to extract minerals from the ground.

Bush burning: Fires can destroy large areas of forest.

Effects of Deforestation

  • It destroys the homes of wild animals.

  • It reduces the number of trees in the environment.

  • It exposes the soil to erosion.

  • It can reduce soil fertility.

  • It contributes to global warming because fewer trees are available to absorb carbon dioxide.

  • It can reduce rainfall in some regions and disturb the water cycle.

  • It can lead to the extinction of some plant and animal species.

  • It can cause desertification in vulnerable areas.

Prevention of Deforestation

  • Plant new trees to replace those that are cut down.

  • Avoid cutting down trees unnecessarily.

  • Practise selective logging instead of clearing entire forests.

  • Establish forest reserves and protect them.

  • Use alternative sources of energy where possible.

  • Recycle and reuse paper and wood products.

  • Enforce laws against illegal logging.

  • Educate people about the importance of forests.

Importance of Forests

  • Forests provide homes for wild animals.

  • Trees absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen during photosynthesis.

  • Forests provide timber, fruits and medicinal plants.

  • Tree roots help hold the soil together.

  • Forests help regulate the water cycle and climate.

  • Forests provide jobs and income for many people.

JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.title: DEPLETION OF OZONE LAYER
JSS 3|First term|Integrated Science.note:
Meaning of the Ozone Layer

The ozone layer is a layer of gas found in the stratosphere, high above the Earth. It contains ozone gas, which helps protect living things by absorbing most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation.

Meaning of Ozone Layer Depletion

Ozone layer depletion is the reduction in the amount of ozone gas in the Earth's stratosphere.

It allows more harmful ultraviolet radiation to reach the Earth's surface.

Causes of Ozone Layer Depletion

Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs): These chemicals were formerly used in some refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol sprays. They can destroy ozone in the stratosphere.

Halons: These chemicals were used in some fire extinguishers and can damage the ozone layer.

Other ozone-depleting chemicals: Some industrial chemicals release substances that destroy ozone.

Improper handling of old equipment: Refrigerators and air conditioners containing ozone-depleting chemicals can release them if not handled properly.

Effects of Ozone Layer Depletion

  • It increases exposure to harmful ultraviolet radiation.

  • It increases the risk of skin cancer.

  • It can cause eye problems such as cataracts.

  • It can weaken the human body's immune system.

  • It can damage crops and reduce plant growth.

  • It can harm tiny aquatic organisms such as phytoplankton.

  • It can disturb food chains in aquatic environments.

Prevention of Ozone Layer Depletion

  • Avoid the unnecessary release of ozone-depleting chemicals.

  • Use refrigerators and air conditioners that do not contain ozone-depleting substances.

  • Ensure old cooling equipment is serviced and disposed of properly by trained professionals.

  • Follow laws controlling ozone-depleting substances.

  • Support the use of safer alternatives in industries.

  • Educate people about protecting the ozone layer.

Importance of the Ozone Layer

  • It absorbs most harmful UV-B radiation from the Sun.

  • It helps protect humans from skin and eye damage.

  • It protects plants from excessive ultraviolet radiation.

  • It helps protect aquatic organisms.

  • It supports the balance of ecosystems.

JSS 3|First term|Business Studies.title: Effective Office Practice
JSS 3|First term|Business Studies.note:
EFFECTIVE OFFICE PRACTICE

Effective office practice refers to the proper methods and procedures used to carry out office duties correctly, quickly and efficiently.

It involves following office rules when handling documents, keeping records, communicating with people and performing daily office activities.

Filing of Documents

This means arranging and keeping documents in the correct places so that they can be found easily when needed.

Record Keeping

This involves recording and storing important business information, such as money received, money spent and goods sold.

Telephone Handling

This means answering telephone calls politely, listening carefully and giving correct information.

Handling Visitors

This involves welcoming visitors politely and directing them to the appropriate people or offices.

Preparation of Documents

This involves preparing letters, reports, invoices, receipts and other official documents.

Office Cleaning

This means keeping the office environment clean, neat and organised.

  • It helps office work to be completed quickly.

  • It reduces mistakes and confusion.

  • It promotes proper record keeping.

  • It saves time and resources.

  • It improves communication.

  • It protects important office documents.

  • It increases workers' productivity.

  • It creates a good image for the business.

Punctuality

This means arriving at work on time.

Honesty

This means being truthful when handling money, documents and information.

Neatness

This means maintaining a clean appearance and keeping the office tidy.

Accuracy

This means ensuring that information and records are correct.

Courtesy

This means treating visitors, customers and colleagues politely.

Confidentiality

This means keeping private office information secret.

Hard Work

This means performing assigned duties diligently.

Responsibility

This means taking duties seriously and completing assigned tasks properly.

Effective office practice involves carrying out office activities correctly and efficiently. It helps to save time, reduce mistakes, maintain accurate records and improve business performance.

JSS 3|First term|Business Studies.title: Office Procedure (Part I)
JSS 3|First term|Business Studies.note:
MEANING OF OFFICE PROCEDURE

Office procedure refers to the established steps, rules and methods followed when carrying out activities in an office. It helps workers perform their duties correctly and efficiently.

TYPES OF OFFICE PROCEDURES

Receiving Correspondence: This involves receiving letters, parcels and other documents sent to an organisation.

Dispatching Correspondence: This means sending letters and documents from an office to other people or organisations.

Filing Procedure: This involves arranging and keeping documents in the correct places for easy retrieval.

Telephone Procedure: This involves answering telephone calls politely and taking messages correctly.

Visitor Reception Procedure: This involves welcoming visitors and directing them to the appropriate persons.

PROCEDURE FOR HANDLING INCOMING MAIL

Incoming mail refers to letters, parcels and documents received by an organisation.

Receiving: Collecting letters and parcels delivered to the office.

Sorting: Separating letters according to their recipients or departments.

Opening: Opening envelopes carefully, except those marked private or confidential.

Date Stamping: Stamping the date of receipt on documents where necessary.

Recording: Entering important details in the mail register.

Distribution: Delivering documents to the appropriate persons.

Filing: Keeping copies of important documents for future reference.

PROCEDURE FOR HANDLING OUTGOING MAIL

Outgoing mail refers to letters and documents sent from an organisation to other people or organisations.

Preparation: Writing and checking the letter for errors.

Approval: Obtaining approval from the authorised officer where necessary.

Signing: Getting the letter signed by the appropriate person.

Enveloping: Placing the letter inside an envelope.

Addressing: Writing the recipient's name and address correctly.

Recording: Entering relevant details in the outgoing mail register.

Dispatching: Sending the letter through an approved delivery method.

IMPORTANCE OF OFFICE PROCEDURE

  • It promotes orderliness.

  • It reduces mistakes.

  • It saves time.

  • It improves communication.

  • It protects important documents.

  • It promotes accountability.

  • It improves workers' efficiency.

JSS 3|First term|Business Studies.title: OFFICE PROCEDURE II
JSS 3|First term|Business Studies.note:
PROCEDURE FOR RECEIVING VISITORS

Visitors are people who come to an organisation to meet staff members or conduct business.

Welcoming: Greeting visitors politely.

Enquiry: Asking visitors the purpose of their visit.

Identification: Finding out the person they wish to see.

Registration: Recording their details where necessary.

Notification: Informing the appropriate staff member about the visitor's arrival.

Waiting: Directing the visitor to the waiting area when necessary.

Direction: Guiding the visitor to the appropriate office.

PROCEDURE FOR MAKING PAYMENTS

Making payments involves following approved steps when an organisation pays for goods or services.

Receiving the Invoice: Obtaining the document showing the amount payable.

Checking: Confirming that the amount and details are correct.

Approval: Obtaining permission from the authorised officer.

Preparing Payment: Preparing the approved payment instruction.

Making Payment: Paying the supplier through an approved method.

Obtaining a Receipt: Collecting evidence of payment.

Recording: Entering the transaction in the appropriate accounting records.

BUSINESS DOCUMENTS USED IN OFFICE PROCEDURE

Invoice: A document showing goods supplied and the amount payable.

Receipt: A document serving as evidence that payment has been received.

Purchase Order: A document used to request goods from a supplier.

Delivery Note: A document showing the goods delivered to a buyer.

Cheque: A written instruction directing a bank to pay a specified amount.

Payment Voucher: A document used to support and authorise a payment.

PROCEDURE FOR FILING DOCUMENTS

Filing is the systematic arrangement and storage of documents for future use.

Collection: Gathering documents to be filed.

Sorting: Separating documents according to their categories.

Classification: Deciding the appropriate filing method.

Labelling: Writing suitable names or descriptions on files.

Storage: Keeping documents in their correct files or cabinets.

Retrieval: Finding and removing documents when needed.

Refiling: Returning documents to their proper places after use.

IMPORTANCE OF FOLLOWING OFFICE PROCEDURES

  • It prevents confusion and delays.

  • It promotes proper handling of money.

  • It helps prevent fraud.

  • It makes documents easy to locate.

  • It improves customer relations.

  • It provides evidence of business transactions.

  • It promotes efficiency and accountability.

JSS 3|First term|Business Studies.title: STORE RECORDS
JSS 3|First term|Business Studies.note:
MEANING OF STORE RECORDS

Store records are documents used to record goods received into a store, goods issued out of the store, and goods remaining in the store.

They help the storekeeper to know the quantity of goods available at any time.

IMPORTANCE OF STORE RECORDS

Store records are important for the following reasons:

  • They show the quantity of goods available in the store.

  • They help to prevent theft and loss of goods.

  • They help the storekeeper know when to order new goods.

  • They provide information about goods received and issued.

  • They help to prevent overstocking and understocking.

  • They make stocktaking easier.

  • They help the business maintain proper records of its goods.

TYPES OF STORE RECORDS

BIN CARD

A bin card is a record kept near or attached to the place where goods are stored. It shows the movement of goods into and out of the store.

A bin card records:

  • Date goods are received.

  • Quantity of goods received.

  • Quantity of goods issued.

  • Balance of goods remaining.

Example:

Date Details Received Issued Balance
1/10/26 Opening stock 50 0 50
3/10/26 Goods received 20 0 70
5/10/26 Goods issued 0 15 55

The balance is calculated by adding the quantity received to the previous balance and subtracting the quantity issued.

STORES LEDGER

A stores ledger is a record used to keep detailed information about goods received, goods issued, and goods remaining in the store.

It may show both the quantities and the values of goods.

GOODS RECEIVED NOTE (GRN)

A goods received note is a document prepared when goods are delivered to a business. It confirms that the goods have been received.

It contains:

  • Date of delivery.

  • Name of the supplier.

  • Description of goods.

  • Quantity received.

  • Condition of the goods.

STORES REQUISITION FORM

A stores requisition form is a document used by a department to request goods from the store.

It tells the storekeeper the type and quantity of goods required.

STOCKTAKING RECORD

A stocktaking record shows the actual quantity of goods counted in the store.

It is used to compare the physical quantity of goods with the quantity shown in the store records.

DIFFERENCES BETWEEN A BIN CARD AND A STORES LEDGER

BIN CARD

  • It is usually kept near the goods in the store.

  • It mainly records quantities of goods.

  • It is commonly maintained by the storekeeper.

STORES LEDGER

  • It is usually kept in the stores or accounts office.

  • It may record both quantities and values of goods.

  • It is commonly maintained by the stores or accounts clerk.

PERSONS RESPONSIBLE FOR STORE RECORDS

STOREKEEPER
The storekeeper receives, stores, issues goods, and updates store records.

STORES CLERK
The stores clerk helps to prepare and maintain store documents.

ACCOUNTANT
The accountant records the financial value of goods and checks relevant records.

INTERNAL AUDITOR
The internal auditor checks records to ensure that they are accurate and properly maintained.

RULES FOR KEEPING STORE RECORDS

  • All goods received must be recorded immediately.

  • All goods issued must be recorded.

  • Store records must be neat and accurate.

  • Documents must be properly filed for future reference.

  • Errors must be corrected properly.

  • Records should be checked regularly against the actual goods available.

SUMMARY

Store records are documents used to record the movement and balance of goods in a store. Examples include bin cards, stores ledgers, goods received notes, stores requisition forms, and stocktaking records.

Proper store records help a business control its goods and reduce losses.

JSS 3|First term|Business Studies.title: STOCKTAKING
JSS 3|First term|Business Studies.note:
MEANING OF STOCKTAKING

Stocktaking is the process of physically counting and checking the goods available in a store to determine the actual quantity of goods remaining.

It helps a business compare the actual goods in the store with the quantities recorded in the store records.

IMPORTANCE OF STOCKTAKING

Stocktaking is important for the following reasons:

  • It helps to determine the actual quantity of goods in the store.

  • It helps to discover missing or stolen goods.

  • It helps to identify damaged or expired goods.

  • It helps to detect errors in store records.

  • It helps to prevent wastage and losses.

  • It helps the business know when to order new goods.

  • It helps to prepare accurate business accounts.

TYPES OF STOCKTAKING

PERIODIC STOCKTAKING

Periodic stocktaking is the counting of goods at specific intervals, such as weekly, monthly, quarterly, or yearly.

CONTINUOUS STOCKTAKING

Continuous stocktaking is the regular checking and counting of goods throughout the year rather than waiting until the end of a particular period.

PROCEDURE FOR STOCKTAKING

  • Prepare a list of goods available in the store.

  • Arrange the goods properly to make counting easy.

  • Count the goods physically.

  • Check the condition of the goods.

  • Record the actual quantity of each item.

  • Compare the actual quantity with the store records.

  • Investigate any differences found.

  • Prepare a stocktaking report.

PERSONS INVOLVED IN STOCKTAKING

STOREKEEPER
The storekeeper arranges the goods and assists in counting them.

STOCKTAKING CLERK
The stocktaking clerk counts the goods and records the quantities.

ACCOUNTANT
The accountant checks the records and helps to identify differences between the actual stock and the recorded stock.

INTERNAL AUDITOR
The internal auditor checks the accuracy of the stocktaking process and the records.

PROBLEMS THAT MAY ARISE DURING STOCKTAKING

  • Goods may be missing or stolen.

  • Goods may be damaged or expired.

  • Errors may occur during counting.

  • Some goods may be counted twice.

  • Store records may contain incorrect information.

  • Stocktaking may take a long time.

  • Business activities may be interrupted during counting.

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN STOCKTAKING AND STORE RECORDS

STOCKTAKING

  • It involves physically counting goods in the store.

  • It shows the actual quantity of goods available.

  • It helps to identify shortages and excess goods.

STORE RECORDS

  • They are documents showing the movement of goods.

  • They show recorded quantities of goods received and issued.

  • They help the storekeeper monitor the balance of goods.

SUMMARY

Stocktaking is the physical counting and checking of goods in a store. It helps a business determine the actual quantity of goods available, discover losses, identify damaged goods, and ensure that store records are accurate.

JSS 3|First term|Business Studies.title: Office Equipment (Part I)

MEANING OF OFFICE EQUIPMENT

Office equipment refers to the machines, tools, and devices used in an office to make work easier, faster, and more efficient.

Office equipment helps workers to perform their duties properly and saves time and energy.

EXAMPLES OF OFFICE EQUIPMENT

TYPEWRITER

A typewriter is a machine used to type letters, reports, and other office documents on paper.

COMPUTER

A computer is an electronic device used to type documents, store information, perform calculations, and communicate.

PRINTER

A printer is a machine used to produce information from a computer on paper.

PHOTOCOPIER

A photocopier is a machine used to make copies of documents quickly.

SCANNER

A scanner is a device used to convert printed documents and pictures into electronic form.

CALCULATOR

A calculator is a device used to perform mathematical calculations quickly and accurately.

TELEPHONE

A telephone is a communication device used to make and receive calls.

FACSIMILE MACHINE (FAX MACHINE)

A fax machine is a device used to send and receive copies of documents through telephone communication systems.

USES OF OFFICE EQUIPMENT

  • It makes office work faster.

  • It saves time and energy.

  • It improves the accuracy of office work.

  • It helps in preparing documents.

  • It makes communication easier.

  • It helps to store and retrieve information.

  • It reduces the amount of manual work.

IMPORTANCE OF OFFICE EQUIPMENT

  • It increases the productivity of office workers.

  • It improves the quality of work.

  • It reduces unnecessary delays.

  • It helps an organisation serve customers better.

  • It makes record keeping easier.

  • It reduces some office operating costs.

CARE AND MAINTENANCE OF OFFICE EQUIPMENT

Care and maintenance of office equipment refer to the activities carried out to keep office machines and devices in good working condition.

Proper care helps office equipment last longer and work efficiently.

WAYS OF CARING FOR OFFICE EQUIPMENT

  • Clean equipment regularly using suitable materials.

  • Keep equipment away from water and excessive moisture.

  • Switch off equipment when it is not in use.

  • Follow the manufacturer's instructions.

  • Handle equipment carefully to prevent damage.

  • Protect equipment from dust.

  • Keep liquids and food away from electrical equipment.

  • Report faults immediately.

  • Allow only trained persons to repair complex machines.

  • Use the correct power supply and suitable accessories.

SAFETY PRECAUTIONS WHEN USING OFFICE EQUIPMENT

  • Read the instructions before using equipment.

  • Do not touch electrical equipment with wet hands.

  • Do not overload electrical sockets.

  • Keep electrical cables in good condition.

  • Do not attempt repairs while equipment is connected to power.

  • Keep equipment away from children and unauthorised persons.

  • Switch off and unplug equipment before cleaning when appropriate.

  • Report electrical faults to a qualified technician.

ADVANTAGES OF PROPER MAINTENANCE

  • It increases the lifespan of equipment.

  • It reduces repair costs.

  • It prevents frequent breakdowns.

  • It improves efficiency.

  • It promotes safety in the office.

  • It reduces delays in office work.

  • It helps the organisation save money.

DISADVANTAGES OF IMPROPER HANDLING OF OFFICE EQUIPMENT

  • Equipment may break down easily.

  • Repair and replacement costs may increase.

  • Office work may be delayed.

  • Important information may be lost.

  • Workers may suffer electrical injuries.

  • The organisation may lose money.

  • The quality of work may decrease.

SUMMARY

Office equipment includes machines and devices used to perform office duties. Examples are computers, printers, photocopiers, scanners, calculators, and telephones. Proper care, maintenance, and safe handling help to prevent damage and ensure efficient office work.
