JSS 3|First term|Business Studies.title: COMMERCE
JSS 3|First term|Business Studies.note:
MEANING OF COMMERCE

Commerce is the process of buying, selling, and distributing goods and services from producers to consumers.

Commerce helps goods and services move from where they are produced to where they are needed.

For example, when a wholesaler buys bags of rice from a producer and sells them to retailers, commerce takes place.

MEANING OF BUSINESS

Business refers to activities carried out by individuals or organisations to produce, buy, or sell goods and services to satisfy human wants and make profit.

RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN COMMERCE AND BUSINESS

Commerce is an important part of business because it helps in the exchange and distribution of goods and services.

Business includes production, buying, selling, and other activities, while commerce mainly deals with trade and the activities that support trade.

WHY COMMERCE IS CALLED THE HEART OF BUSINESS

Commerce is called the heart of business for the following reasons:

  • It connects producers with consumers.

  • It helps goods reach different markets.

  • It makes buying and selling easier.

  • It promotes the exchange of goods and services.

  • It creates employment opportunities.

  • It encourages production by providing markets for goods.

  • It helps businesses earn income and make profit.

  • It promotes trade between different towns and countries.

  • It supports the growth and development of businesses.

COMPONENTS OF COMMERCE

Commerce has two major components: trade and aids to trade.

TRADE

Trade is the buying and selling of goods and services.

Trade can be divided into two main types.

HOME TRADE
Home trade is the buying and selling of goods and services within a country.

Examples include a trader selling rice in Lagos and a shopkeeper selling exercise books in Ibadan.

FOREIGN TRADE
Foreign trade is the buying and selling of goods and services between different countries.

Examples include Nigeria exporting cocoa to another country and importing cars from abroad.

AIDS TO TRADE

Aids to trade are activities and services that make buying and selling easier.

The major aids to trade are:

TRANSPORT
Transport moves goods and people from one place to another.

Examples include road, rail, air, and water transport.

BANKING
Banking provides financial services such as keeping money safe, making payments, and giving loans to businesses.

INSURANCE
Insurance protects businesses against certain risks and losses, depending on the policy.

WAREHOUSING
Warehousing involves keeping goods safely until they are needed.

ADVERTISING
Advertising informs people about goods and services and encourages them to buy.

COMMUNICATION
Communication helps buyers, sellers, and other business people exchange information quickly.

TOURISM AND TRAVEL SERVICES
These services help people move from one place to another for business and other purposes, supporting commercial activities.

FUNCTIONS OF COMMERCE

  • It facilitates the exchange of goods and services.

  • It links producers and consumers.

  • It helps goods reach the people who need them.

  • It creates employment for traders and other workers.

  • It encourages specialisation and large-scale production.

  • It improves the standard of living by making goods available.

  • It generates income for individuals and businesses.

  • It promotes local and international trade.

  • It supports economic growth and development.

IMPORTANCE OF COMMERCE TO NIGERIA

  • It creates jobs for Nigerians.

  • It provides markets for locally produced goods.

  • It generates income for individuals and government through economic activities and taxes.

  • It encourages the development of roads, ports, banks, and communication systems.

  • It promotes trade between Nigeria and other countries.

  • It helps make goods from different parts of the country available to consumers.

  • It encourages entrepreneurship and investment.

DIFFERENCES BETWEEN TRADE AND COMMERCE

TRADE

  • Trade means buying and selling goods and services.

SS 2|First term|Mathematics.title: SIMULTENOUS LINEAR EQUATIONS
SS 2|First term|Mathematics.note:
Meaning of Simultaneous Linear Equations

Simultaneous linear equations are two or more linear equations that contain the same unknown quantities and are solved together to find values that satisfy all the equations.

A linear equation is an equation in which the highest power of the unknown is 1.

Examples:

\[ x+y=10 \]
\[ 2x+y=14 \]

These are simultaneous equations because they contain the same unknowns, \(x\) and \(y\).

The solution is the pair of values that makes both equations correct.

METHODS OF SOLVING SIMULTANEOUS EQUATIONS

The two common methods are:

  • Substitution method

  • Elimination method

SUBSTITUTION METHOD

The substitution method involves making one unknown the subject of one equation and substituting its value or expression into the other equation.

Example 1

Solve the equations:

\[ x+y=7 \qquad (1) \]
\[ x-y=3 \qquad (2) \]

Step 1: Make one unknown the subject.

From equation (1):

\[ x=7-y \]

Step 2: Substitute into equation (2).

\[ (7-y)-y=3 \]

Remove the brackets:

\[ 7-y-y=3 \]

Collect like terms:

\[ 7-2y=3 \]
\[ -2y=3-7 \]
\[ -2y=-4 \]

Divide both sides by \(-2\):

\[ y=\frac{-4}{-2}=2 \]

Step 3: Find the value of \(x\).

Substitute \(y=2\) into equation (1):

\[ x+2=7 \]
\[ x=7-2 \]
\[ x=5 \]

Answer:

\[ \boxed{x=5,\quad y=2} \]

ELIMINATION METHOD

The elimination method involves adding or subtracting equations to eliminate one unknown, making it possible to find the other unknown.

Example 2

Solve the equations:

\[ 2x+y=11 \qquad (1) \]
\[ x+y=7 \qquad (2) \]

Step 1: Arrange the equations.

\[ 2x+y=11 \]
\[ x+y=7 \]

Step 2: Subtract equation (2) from equation (1).

\[ (2x+y)-(x+y)=11-7 \]

Expand the brackets:

\[ 2x+y-x-y=4 \]

Collect like terms:

\[ x=4 \]

Step 3: Find the value of \(y\).

Substitute \(x=4\) into equation (2):

\[ 4+y=7 \]
\[ y=7-4 \]
\[ y=3 \]

Answer:

\[ \boxed{x=4,\quad y=3} \]

SOLVING BY ELIMINATION WHEN THE COEFFICIENTS ARE DIFFERENT

Sometimes, the coefficients of the unknowns are not equal. In such cases, multiply one or both equations by suitable numbers before adding or subtracting.

Example 3

Solve:

\[ 2x+3y=13 \qquad (1) \]
\[ 3x+2y=12 \qquad (2) \]

Step 1: Make the coefficients of \(y\) equal.

Multiply equation (1) by 2:

\[ 4x+6y=26 \qquad (3) \]

Multiply equation (2) by 3:

\[ 9x+6y=36 \qquad (4) \]

Step 2: Subtract equation (3) from equation (4).

\[ 9x-4x=36-26 \]
\[ 5x=10 \]
\[ x=\frac{10}{5}=2 \]

Step 3: Find \(y\).

Substitute \(x=2\) into equation (1):

\[ 2(2)+3y=13 \]
\[ 4+3y=13 \]
\[ 3y=13-4 \]
\[ 3y=9 \]
\[ y=3 \]

Answer:

\[ \boxed{x=2,\quad y=3} \]

WORD PROBLEMS INVOLVING SIMULTANEOUS EQUATIONS

Simultaneous equations can be used to solve everyday problems involving numbers, ages, prices and quantities.

Example 4

The sum of two numbers is 20, and their difference is 4. Find the numbers.

Step 1: Represent the unknowns.

Let the first number be \(x\) and the second number be \(y\).

From the question:

\[ x+y=20 \qquad (1) \]
\[ x-y=4 \qquad (2) \]

Step 2: Add the equations.

\[ (x+y)+(x-y)=20+4 \]
\[ 2x=24 \]
\[ x=12 \]

Step 3: Find the second number.

Substitute \(x=12\) into equation (1):

\[ 12+y=20 \]
\[ y=20-12 \]
\[ y=8 \]

Answer: The two numbers are 12 and 8.

CHECKING THE ANSWERS

After solving simultaneous equations, substitute the values obtained into the original equations to confirm that both equations are satisfied.

For example, if \(x=5\) and \(y=2\):

\[ x+y=5+2=7 \]
\[ x-y=5-2=3 \]

Both equations are correct.

CLASSWORK

SS 2|First term|Mathematics.title: FORMATION OF QUADRATIC EQUATIONS
SS 2|First term|Mathematics.note:
MEANING OF A QUADRATIC EQUATION

A quadratic equation is an equation in which the highest power of the unknown is 2.

The general form of a quadratic equation is:

\[ ax^2+bx+c=0 \]

Where:

  • \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are constants.

  • \(a\neq 0\).

  • \(x\) is the unknown.

Examples of quadratic equations are:

\[ x^2+5x+6=0 \]
\[ 2x^2-3x-2=0 \]

FORMATION OF QUADRATIC EQUATIONS FROM GIVEN ROOTS

The roots of a quadratic equation are the values of the unknown that satisfy the equation.

If the roots are \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), the quadratic equation is formed using:

\[ (x-\alpha)(x-\beta)=0 \]

Expanding gives:

\[ \boxed{x^2-(\alpha+\beta)x+\alpha\beta=0} \]

Therefore:

  • Sum of roots = \(\alpha+\beta\)

  • Product of roots = \(\alpha\beta\)

Example 1: Form a quadratic equation whose roots are 2 and 5.

Solution

Let the roots be 2 and 5.

Using the formula:

\[ (x-2)(x-5)=0 \]

Expand the brackets:

\[ x^2-5x-2x+10=0 \]

Collect like terms:

\[ \boxed{x^2-7x+10=0} \]

Example 2: Form a quadratic equation whose roots are −3 and 4.

Solution

\[ (x+3)(x-4)=0 \]

Expand:

\[ x^2-4x+3x-12=0 \]

Simplify:

\[ \boxed{x^2-x-12=0} \]

FORMATION USING THE SUM AND PRODUCT OF ROOTS

A quadratic equation can be formed when the sum and product of its roots are given.

The formula is:

\[ \boxed{x^2-Sx+P=0} \]

Where:

  • \(S\) = sum of the roots.

  • \(P\) = product of the roots.

Example 3: Form a quadratic equation whose roots have a sum of 7 and a product of 12.

Solution

Given:

Sum = 7

Product = 12

Substitute into the formula:

\[ x^2-Sx+P=0 \]
\[ x^2-7x+12=0 \]

Answer:

\[ \boxed{x^2-7x+12=0} \]

Example 4: Form a quadratic equation whose roots have a sum of −2 and a product of −15.

Solution

Given:

\(S=-2\), \(P=-15\)

Substitute:

\[ x^2-(-2)x+(-15)=0 \]

Simplify:

\[ \boxed{x^2+2x-15=0} \]

FORMATION FROM WORD PROBLEMS

Quadratic equations can be formed from problems involving numbers, ages, areas and other real-life situations.

The unknown quantity is represented by a letter, and the information in the question is translated into an equation.

Example 5: The product of two consecutive positive integers is 42. Form a quadratic equation to find the integers.

Solution

Let the first integer be \(x\).

The next consecutive integer is \(x+1\).

Their product is 42.

Therefore:

\[ x(x+1)=42 \]

Expand:

\[ x^2+x=42 \]

Bring all terms to one side:

\[ \boxed{x^2+x-42=0} \]

Example 6: The length of a rectangle is 3 cm more than its width. If its area is 40 cm², form a quadratic equation to find its dimensions.

Solution

Let the width be \(x\) cm.

Length = \(x+3\) cm.

Area of a rectangle = length × width.

Therefore:

\[ x(x+3)=40 \]

Expand:

\[ x^2+3x=40 \]

Bring all terms to one side:

\[ \boxed{x^2+3x-40=0} \]

IMPORTANT RULES TO REMEMBER

  • When roots are given, use \((x-\alpha)(x-\beta)=0\).

  • When the sum and product are given, use \(x^2-Sx+P=0\).

  • The coefficient of \(x^2\) is usually made positive.

  • Always expand brackets correctly.

  • Write the final equation in the form \(ax^2+bx+c=0\).

CLASSWORK

  1. The roots are 3 and 6.

  2. The roots are −2 and 5.

  3. The sum of the roots is 9 and the product is 20.

  4. The sum of the roots is −4 and the product is 3.

  5. The product of two consecutive positive integers is 72. Form a quadratic equation to represent the problem.

  4. The sum of the roots is −3 and their product is −10.

  5. The length of a rectangle is 5 cm more than its width. If its area is 84 cm², form a quadratic equation to represent the problem.

1. NOMINALIZATION OF ADJECTIVES AND VERBS

Meaning of Nominalization

Nominalization is the process of changing a verb or an adjective into a noun.

A noun is the name of a person, animal, place, thing or idea.

Nominalization of Adjectives

An adjective describes a noun. It can be changed into a noun by adding certain endings or by changing its form.

Examples:

Adjective

Noun

Happy

Happiness

Kind

Kindness

Weak

Weakness

Honest

Honesty

Beautiful

Beauty

Able

Ability

Dark

Darkness

Strong

Strength

Nominalization of Verbs

A verb expresses an action or state. Some verbs can be changed into nouns by adding endings such as -tion, -ment, -ance or -al.

Examples:

Verb

Noun

Educate

Education

Develop

Development

Perform

Performance

Arrive

Arrival

Inform

Information

Move

Movement

Decide

Decision

Improve

Improvement

Examples in Sentences

  • Her kindness made everyone happy.

  • The development of the school is important.

  • His honesty earned him respect.

  • The teacher praised our performance.

Importance of Nominalization

  • It helps us express ideas clearly.

  • It makes formal writing more effective.

  • It helps us form different types of words.

  • It improves our vocabulary.

2. ORAL ENGLISH: VOICED AND VOICELESS CONSONANT SOUNDS

Meaning of Consonant Sounds

Consonant sounds are speech sounds produced when air is blocked or restricted as it passes through the mouth.

Consonant sounds are divided into voiced and voiceless sounds.

Voiced Consonant Sounds

Voiced consonants are produced when the vocal cords vibrate during speech.

Examples:

/b/ as in boy

/d/ as in dog

/g/ as in go

/v/ as in van

/z/ as in zoo

/m/ as in man

/n/ as in net

/l/ as in leg

Voiceless Consonant Sounds

Voiceless consonants are produced without vibration of the vocal cords.

Examples:

/p/ as in pen

/t/ as in ten

/k/ as in kite

/f/ as in fan

/s/ as in sun

/h/ as in hat

/ʃ/ as in ship

/tʃ/ as in chair

How to Identify Voiced and Voiceless Sounds

Place your fingers gently on your throat and pronounce the sounds.

  • If you feel vibration, the sound is voiced.

  • If you do not feel vibration, the sound is voiceless.

Pairs of Voiced and Voiceless Sounds

Voiceless sound

Voiced sound

/p/ as in pin

/b/ as in bin

/t/ as in ten

/d/ as in den

/k/ as in cap

/g/ as in gap

/f/ as in fan

/v/ as in van

/s/ as in sip

/z/ as in zip

/θ/ as in thin

/ð/ as in this

3. SUMMARY WRITING

Meaning of Summary Writing

Summary writing is the act of reducing a passage to its main points using fewer words without changing the original meaning.

A summary contains only the important information in a passage.

Rules of Summary Writing

  • Read the passage carefully.

  • Identify the main ideas.

  • Remove unnecessary examples and repetitions.

  • Use your own words where possible.

  • Write only the required points.

  • Use clear and correct sentences.

  • Do not add your personal opinion.

  • Follow the required number of sentences or words.

Example

Original passage:

Many students fail their examinations because they do not study regularly. Some spend too much time watching television and using their phones. Students who prepare a timetable and follow it carefully are more likely to perform well in their examinations.

Summary:

Students perform better when they study regularly, avoid distractions and follow a study timetable.

Qualities of a Good Summary

  • It is brief.

  • It contains the main ideas.

  • It is written clearly.

  • It does not contain unnecessary details.

  • It preserves the meaning of the original passage.

4. VOCABULARY DEVELOPMENT

Meaning of Vocabulary Development

Vocabulary development is the process of learning new words and understanding how to use them correctly.

A good vocabulary helps students to speak, read and write effectively.

Importance of Vocabulary Development

SS 2|First term|English.title: CONSONANT CLUSTERS
SS 2|First term|English.note:
CONSONANT CLUSTERS

Meaning of Consonant Clusters

A consonant cluster is a group of two or more consonant sounds that occur together in a word without a vowel sound between them.

Examples:

  • Black — /bl/

  • Street — /str/

  • Plant — /pl/

  • School — /sk/

  • Spring — /spr/

A consonant cluster can occur at the beginning or at the end of a word.

Consonant Clusters at the Beginning of Words

These are consonant sounds that occur together at the beginning of a word.

Cluster

Examples

/bl/

Black, blue, blame

/br/

Bread, bring, brown

/st/

Stop, stand, stone

/str/

Street, strong, strange

/pl/

Plant, play, please

/spr/

Spring, spray, spread

/sk/

School, skin, skill

/tr/

Tree, train, travel

Consonant Clusters at the End of Words

These are consonant sounds that occur together at the end of a word.

Cluster

Examples

/nd/

Hand, land, send

/st/

Best, first, past

/mp/

Lamp, camp, jump

/ŋk/

Bank, thank, think

/ld/

Cold, field, child

/kt/

Act, fact, strict

/ft/

Left, gift, soft

Two-Consonant Clusters

These contain two consonant sounds together.

Examples: play, black, stop, hand, lamp.

Three-Consonant Clusters

These contain three consonant sounds together.

Examples: street, spring, splash, strong.

Four-Consonant Clusters

Examples: texts /ksts/ and sixths /ksθs/ in varieties of English where these pronunciations occur.

Five-Consonant Clusters

Five-consonant clusters are rare. They may occur in complex word endings, depending on the speaker's pronunciation.

Example: glimpsed may end with a cluster of several consonant sounds.

Importance of Consonant Clusters

  • They help students pronounce words correctly.

  • They improve oral communication.

  • They help students read unfamiliar words.

  • They improve spelling and listening skills.

VOCABULARY DEVELOPMENT: WORDS ASSOCIATED WITH THE HUMAN BODY SYSTEMS AND THEIR FUNCTIONS

COMPREHENSION: GAP-FILLING EXERCISE

Meaning of Comprehension

Comprehension is the ability to read or listen to a passage and understand its meaning.

A gap-filling exercise is a passage in which some words have been removed. The student must supply the correct words to complete the passage.

How to Answer Gap-Filling Questions

  • Read the entire passage first.

  • Look at the words before and after each gap.

  • Identify the type of word needed, such as a noun, verb, adjective or preposition.

  • Consider the meaning of the whole sentence.

  • Check that the completed sentence is grammatically correct.

  • Read the passage again after filling in the gaps.

Example

Complete the passage with the correct words.

Good health is important to every student. Students should eat a balanced (1) ______ and drink clean water. Regular exercise helps the body remain (2) ______. They should also get enough (3) ______ every night. Personal hygiene helps to prevent the spread of (4) ______. A healthy student is more likely to concentrate during (5) ______.

Answers

  1. Diet

  2. Fit

  3. Sleep

  4. Diseases

  5. Lessons

Tips for Success

  • Do not choose a word simply because it sounds familiar.

  • Pay attention to singular and plural forms.

  • Check the tense of the sentence.

  • Use context to determine the correct answer.

EXPOSITORY ESSAY WRITING

Meaning of Expository Essay

An expository essay is a type of essay that explains a subject or gives information about a topic in a clear and organised way.

Its main purpose is to explain, inform or describe how something works.

Features of an Expository Essay

  • It has a clear introduction.

  • It explains the topic with facts and relevant details.

  • It presents ideas in a logical order.

  • It uses clear and simple language.

  • It has a conclusion that summarises the main ideas.

Structure of an Expository Essay

Introduction

The introduction introduces the topic and tells the reader what the essay is about.

Body

The body contains paragraphs explaining the main points. Each paragraph should focus on one major idea.

Conclusion

The conclusion summarises the discussion and brings the essay to a proper end.

Example of an Expository Essay

Topic: How Students Can Maintain Good Health

Good health is important to every student because it helps students learn effectively and participate in school activities. Every student should develop healthy habits to remain physically and mentally fit.

First, students should eat balanced meals containing carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins, minerals and other essential nutrients. They should also drink clean water regularly to prevent dehydration.

Secondly, regular exercise helps to strengthen the body and improve fitness. Students can participate in activities such as walking, running, football and other sports.

Another important habit is personal hygiene. Students should bathe regularly, wash their hands before eating and keep their surroundings clean. These practices help to reduce the spread of diseases.

Finally, students should get enough sleep and rest. Adequate sleep helps the body recover and improves concentration in the classroom.

In conclusion, students can maintain good health by eating balanced meals, exercising regularly, practising personal hygiene and getting enough rest.

Other Examples of Expository Essay Topics

  • The importance of education.

  • Causes and effects of environmental pollution.

  • How to prevent the spread of communicable diseases.

  • The importance of regular exercise.

  • How students can manage their time effectively.

MEANING OF NOUNS

A noun is a word used to name a person, animal, place, thing or idea.

Examples:
Person: teacher, doctor, student.
Animal: goat, lion, dog.
Place: Lagos, school, market.
Thing: book, table, pen.
Idea: love, honesty, happiness.

TYPES OF NOUNS

Common Nouns
These are general names given to people, animals, places or things.
Examples: boy, girl, school, town, chair.

Proper Nouns
These are special names given to particular people, places or things. They begin with capital letters.
Examples: John, Lagos, Nigeria, Monday.

Collective Nouns
These are names given to groups of people, animals or things.
Examples: team, class, crowd, flock.

Abstract Nouns
These are names of qualities, feelings or ideas that cannot be touched physically.
Examples: kindness, honesty, wisdom, fear.

Concrete Nouns
These are nouns that name things we can experience through our senses.
Examples: stone, water, flower, bell.

Countable Nouns
These are nouns that can be counted.
Examples: one book, two pens, five chairs.

Uncountable Nouns
These are nouns that are not usually counted individually.
Examples: water, rice, sugar, information, advice.

MEANING OF A NOUN PHRASE

A noun phrase is a group of words that performs the function of a noun in a sentence. It usually has a noun as its main word.

Examples:
The intelligent student
A beautiful house
My English teacher
The tall boy in the classroom
Those new school bags

Sentences:
The intelligent student won the prize.
A beautiful house stood beside the road.
My English teacher explained the lesson.

PARTS OF A NOUN PHRASE

Determiner
A determiner comes before a noun to identify it.
Examples: a, an, the, this, that, my, some.

Modifier
A modifier gives more information about a noun.
Examples: tall, beautiful, intelligent, old.

Head Noun
The head noun is the main noun in a noun phrase.

Examples:
The tall boy — determiner: the; modifier: tall; head noun: boy.
My new book — determiner: my; modifier: new; head noun: book.
A beautiful girl — determiner: a; modifier: beautiful; head noun: girl.

Not every noun phrase contains all three parts. For example, “students” can function as a noun phrase on its own.

FUNCTIONS OF NOUN PHRASES

As the Subject
The subject tells us who or what performs an action or what the sentence is about.
Example: The young teacher entered the classroom.

As the Object
The object receives the action of the verb.
Example: The boy kicked the red ball.

As the Complement
A noun phrase can identify the subject after a linking verb.
Example: My father is a hardworking farmer.

As the Object of a Preposition
A noun phrase can follow a preposition such as in, on, under or beside.
Example: The book is on the wooden table.

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A NOUN PHRASE AND A NOUN CLAUSE

A noun phrase is a group of words that functions as a noun but does not contain a subject and verb forming a clause.
Examples: the clever boy, my new school, the beautiful woman.

A noun clause contains a subject and a verb and performs the function of a noun.
Examples:
What he said surprised me.
I know what you want.

In “What he said surprised me,” the words “What he said” form a noun clause and function as the subject of the sentence.

IMPORTANCE OF NOUNS AND NOUN PHRASES

They help us identify people, places, things and ideas.
They make sentences clearer and more meaningful.
They provide more information about people and things.
They improve speaking and writing skills.
They help us construct grammatically correct sentences.

CLASSWORK

2. Explain four types of nouns with two examples each.
3. What is a noun phrase? Give five examples.
4. Identify the noun phrase in this sentence: The hardworking student completed his assignment.
5. Explain the difference between a noun phrase and a noun clause, giving one example of each.

ASSIGNMENT

2. Identify the head noun in these phrases: the tall man, my new shoes, a beautiful house, those clever students.
3. State four functions of noun phrases and give one sentence for each.
4. Identify the noun phrase in these sentences:
   a. The little girl is crying.
   b. My English teacher is kind.
   c. We visited the new hospital.
   d. The books are on the wooden shelf.
   e. A group of students entered the hall.
5. Write five sentences containing noun phrases and underline the noun phrase in each sentence.

Comprehension is the ability to read a passage and understand its meaning. It involves identifying important information and answering questions based on what has been read.

  • It improves reading and understanding.

  • It helps students identify the main ideas in a passage.

  • It develops vocabulary.

  • It improves students' ability to answer examination questions.

  • It helps students understand written information.

Literal Questions

These questions ask for information directly stated in the passage.

Example: Where did the boy go?

Inferential Questions

These questions require students to use clues in a passage to understand information that is not directly stated.

Example: Why do you think the boy was afraid?

Vocabulary Questions

These questions ask for the meanings of words as used in a passage.

Example: What does the word exhausted mean as used in the passage?

Main Idea Questions

These questions ask students to identify the central message of a passage.

  • Read the passage carefully.

  • Identify the main points.

  • Read each question and understand what it requires.

  • Use information from the passage to answer.

  • Write clear and complete answers.

  • Avoid adding information that is not in the passage.

  • Check your answers before submitting.

Summary writing is the process of presenting the main ideas of a passage in a shorter form without changing the original meaning.

  • It is brief and clear.

  • It contains only the important points.

  • It avoids unnecessary examples and repetitions.

  • It does not contain personal opinions.

  • It uses correct grammar.

  • It maintains the original meaning of the passage.

  • Read the passage carefully.

  • Identify the important points.

  • Remove unnecessary details and repetitions.

  • Use your own words where possible.

  • Write only the required number of sentences or points.

  • Do not introduce ideas that are not in the passage.

  • Check your grammar and spelling.

Comprehension tests how well a reader understands a passage and answers questions about it.

Summary writing requires the reader to shorten a passage by presenting its main ideas in fewer words.

Vocabulary development is the process of learning new words, understanding their meanings and using them correctly in speech and writing.

Patient: A person receiving medical care.

Physician: A qualified medical doctor.

Nurse: A trained person who cares for sick people.

Diagnosis: The identification of a disease or medical condition.

Prescription: Instructions from a medical professional about the medicine a patient should take.

Treatment: The care given to a person to cure or manage an illness.

Vaccine: A substance that helps protect the body against a particular disease.

Infection: The invasion and multiplication of harmful microorganisms in the body.

Prevention: Action taken to stop something harmful from happening.

Hygiene: Practices that help maintain cleanliness and good health.

Emergency: A serious situation requiring immediate attention.

Pharmacy: A place where medicines are prepared or supplied.

Symptom: A sign of an illness experienced by a patient.

Recovery: The process of becoming healthy again after an illness.

Immunisation: The process of making a person resistant to certain diseases, usually through vaccination.

  • The patient visited the hospital for treatment.

  • The physician examined the patient.

  • The nurse cared for the sick child.

  • The doctor made a diagnosis after examining the patient.

  • The pharmacist supplied the prescribed medicine.

  • Good hygiene helps prevent the spread of infections.

  • Vaccination helps protect people against certain diseases.

  • The patient made a full recovery after treatment.

Good health is important to every individual. A healthy person can work, study and take part in daily activities without unnecessary difficulty. To maintain good health, people must eat balanced meals, drink clean water and exercise regularly.

Personal hygiene is also necessary for good health. People should wash their hands before eating and after using the toilet. They should keep their homes and surroundings clean to reduce the spread of diseases.

When people become sick, they should seek help from qualified medical professionals. Doctors examine patients, diagnose illnesses and recommend suitable treatment. Patients should follow medical instructions and avoid taking medicines without proper guidance.

In addition, communities should support health education and immunisation programmes. These measures help people understand how to prevent diseases and protect themselves and others.

Good health is not only the responsibility of medical workers. Every individual has a role to play by practising healthy habits and keeping the environment clean.

  • What is the importance of good health?

  • Mention three ways people can maintain good health.

  • Why should people wash their hands regularly?

  • What do doctors do when patients visit them?

  • State two ways communities can help prevent diseases.

Summarise the passage The Importance of Good Health in three sentences, explaining how individuals and communities can maintain good health.

  2. State four rules for answering comprehension questions.

  3. Explain summary writing and mention four features of a good summary.

SS 2|First term|English.title: ESSAY WRITING
SS 2|First term|English.note:
MEANING OF AN ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY

An argumentative essay is a type of essay in which the writer presents reasons to support or oppose a particular opinion or idea.

The aim is to convince the reader to agree with the writer's point of view.

Examples of argumentative essay topics:

  • Boarding schools are better than day schools.

  • Social media does more harm than good.

  • Education is more important than wealth.

  • Students should be allowed to use mobile phones in school.

FEATURES OF AN ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY

Clear Position

The writer must clearly state whether they agree or disagree with the topic.

Strong Arguments

The writer must give reasons to support their position.

Facts and Examples

The writer should use relevant facts and examples to support their arguments.

Logical Arrangement

Ideas should be arranged in a clear and sensible order.

Formal Language

The writer should use clear and respectful language.

Conclusion

The essay should end with a conclusion that restates the writer's position.

STRUCTURE OF AN ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY

INTRODUCTION

The introduction presents the topic and states the writer's position.

Example:

Education is an important part of human development. However, people have different opinions about whether boarding schools are better than day schools. I strongly believe that boarding schools offer several advantages over day schools.

BODY OF THE ESSAY

The body contains paragraphs explaining the writer's arguments.

Each paragraph should focus on one major point and support it with explanations or examples.

Useful expressions include:

  • Firstly

  • Secondly

  • Furthermore

  • In addition

  • For example

  • Moreover

  • Finally

CONCLUSION

The conclusion summarises the main arguments and restates the writer's position.

Useful expressions include:

  • In conclusion

  • To sum up

  • For these reasons

  • Therefore

HOW TO DEVELOP STRONG ARGUMENTS

A good argument should contain a point, an explanation and an example where necessary.

Point: Boarding schools encourage independence.

Explanation: Students learn to manage their time and take responsibility for their personal needs.

Example: A boarding student learns to organise study time and keep personal belongings in order.

This method makes an argument clearer and more convincing.

EXAMPLE OF AN ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY

TOPIC: BOARDING SCHOOLS ARE BETTER THAN DAY SCHOOLS

Education is important in the development of every child. There has been much discussion about whether boarding schools are better than day schools. In my opinion, boarding schools have several advantages over day schools.

Firstly, boarding schools provide students with more time to study. Since students live within the school environment, they can follow a regular timetable and attend supervised evening lessons. This can help them prepare better for examinations.

Secondly, boarding schools encourage independence and responsibility. Students learn to manage their time, organise their belongings and take care of their personal needs.

Furthermore, boarding schools allow students to interact with people from different backgrounds. This helps them develop friendships, cooperation and respect for others.

Another advantage is that students may experience fewer distractions from activities outside school. With proper supervision, they can concentrate more on their academic work.

However, day schools also have advantages. Students can spend more time with their families and receive personal care at home. Nevertheless, boarding schools can provide an organised learning environment for students who adapt well to boarding life.

In conclusion, I believe boarding schools are better than day schools because they encourage independence, provide structured study time and promote social development. However, the best choice depends on the needs of each student.

COMMON MISTAKES IN ARGUMENTATIVE ESSAY WRITING

  • Failing to state a clear position.

  • Giving arguments without explaining them.

  • Repeating the same point several times.

  • Using informal language.

  • Arranging ideas without a logical order.

  • Writing a conclusion that does not support the essay's position.

CONTINUOUS ASSESSMENT

Continuous assessment is the regular evaluation of students' learning throughout the school term.

It helps teachers determine whether students understand what they have been taught.

METHODS OF CONTINUOUS ASSESSMENT

Class Tests

Short tests given during lessons.

Assignments

Exercises completed by students outside classroom teaching.

Classwork

Questions answered during lessons.

Oral Assessment

Evaluation of students' speaking and reading skills.

Projects

Tasks that require students to research and present information.

IMPORTANCE OF CONTINUOUS ASSESSMENT

  • It helps teachers identify students' strengths and weaknesses.

  • It encourages students to study regularly.

  • It helps teachers improve their teaching methods.

  • It measures students' progress throughout the term.

  • It prepares students for major examinations.

CLASSWORK

  1. Define an argumentative essay.

  2. State five features of an argumentative essay.

  3. Explain the three main parts of an argumentative essay.

  4. Give three expressions used to introduce arguments and two expressions used to conclude an essay.

  5. Write an argumentative essay of about 200 words on the topic: Social Media Does More Harm Than Good.

ASSIGNMENT

  1. Explain the difference between an argumentative essay and an expository essay.

  2. State five common mistakes students make when writing argumentative essays.

  3. Explain how a writer can develop a strong argument.

  4. Write an argumentative essay of about 250 words on the topic: Students Should Be Allowed to Use Mobile Phones in School.

  5. Define continuous assessment and state four reasons why it is important in schools.

SS 2|First term|English.title: GRAMMER AND SPEECH
SS 2|First term|English.note:
RELATIVE PRONOUNS

MEANING OF RELATIVE PRONOUNS

Relative pronouns are words used to join sentences and give more information about a noun or pronoun.

Examples of relative pronouns are who, whom, whose, which, and that.

TYPES AND USES OF RELATIVE PRONOUNS

Who: Used when referring to people.

Example: The girl who won the prize is my sister.

Whom: Used to refer to a person who receives an action.

Example: The man whom I greeted is our teacher.

Whose: Used to show possession or ownership.

Example: The boy whose bag was missing is here.

Which: Used when referring to animals or things.

Example: This is the book which I bought yesterday.

That: Used to refer to people, animals, or things in certain sentences.

Example: The food that she cooked was delicious.

FUNCTIONS OF RELATIVE PRONOUNS

  • They join sentences together.

  • They provide more information about people, animals, or things.

  • They help to avoid unnecessary repetition.

Example:

Two sentences: The boy is my friend. The boy won the competition.

Joined sentence: The boy who won the competition is my friend.

PLURAL NOUNS

MEANING OF PLURAL NOUNS

A plural noun is a noun that refers to more than one person, animal, place, or thing.

Examples: boys, girls, books, chairs, and houses.

A singular noun refers to one person or thing, while a plural noun refers to more than one.

RULES FOR FORMING PLURAL NOUNS

Adding -s

Most nouns form their plurals by adding -s.

Examples:

  • Book — Books

  • Girl — Girls

  • Chair — Chairs

  • Table — Tables

Adding -es

Nouns ending in s, sh, ch, x, and some nouns ending in o often take -es.

Examples:

  • Bus — Buses

  • Brush — Brushes

  • Church — Churches

  • Box — Boxes

  • Tomato — Tomatoes

Changing -y to -ies

When a noun ends in a consonant followed by y, change y to ies.

Examples:

  • Baby — Babies

  • City — Cities

  • Lady — Ladies

When a noun ends in a vowel followed by y, simply add -s.

Examples:

  • Boy — Boys

  • Key — Keys

  • Toy — Toys

Changing -f or -fe to -ves

Some nouns ending in -f or -fe change to -ves.

Examples:

  • Leaf — Leaves

  • Wife — Wives

  • Knife — Knives

Not all nouns follow this rule. For example, roof becomes roofs.

Irregular plural nouns

Some nouns change their forms completely.

Singular

Plural

Man

Men

Woman

Women

Child

Children

Foot

Feet

Tooth

Teeth

Mouse

Mice

Person

People

Nouns with the same singular and plural forms

Some nouns do not change in the plural.

Examples:

  • Sheep — Sheep

  • Deer — Deer

  • Fish — Fish

UNSTRESSED VOWEL SOUNDS

MEANING OF STRESS IN SPEECH

Stress is the extra force used when pronouncing a syllable in a word.

A stressed syllable is pronounced more strongly, while an unstressed syllable is pronounced more weakly.

Example: In the word about, the second syllable receives more stress: a-BOUT.

THE SCHWA SOUND /ə/

The schwa sound is a common unstressed vowel sound in English. It is represented by the symbol /ə/.

It sounds like a short, weak “uh” sound.

Examples:

  • About — /əˈbaʊt/

  • Teacher — /ˈtiːtʃə/

  • Doctor — /ˈdɒktə/

  • Sofa — /ˈsəʊfə/

The schwa sound can be represented by different vowel letters, including a, e, o, and u, depending on the word.

FEATURES OF UNSTRESSED VOWEL SOUNDS

  • They are pronounced weakly.

  • They are usually shorter than stressed vowel sounds.

  • They often occur in unstressed syllables.

  • The schwa sound /ə/ is common in unstressed syllables.

IMPORTANCE OF LEARNING UNSTRESSED VOWEL SOUNDS

  • It improves pronunciation.

  • It helps students speak English more naturally.

  • It improves listening and understanding.

  • It helps students identify syllable stress in words.

CLASSWORK

  1. Define a relative pronoun and give four examples.

  2. Fill in the blank: The woman _____ teaches us English is kind.

  3. Write the plural forms of child, knife, city, box, and man.

  4. Explain the difference between singular and plural nouns.

  5. What is an unstressed vowel sound? Give three examples of words containing the schwa sound /ə/.

ASSIGNMENT

  2. Write the plural forms of woman, tooth, baby, church, sheep, and leaf.

  3. State five rules for forming plural nouns and give two examples for each.

  5. Join each pair of sentences using a suitable relative pronoun:

    • The girl is my cousin. The girl lives in Lagos.

    • I bought a phone. The phone is expensive.

    • The man is a doctor. His car was stolen.

SS 2|First term|English.title: ADJECTIVES, ADVERBS AND EXPOSITORY ESSAY
SS 2|First term|English.note:
MEANING OF ADJECTIVES

An adjective is a word that describes a noun or pronoun. It tells us more about a person, animal, place or thing.

Examples:

  • The beautiful girl is singing.

  • I have a red bag.

  • He is a tall boy.

  • She bought five oranges.

The words beautiful, red, tall, and five are adjectives.

TYPES OF ADJECTIVES

Descriptive Adjectives

These describe the qualities of a person or thing.

Examples: beautiful, tall, short, clever, honest, big.

Sentence: The clever boy answered the question.

Adjectives of Quantity

These tell us the amount of something.

Examples: some, much, little, enough.

Sentence: There is some water in the cup.

Adjectives of Number

These tell us the number or order of people or things.

Examples: one, two, many, first, second.

Sentence: She came first in the competition.

Demonstrative Adjectives

These point out specific people or things.

Examples: this, that, these, those.

Sentence: Those students are hardworking.

Possessive Adjectives

These show ownership.

Examples: my, your, his, her, its, our, their.

Sentence: My teacher is kind.

Interrogative Adjectives

These are used to ask questions about nouns.

Examples: which, what, whose.

Sentences:

  • Which book do you want?

  • Whose bag is this?

DEGREES OF COMPARISON

Adjectives can compare people or things in three ways.

Positive Degree: Describes one person or thing.

Example: John is tall.

Comparative Degree: Compares two people or things. We often add -er or use more.

Example: John is taller than Peter.

Superlative Degree: Compares three or more people or things. We often add -est or use most.

Example: John is the tallest boy in the class.

More examples:

Positive

Comparative

Superlative

Tall

Taller

Tallest

Big

Bigger

Biggest

Small

Smaller

Smallest

Beautiful

More beautiful

Most beautiful

Good

Better

Bad

Worse

Worst

FUNCTIONS OF ADJECTIVES

Adjectives help us to:

  • Describe people and things.

  • Show the colour, size or shape of something.

  • Tell us the number or quantity of things.

  • Compare people or things.

  • Make sentences more meaningful.

CLASSWORK

Identify the adjectives in these sentences.

  • The fat man entered the room.

  • I bought three pencils.

  • Her dress is beautiful.

  • Those boys are playing football.

  • This is my book.

ASSIGNMENT

  • Define an adjective.

  • State five types of adjectives.

  • Give five examples of descriptive adjectives.

  • State the three degrees of comparison.

  • Use the words good, tall, and beautiful to show the degrees of comparison.

TOPIC: ADVERBS

MEANING OF ADVERBS

An adverb is a word that describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb.

An adverb can tell us how, when, where or how often something happens.

Examples:

  • She sings beautifully.

  • He arrived yesterday.

  • The children are playing outside.

  • I always read my books.

The words beautifully, yesterday, outside, and always are adverbs.

TYPES OF ADVERBS

Adverbs of Manner

These tell us how an action is performed.

Examples: slowly, quickly, carefully, beautifully.

Sentence: The girl writes neatly.

Adverbs of Time

These tell us when an action happens.

Examples: yesterday, today, tomorrow, soon, now.

Sentence: We shall travel tomorrow.

Adverbs of Place

These tell us where an action happens.

Examples: here, there, outside, inside, everywhere.

Sentence: The children are waiting outside.

Adverbs of Frequency

These tell us how often an action happens.

Examples: always, often, sometimes, rarely, never.

Sentence: She always comes to school early.

Adverbs of Degree

These tell us the level or extent of an action or quality.

Examples: very, too, quite, extremely, almost.

Sentences:

  • The water is very cold.

  • He is too weak to walk.

FORMATION OF ADVERBS

Many adverbs are formed by adding -ly to adjectives.

Adjective

Adverb

Quick

Quickly

Slow

Slowly

Careful

Carefully

Beautiful

Beautifully

Happy

Happily

Easy

Easily

However, not all adverbs end in -ly.

Examples: fast, well, hard, late.

Sentences:

  • He runs fast.

  • She sings well.

  • They worked hard.

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN ADJECTIVES AND ADVERBS

An adjective describes a noun or pronoun, while an adverb describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb.

Examples:

  • She is a careful driver. (Careful describes the noun driver.)

  • She drives carefully. (Carefully describes the verb drives.)

Another example:

  • He is a slow runner.

  • He runs slowly.

CLASSWORK

Identify the adverbs in these sentences.

  • The boy ran quickly.

  • We shall meet tomorrow.

  • The children are playing outside.

  • She always helps her mother.

  • The food is very hot.

ASSIGNMENT

  • Define an adverb.

  • State five types of adverbs.

  • Give five examples of adverbs of manner.

  • Explain the difference between an adjective and an adverb.

  • Write five sentences containing different types of adverbs.

TOPIC: EXPOSITORY ESSAY

MEANING OF EXPOSITORY ESSAY

An expository essay is a type of essay that explains a topic clearly and gives information to help readers understand it.

The purpose is to explain, inform or describe how something works. It is not mainly written to tell a fictional story.

Examples of expository essay topics include:

  • The Importance of Education

  • Causes of Drug Abuse

  • How to Keep Our Environment Clean

  • The Effects of Examination Malpractice

  • The Importance of Good Health

FEATURES OF AN EXPOSITORY ESSAY

Clear Introduction

The introduction presents the topic and tells the reader what the essay is about.

Body Paragraphs

These contain the main explanations, facts, reasons and examples about the topic.

Conclusion

The conclusion summarises the main points and brings the essay to a proper end.

Simple and Clear Language

The writer uses understandable words and sentences to explain the topic.

Facts and Examples

The essay uses relevant facts and examples to make the explanation clearer.

STRUCTURE OF AN EXPOSITORY ESSAY

An expository essay has three main parts.

Introduction

Introduce the topic and explain its meaning.

Body

Explain the main points in separate paragraphs. Each paragraph should focus on one important idea.

Conclusion

Summarise the main ideas and provide a final statement about the topic.

STEPS IN WRITING AN EXPOSITORY ESSAY

  • Understand the topic.

  • Identify the main points you want to explain.

  • Arrange your points in a logical order.

  • Write an introduction.

  • Explain each point in the body paragraphs.

  • End with a conclusion.

  • Check your spelling, grammar and punctuation.

SAMPLE EXPOSITORY ESSAY

THE IMPORTANCE OF EDUCATION

Education is the process of acquiring knowledge, skills and good character. It helps people to understand the world around them and prepares them for the future. Education is important to individuals and society.

Firstly, education helps people to read and write. A person who can read and write can understand books, newspapers, instructions and other important information. This makes everyday life easier.

Secondly, education helps people to develop useful skills. Students learn different subjects that prepare them for future careers. For example, a person who studies medicine may become a doctor, while someone who studies teaching may become a teacher.

Furthermore, education helps to reduce ignorance and poverty. Educated people can make better decisions, identify opportunities and contribute to the development of their communities.

Education also teaches discipline, responsibility and cooperation. In school, students learn to obey rules, respect others and work together to achieve common goals.

In conclusion, education is very important because it provides knowledge, develops skills and prepares people for a better future. Therefore, every child should have the opportunity to receive a good education.

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN EXPOSITORY AND NARRATIVE ESSAYS

Expository Essay

Narrative Essay

Explains a topic.

Tells a story.

Gives facts and information.

Describes events and experiences.

Focuses on explaining ideas.

Focuses on what happened.

Example: The Importance of Education.

Example: My First Day at School.

CLASSWORK

  • Define an expository essay.

  • State the three main parts of an expository essay.

  • Mention four features of an expository essay.

  • Give three examples of expository essay topics.

  • Write an expository essay on The Importance of Keeping Our School Clean.

ASSIGNMENT

  • Explain the meaning of an expository essay.

  • State five steps involved in writing an expository essay.

  • Explain the functions of the introduction, body and conclusion.

  • State three differences between expository and narrative essays.

  • Write an expository essay of at least 200 words on The Causes and Effects of Drug Abuse Among Students.

SS 2|First term|Account.title: TRADING PROFIT AND LOSS ACCOUNT
SS 2|First term|Account.note:
MEANING OF TRADING, PROFIT AND LOSS ACCOUNT

A Trading, Profit and Loss Account is a financial statement prepared by a business to determine its gross profit or gross loss and net profit or net loss over a particular period.

It is usually prepared at the end of an accounting period, such as a month or a year.

The account has two main sections:

  • Trading Account: Used to calculate gross profit or gross loss.

  • Profit and Loss Account: Used to calculate net profit or net loss.

MEANING OF GROSS PROFIT AND GROSS LOSS

Gross Profit

Gross profit is the excess of net sales over the cost of goods sold.

\[ \text{Gross Profit}=\text{Net Sales}-\text{Cost of Goods Sold} \]

Gross Loss

Gross loss occurs when the cost of goods sold is greater than net sales.

\[ \text{Gross Loss}=\text{Cost of Goods Sold}-\text{Net Sales} \]

MEANING OF NET PROFIT AND NET LOSS

Net Profit

Net profit is the amount remaining after all business expenses have been deducted from gross profit, taking other incomes into account.

\[ \text{Net Profit}=\text{Gross Profit}+\text{Other Income}-\text{Expenses} \]

Net Loss

Net loss occurs when total expenses exceed gross profit plus other income.

ITEMS FOUND IN THE TRADING ACCOUNT

Opening Stock

This is the value of goods available for sale at the beginning of the accounting period.

Purchases

These are goods bought for resale during the accounting period.

Returns Outwards

These are goods returned to suppliers. They are deducted from purchases.

Carriage Inwards

This is the cost of transporting purchased goods to the business premises. It is added to the cost of purchases.

Closing Stock

This is the value of goods remaining unsold at the end of the accounting period.

Sales

These are goods sold to customers during the accounting period.

Returns Inwards

These are goods returned by customers. They are deducted from sales.

CALCULATION OF NET SALES

Net sales are calculated by deducting returns inwards from total sales.

\[ \text{Net Sales}=\text{Sales}-\text{Returns Inwards} \]

Example:

Sales = ₦500,000

Returns inwards = ₦20,000

\[ \text{Net Sales}=500,000-20,000 \]
\[ \boxed{\text{Net Sales}=₦480,000} \]

CALCULATION OF NET PURCHASES

Net purchases are calculated by deducting returns outwards from total purchases.

\[ \text{Net Purchases}=\text{Purchases}-\text{Returns Outwards} \]

Example:

Purchases = ₦300,000

Returns outwards = ₦15,000

\[ \text{Net Purchases}=300,000-15,000 \]
\[ \boxed{\text{Net Purchases}=₦285,000} \]

CALCULATION OF COST OF GOODS SOLD

Cost of goods sold is the total cost of goods that were sold during the accounting period.

The formula is:

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{Cost of Goods Sold}={}&\text{Opening Stock}\\ &+\text{Net Purchases}\\ &+\text{Carriage Inwards}\\ &-\text{Closing Stock} \end{aligned} \]

Example

Opening stock = ₦80,000

Purchases = ₦250,000

Returns outwards = ₦10,000

Carriage inwards = ₦5,000

Closing stock = ₦60,000

Solution:

Net purchases:

\[ 250,000-10,000=₦240,000 \]

Cost of goods sold:

\[ 80,000+240,000+5,000-60,000 \]
\[ \boxed{\text{Cost of Goods Sold}=₦265,000} \]

SS 2|First term|Chemistry.title: ELECTRODE POTENTIAL
SS 2|First term|Chemistry.note:
Meaning of Electrode Potential

Electrode potential is the tendency of an electrode to lose or gain electrons when it is placed in a solution containing its ions.

An electrode is a conductor, usually a metal or graphite, through which electric current enters or leaves an electrolyte.

Electrode potential develops when an electrode is placed in contact with an electrolyte due to the transfer of electrons between the electrode and the ions in the solution.

Types of Electrode Potential

Oxidation Potential

This is the tendency of an electrode to lose electrons and form positive ions.

Example:

\[ \mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-} \]

Zinc loses two electrons to form zinc ions.

Reduction Potential

This is the tendency of an electrode to gain electrons or accept electrons from another substance.

Example:

\[ \mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu} \]

Copper ions gain two electrons to form copper metal.

Standard Electrode Potential

Standard electrode potential is the potential difference of an electrode measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode under standard conditions.

The standard conditions are:

  • Temperature: 25°C or 298 K.

  • Concentration of solution: 1 mol/dm³.

  • Gas pressure: 1 atmosphere (approximately 100 kPa).

Standard electrode potential is represented by \(E^\circ\) and measured in volts (V).

The Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE)

The standard hydrogen electrode is used as the reference electrode for measuring the electrode potentials of other electrodes.

Its standard electrode potential is defined as:

\[ E^\circ = 0.00\text{ V} \]

It consists of a platinum electrode in contact with a solution containing hydrogen ions, while hydrogen gas is passed over the platinum surface.

The half-cell reaction is:

\[ \mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons H_2} \]

The Electrochemical Series

The electrochemical series is a list of elements or electrodes arranged according to their standard reduction potentials.

Examples of standard reduction potentials are shown below.

Electrode reaction

Standard potential (V)

Li⁺ + e⁻ → Li

−3.04

Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn

−0.76

Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Fe

−0.44

2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂

0.00

Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu

+0.34

Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag

+0.80

These are approximate standard reduction potential values.

Importance of the Electrochemical Series

  • It helps predict which substances can act as oxidizing or reducing agents.

  • It helps predict whether a redox reaction is feasible under standard conditions.

  • It helps determine the direction of electron flow in an electrochemical cell.

  • It helps calculate the standard electromotive force (EMF) of a cell.

  • It helps compare the tendencies of metals to lose electrons.

Electrochemical Cells

An electrochemical cell is a device in which chemical energy is converted into electrical energy through a spontaneous redox reaction.

A simple cell consists of two electrodes connected by an external wire and electrolytes connected by a salt bridge.

Example: Zinc–Copper Cell

The zinc electrode loses electrons:

\[ \mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-} \]

The copper ions gain electrons:

\[ \mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu} \]

Overall reaction:

\[ \mathrm{Zn + Cu^{2+} \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + Cu} \]

Electrons flow through the external wire from zinc to copper.

Calculation of Standard Cell Potential

The standard cell potential is calculated using:

\[ E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}} \]

Where:

  • \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}}\) = standard cell potential.

  • \(E^\circ_{\text{cathode}}\) = standard reduction potential of the cathode.

  • \(E^\circ_{\text{anode}}\) = standard reduction potential of the anode.

Example

Calculate the standard cell potential of a zinc–copper cell.

Given:

  • Copper: \(+0.34\text{ V}\)

  • Zinc: \(-0.76\text{ V}\)

Solution:

\[ E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=0.34-(-0.76) \]
\[ E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=0.34+0.76 \]
\[ \boxed{E^\circ_{\text{cell}}=+1.10\text{ V}} \]

Therefore, the standard cell potential is +1.10 V.

A positive standard cell potential indicates that the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.

Difference Between Electrode Potential and Cell Potential

Electrode potential

Cell potential

Refers to the potential of one electrode relative to a reference electrode.

Refers to the potential difference between two electrodes.

It is measured relative to a reference electrode, such as the SHE.

It is calculated from the potentials of the two half-cells.

It describes the tendency for oxidation or reduction at an electrode.

It indicates the driving force for the overall cell reaction.

SS 2|First term|Biology.title: DIGESTIVE SYSTEM I
SS 2|First term|Biology.note:
The digestive system is the group of organs in the body that work together to break down food into simple substances that the body can absorb and use.

Food contains nutrients that provide energy, help the body grow, and repair damaged tissues. However, most food substances are too large to be absorbed directly into the blood. Digestion breaks them down into smaller, soluble substances.

Digestion is the process by which large, complex food substances are broken down into smaller, simple, soluble substances that can be absorbed by the body.

For example, starch is broken down into simple sugars, while proteins are broken down into amino acids.

There are two main types of digestion.

Mechanical digestion

This is the physical breakdown of food into smaller pieces without changing its chemical composition.

Examples:

  • Chewing food with the teeth.

  • Churning of food in the stomach.

  • Mixing food with digestive juices.

Chemical digestion

This is the breakdown of complex food substances into simpler substances through the action of enzymes.

Examples:

  • Starch is broken down into simpler sugars by amylase.

  • Proteins are broken down into smaller peptides and amino acids by proteases.

The human digestive system consists of the alimentary canal and the associated digestive organs.

The alimentary canal

The alimentary canal is a long tube through which food passes from the mouth to the anus.

Its main parts are:

  • Mouth

  • Pharynx

  • Oesophagus

  • Stomach

  • Small intestine

  • Large intestine

  • Rectum

  • Anus

Associated digestive organs

These organs produce or store substances that help digestion.

They include:

  • Salivary glands

  • Liver

  • Gall bladder

  • Pancreas

Mouth

The mouth is where digestion begins.

Functions:

  • Receives food.

  • Teeth cut and grind food into smaller pieces.

  • The tongue mixes food with saliva.

  • Saliva moistens food and makes swallowing easier.

  • Salivary amylase begins the digestion of starch.

Pharynx

The pharynx is the passage that carries swallowed food from the mouth towards the oesophagus.

Oesophagus

The oesophagus is a muscular tube that carries food from the pharynx to the stomach.

Food moves through it by a process called peristalsis.

Peristalsis is the wave-like contraction and relaxation of muscles that pushes food along the digestive tract.

Stomach

The stomach is a muscular, bag-like organ that temporarily stores food.

Functions:

  • Churns and mixes food.

  • Produces hydrochloric acid.

  • Provides a suitable acidic medium for the action of pepsin.

  • Begins the digestion of proteins.

  • Helps kill many harmful microorganisms swallowed with food.

Small intestine

The small intestine is the main site of chemical digestion and absorption of digested nutrients.

Functions:

  • Completes the digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

  • Receives bile from the liver through the bile duct.

  • Receives pancreatic juice from the pancreas.

  • Absorbs digested nutrients into the blood and lymph.

Large intestine

The large intestine receives undigested food materials from the small intestine.

Functions:

  • Absorbs water and mineral salts.

  • Helps form faeces.

  • Contains bacteria that act on some undigested materials.

Rectum

The rectum temporarily stores faeces before they are removed from the body.

Anus

The anus is the opening through which faeces leave the body. This process is called egestion or defaecation.

  • The digestive system breaks down food into substances the body can absorb.

  • Mechanical digestion involves physical breakdown of food.

  • Chemical digestion involves enzymes.

  • The alimentary canal extends from the mouth to the anus.

  • The small intestine is the major site of digestion and nutrient absorption.

  • The large intestine absorbs water and helps form faeces.

  5. State four functions of the stomach.

SS 2|First term|Biology.title: DIGESTIVE SYSTEM II
SS 2|First term|Biology.note:
Digestive juices are liquids produced by different organs of the digestive system. They contain substances, including enzymes, that help break down food.

The main digestive juices are saliva, gastric juice, pancreatic juice and intestinal juice. Bile also helps digestion, although it does not contain digestive enzymes.

Digestive enzymes are special proteins that speed up the breakdown of food into simpler substances.

Different enzymes act on different food substances.

Saliva

Saliva is produced by the salivary glands in the mouth.

Functions:

  • Moistens food.

  • Makes swallowing easier.

  • Contains salivary amylase, which begins the digestion of starch.

Gastric juice

Gastric juice is produced by glands in the stomach.

It contains hydrochloric acid and enzymes such as pepsin.

Functions:

  • Hydrochloric acid provides the acidic condition needed for pepsin to work.

  • Hydrochloric acid helps kill many microorganisms.

  • Pepsin begins the digestion of proteins into smaller peptides.

Pancreatic juice

Pancreatic juice is produced by the pancreas and released into the small intestine.

It contains enzymes that digest carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

Examples:

  • Pancreatic amylase digests starch.

  • Trypsin digests proteins and peptides.

  • Pancreatic lipase digests fats into fatty acids and monoglycerides.

Intestinal juice

Intestinal juice is produced by glands in the small intestine.

Its enzymes complete the digestion of food.

Examples:

  • Maltase breaks maltose into glucose.

  • Sucrase breaks sucrose into glucose and fructose.

  • Lactase breaks lactose into glucose and galactose.

  • Peptidases break small peptides into amino acids.

Bile is a yellowish-green digestive fluid produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

Bile does not contain digestive enzymes.

Functions of bile:

  • Emulsifies fats by breaking large fat globules into smaller droplets.

  • Helps neutralise the acidic food coming from the stomach.

  • Provides a more suitable alkaline condition for enzymes acting in the small intestine.

Emulsification increases the surface area of fats, making it easier for lipase to digest them.

Absorption is the movement of digested, soluble food substances through the wall of the digestive tract into the blood or lymph.

Most absorption takes place in the small intestine.

Adaptations of the small intestine for absorption

The small intestine is well suited for absorption because:

  • It is long, providing enough time and space for absorption.

  • Its inner surface has many tiny finger-like projections called villi.

  • Each villus has tiny projections called microvilli, which further increase the surface area.

  • The walls of the villi are thin, allowing nutrients to pass through easily.

  • Each villus contains blood capillaries that absorb glucose, amino acids and other water-soluble nutrients.

  • Each villus contains a lymph vessel called a lacteal, which absorbs most products of fat digestion.

Fate of absorbed food

  • Glucose is used for energy or stored as glycogen.

  • Amino acids are used for growth and tissue repair.

  • Fatty acids and other fat digestion products are used to build fats and cell structures or stored for later use.

  • Vitamins, mineral salts and water are used for various body functions.

Assimilation is the process by which absorbed nutrients are used by body cells.

Examples:

  • Glucose is used in respiration to release energy.

  • Amino acids are used to make new proteins for growth and repair.

  • Excess glucose may be stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles.

Egestion is the removal of undigested and unabsorbed food materials from the body through the anus as faeces.

Egestion is different from excretion. Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste products, such as urea and carbon dioxide.

Constipation: Difficulty passing faeces, often associated with hard stools.

Diarrhoea: Frequent passage of loose or watery faeces.

Peptic ulcer: A sore in the lining of the stomach or upper small intestine.

Indigestion: Discomfort associated with the digestion of food.

Tooth decay: Damage to the teeth caused by acids produced by bacteria acting on sugars in the mouth.

  • Eat a balanced diet.

  • Drink enough clean water.

  • Eat fruits and vegetables rich in fibre.

  • Wash hands before eating and after using the toilet.

  • Wash fruits and vegetables properly.

  • Chew food properly.

  • Maintain good oral hygiene.

  • Avoid eating contaminated food.

  • Exercise regularly.

SS 2|First term|Biology.title: TRANSPORT SYSTEM I
SS 2|First term|Biology.note:
BIOLOGY NOTE FOR SS2

TRANSPORT SYSTEM — PART ONE

MEANING OF TRANSPORT SYSTEM

The transport system is the system that moves substances such as water, food, oxygen and waste products from one part of a living organism to another.

The transport system is important because every living cell needs materials for growth, respiration and survival.

TRANSPORT SYSTEM IN PLANTS

Plants need water and mineral salts from the soil. They also manufacture food in their leaves. These substances must be transported to different parts of the plant.

The two main transport tissues in plants are xylem and phloem.

XYLEM

Xylem is the tissue that transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the stem and leaves.

Functions of xylem

  • Transports water from the roots to the leaves.

  • Transports mineral salts.

  • Provides support for the plant.

PHLOEM

Phloem is the tissue that transports manufactured food from the leaves to other parts of the plant.

Functions of phloem

  • Transports food to the roots.

  • Supplies food to growing parts of the plant.

  • Carries food to fruits and storage organs.

DIFFERENCES BETWEEN XYLEM AND PHLOEM

XylemPhloem
Transports water and mineral salts.Transports manufactured food.
Movement is mainly upwards from the roots.Movement can occur in different directions.
Most conducting cells are dead at maturity.The main conducting cells are living.
Provides support for the plant.Mainly transports food.

MOVEMENT OF WATER IN PLANTS

Root pressure

Root pressure is the pressure produced when water enters the roots. It helps push water upwards through the xylem.

Capillary action

Capillary action is the movement of water through narrow tubes. It helps water move through the narrow xylem vessels.

Transpiration pull

Transpiration pull is the force that draws water upwards when water evaporates from the leaves.

TRANSPIRATION

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata in the leaves.

Importance of transpiration

  • Helps pull water from the roots to the leaves.

  • Helps transport mineral salts.

  • Cools the plant.

  • Maintains the movement of water through the plant.

TRANSLOCATION

Translocation is the movement of manufactured food from one part of a plant to another through the phloem.

For example, food made in the leaves can be transported to the roots for storage.

TRANSPORT SYSTEM IN ANIMALS

Animals need a transport system to carry oxygen and digested food to their cells and remove waste products.

In humans, the transport system consists of the heart, blood and blood vessels.

THE HEART

The heart is a muscular organ that pumps blood around the body.

The human heart has four chambers.

Right atrium: Receives oxygen-poor blood from the body.

Right ventricle: Pumps oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.

Left atrium: Receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs.

Left ventricle: Pumps oxygen-rich blood to the rest of the body.

Valves: Prevent blood from flowing backwards.

Septum: Separates the right and left sides of the heart.

BLOOD VESSELS

Blood vessels are tubes through which blood moves around the body.

There are three main types of blood vessels.

Arteries

Arteries carry blood away from the heart.

Characteristics of arteries:

  • They have thick, strong and elastic walls.

  • Blood flows through them under high pressure.

  • They generally do not have valves along their length.

Most arteries carry oxygen-rich blood, but the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood to the lungs.

Veins

Veins carry blood towards the heart.

Characteristics of veins:

  • They have thinner walls than arteries.

  • They have a wider internal space.

  • They usually contain valves.

  • Blood flows through them under low pressure.

Most veins carry oxygen-poor blood, but the pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the heart.

Capillaries

Capillaries are very tiny blood vessels that connect small arteries to small veins.

Characteristics of capillaries:

  • Their walls are one cell thick.

  • They allow the exchange of oxygen, nutrients and waste products.

  • They are found throughout the body.
