SS 2|First term|Biology.title: TRANSPORT SYSTEM II
SS 2|First term|Biology.note:
BIOLOGY NOTE FOR SS2

TRANSPORT SYSTEM — PART TWO

BLOOD AND ITS COMPONENTS

Blood is a fluid connective tissue that transports substances around the body.

Blood has four main components: plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

PLASMA

Plasma is the pale-yellow liquid part of blood.

Functions of plasma

  • Transports digested food.

  • Carries hormones.

  • Transports waste products such as urea.

  • Distributes heat around the body.

  • Carries dissolved substances.

RED BLOOD CELLS

Red blood cells contain a red pigment called haemoglobin, which carries oxygen.

Functions of red blood cells

  • Transport oxygen from the lungs to body tissues.

  • Help transport some carbon dioxide from body tissues.

WHITE BLOOD CELLS

White blood cells protect the body against diseases.

Functions of white blood cells

  • Destroy harmful microorganisms.

  • Produce antibodies through certain types of white blood cells.

  • Protect the body against infections.

PLATELETS

Platelets are small cell fragments found in blood.

Function of platelets

Platelets help blood to clot when a blood vessel is damaged. This prevents excessive bleeding.

TYPES OF CIRCULATION IN HUMANS

Pulmonary circulation

Pulmonary circulation is the movement of blood from the heart to the lungs and back to the heart.

Pathway:

Right ventricle → Pulmonary artery → Lungs → Pulmonary veins → Left atrium.

In the lungs, blood releases carbon dioxide and receives oxygen.

Systemic circulation

Systemic circulation is the movement of blood from the heart to the rest of the body and back to the heart.

Pathway:

Left ventricle → Aorta → Body tissues → Venae cavae → Right atrium.

In the body tissues, blood supplies oxygen and nutrients and collects waste products.

DOUBLE CIRCULATION

Double circulation is a type of circulation in which blood passes through the heart twice during one complete journey around the body.

It consists of pulmonary circulation and systemic circulation.

Advantages of double circulation

  • Supplies oxygen efficiently to body cells.

  • Prevents the direct mixing of oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood.

  • Allows blood to be pumped to the body at relatively high pressure.

  • Supports the high energy needs of humans.

THE LYMPHATIC SYSTEM

The lymphatic system is a network of vessels and organs that transports lymph around the body.

Lymph is a fluid formed from tissue fluid.

Functions of the lymphatic system

  • Returns excess tissue fluid to the bloodstream.

  • Transports most products of fat digestion from the small intestine.

  • Helps protect the body against infections.

IMPORTANCE OF THE TRANSPORT SYSTEM

The transport system is important because it:

  • Supplies oxygen to body cells.

  • Carries digested food to different parts of the body.

  • Transports hormones to target organs.

  • Removes waste products from cells.

  • Distributes heat around the body.

  • Transports water and mineral salts in plants.

  • Distributes manufactured food in plants.

  • Helps protect the body against infections.

CLASSWORK

Answer the following questions.

  1. List the four main components of blood.

  2. State three functions of plasma.

  3. Differentiate between pulmonary circulation and systemic circulation.

  4. What is double circulation? State two advantages.

  5. State three functions of the lymphatic system.

ASSIGNMENT

  1. Explain the functions of red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

  2. Describe the pathway of blood during pulmonary circulation.

  3. Describe the pathway of blood during systemic circulation.

  4. State four advantages of double circulation in humans.

  5. Explain five ways the transport system supports life in plants and animals.

SS 2|First term|Biology.title: RESPIRATORY SYSTEM I
SS 2|First term|Biology.note:
MEANING OF RESPIRATORY SYSTEM

The respiratory system is the system responsible for taking oxygen into the body and removing carbon dioxide from the body.

Oxygen is needed by body cells to release energy from food during respiration.

MEANING OF RESPIRATION

Respiration is the process by which living cells break down food substances to release energy.

There are two main types of respiration.

AEROBIC RESPIRATION

Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen to release energy.

Word equation:

Glucose + Oxygen → Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy

ANAEROBIC RESPIRATION

Anaerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose to release energy without using oxygen.

In human muscles, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid.

Word equation:

Glucose → Lactic acid + Energy

In yeast, anaerobic respiration produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN BREATHING AND RESPIRATION

Breathing: This is the physical process of taking air into and pushing air out of the lungs.

Respiration: This is the chemical process by which cells release energy from food.

PARTS OF THE HUMAN RESPIRATORY SYSTEM

The main parts of the human respiratory system are the nostrils, nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli and lungs.

NOSTRILS AND NASAL CAVITY

The nostrils are the openings through which air enters and leaves the nose.

The nasal cavity is the space inside the nose.

Functions

  • Allow air to enter the respiratory system.

  • Filter dust and other particles from the air.

  • Warm incoming air.

  • Moisten incoming air.

PHARYNX

The pharynx is a passage that carries air from the nasal cavity towards the larynx.

LARYNX

The larynx is also called the voice box.

Functions

  • Allows air to pass into the trachea.

  • Contains the vocal cords, which produce sound.

TRACHEA

The trachea is also called the windpipe. It carries air from the larynx to the bronchi.

Functions

  • Provides a passage for air.

  • Contains rings of cartilage that prevent it from collapsing.

  • Contains mucus and cilia that help remove dust and particles.

BRONCHI

The bronchi are the two main branches of the trachea. One enters each lung.

Function

They carry air into the lungs.

BRONCHIOLES

Bronchioles are smaller branches of the bronchi found inside the lungs.

Function

They distribute air to the alveoli.

ALVEOLI

Alveoli are tiny air sacs found at the ends of the bronchioles.

Functions

  • Allow oxygen to move into the blood.

  • Allow carbon dioxide to move from the blood into the air sacs.

LUNGS

The lungs are the main organs of breathing. They contain bronchioles and millions of alveoli.

Functions

  • Take oxygen into the body.

  • Remove carbon dioxide from the body.

  • Provide a large surface for gaseous exchange.

MECHANISM OF BREATHING

Breathing takes place through two processes: inhalation and exhalation.

INHALATION

Inhalation is the process of taking air into the lungs.

During inhalation:

  • The diaphragm contracts and flattens.

  • The external intercostal muscles contract.

  • The ribs move upwards and outwards.

  • The chest cavity increases in volume.

  • Pressure inside the lungs decreases.

  • Air enters the lungs.

EXHALATION

Exhalation is the process of pushing air out of the lungs.

During normal exhalation:

  • The diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped.

  • The external intercostal muscles relax.

  • The ribs move downwards and inwards.

  • The chest cavity decreases in volume.

  • Pressure inside the lungs increases.

  • Air moves out of the lungs.

CLASSWORK

Answer the following questions.

  1. Define the respiratory system.

  2. Differentiate between breathing and respiration.

  3. State the functions of the nasal cavity, trachea and lungs.

  4. Explain the meaning of aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

  5. Describe the processes of inhalation and exhalation.

ASSIGNMENT

  1. Draw and label the human respiratory system.

  2. State five parts of the respiratory system and explain their functions.

  3. Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.

  4. Explain how the diaphragm and ribs move during inhalation.

  5. State four differences between inhalation and exhalation.

SS 2|First term|Biology.title: RESPIRATORY SYSTEM II
SS 2|First term|Biology.note:
GASEOUS EXCHANGE

Gaseous exchange is the process by which oxygen and carbon dioxide move between an organism and its environment.

In humans, gaseous exchange takes place mainly in the alveoli of the lungs.

Oxygen moves from the air in the alveoli into the blood, while carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the alveoli to be breathed out.

ADAPTATIONS OF THE ALVEOLI FOR GASEOUS EXCHANGE

The alveoli are suitable for gaseous exchange because:

  • They are numerous and provide a large surface area.

  • Their walls are thin, allowing gases to diffuse quickly.

  • Their surfaces are moist, allowing gases to dissolve.

  • They are surrounded by many blood capillaries.

  • Continuous breathing helps maintain differences in gas concentration.

TRANSPORT OF OXYGEN

Oxygen enters the blood through the alveoli.

Most oxygen combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells to form oxyhaemoglobin.

Oxyhaemoglobin carries oxygen to body tissues, where the oxygen is released for cellular respiration.

TRANSPORT OF CARBON DIOXIDE

Carbon dioxide is produced during cellular respiration.

It is transported from body tissues to the lungs mainly in the form of bicarbonate ions in the blood. Some is attached to haemoglobin, while a small amount dissolves directly in the plasma.

In the lungs, carbon dioxide moves into the alveoli and leaves the body during exhalation.

RESPIRATORY SURFACES IN OTHER ORGANISMS

Different organisms use different structures for gaseous exchange.

Fish

Fish use gills to absorb dissolved oxygen from water and release carbon dioxide.

Insects

Insects use air tubes called tracheae. Air enters through openings called spiracles.

Earthworms

Earthworms exchange gases through their moist skin.

Amphibians

Adult frogs use their lungs and moist skin for gaseous exchange. Their larvae generally use gills.

Plants

Plants exchange gases mainly through stomata in their leaves and lenticels in woody stems.

AEROBIC AND ANAEROBIC RESPIRATION

Aerobic respiration

  • Requires oxygen.

  • Completely breaks down glucose.

  • Releases a large amount of energy.

  • Produces carbon dioxide and water.

Anaerobic respiration

  • Does not require oxygen.

  • Incompletely breaks down glucose.

  • Releases less energy than aerobic respiration.

  • Produces different end products depending on the organism.

In human muscles, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid. In yeast, it produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

RESPIRATORY DISORDERS

Asthma

Asthma is a condition in which the airways become inflamed and narrowed, making breathing difficult.

Bronchitis

Bronchitis is the inflammation of the lining of the bronchi. It may cause coughing and mucus production.

Pneumonia

Pneumonia is an infection that causes inflammation of the lungs. The alveoli may fill with fluid or pus, making breathing difficult.

Tuberculosis (TB)

Tuberculosis is a bacterial disease that commonly affects the lungs. It can spread through the air when an infected person releases infectious particles.

Lung cancer

Lung cancer is the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells in the lungs. Smoking is a major risk factor.

WAYS OF MAINTAINING A HEALTHY RESPIRATORY SYSTEM

  • Avoid smoking and vaping.

  • Avoid inhaling harmful dust and chemicals.

  • Keep rooms well ventilated.

  • Exercise regularly.

  • Avoid prolonged exposure to air pollution.

  • Practise good hygiene.

  • Seek medical attention for persistent breathing difficulties or coughing.

CLASSWORK

Answer the following questions.

  1. Define gaseous exchange.

  2. State four adaptations of the alveoli for gaseous exchange.

  3. Explain how oxygen is transported from the lungs to body tissues.

  4. State the respiratory organs used by fish, insects and earthworms.

  5. Mention five respiratory disorders.

ASSIGNMENT

  1. Explain how carbon dioxide is transported from body tissues to the lungs.

  2. Differentiate between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

  3. Explain gaseous exchange in fish and insects.

  4. State five ways of maintaining a healthy respiratory system.

  5. Explain the causes or characteristics of asthma, bronchitis and pneumonia.

SS 2|First term|Biology.title: EXCRETORY SYSTEM
SS 2|First term|Biology.note:
MEANING OF EXCRETION

Excretion is the process by which living organisms remove metabolic waste products from their bodies.

Metabolic waste products are substances produced during activities inside the cells. If these substances accumulate in the body, they may become harmful.

Examples of excretory products include carbon dioxide, urea, excess water and mineral salts.

MEANING OF THE EXCRETORY SYSTEM

The excretory system is the group of organs responsible for removing metabolic waste products from the body and maintaining the proper balance of water and mineral salts.

DIFFERENCE BETWEEN EXCRETION AND EGESTION

Excretion: The removal of metabolic waste products from the body.

Example: Removal of urea through urine.

Egestion: The removal of undigested food materials from the digestive tract through the anus.

Example: Passing out faeces.

EXCRETORY ORGANS IN HUMANS

The major excretory organs in humans are the kidneys, lungs, skin and liver.

THE KIDNEYS

The kidneys are two bean-shaped organs located at the back of the abdominal cavity, one on each side of the backbone.

Their major function is to filter the blood and remove waste products in the form of urine.

Functions of the kidneys

  • Remove urea from the blood.

  • Remove excess water and mineral salts.

  • Help maintain the balance of water in the body.

  • Help maintain the balance of salts in the blood.

  • Help maintain the body's acid-base balance.

STRUCTURE OF THE KIDNEY

The main parts of the kidney include the following.

Cortex: The outer region of the kidney. It contains parts of the nephrons where filtration begins.

Medulla: The inner region of the kidney. It contains structures involved in concentrating urine.

Renal pelvis: A space that collects urine before it passes into the ureter.

Ureter: A tube that carries urine from the kidney to the urinary bladder.

Urinary bladder: An organ that temporarily stores urine.

Urethra: The tube through which urine leaves the body.

THE NEPHRON

The nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney. It filters blood and helps produce urine.

Main parts of the nephron

  • Glomerulus: A network of tiny blood capillaries where filtration takes place.

  • Bowman's capsule: A cup-shaped structure that collects the fluid filtered from the blood.

  • Proximal convoluted tubule: Reabsorbs useful substances such as glucose, amino acids, salts and water.

  • Loop of Henle: Helps the kidney conserve water and regulate salt concentration.

  • Distal convoluted tubule: Helps regulate salt, water and acid-base balance.

  • Collecting duct: Collects fluid from nephrons and helps determine the final concentration of urine.

FORMATION OF URINE

Urine is formed in the kidneys through three main processes.

Ultrafiltration

Ultrafiltration is the process by which water and small dissolved substances are forced out of the blood in the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule.

Blood cells and most large proteins remain in the blood.

Selective reabsorption

Selective reabsorption is the process by which useful substances are taken back into the blood from the fluid inside the kidney tubules.

Examples include glucose, amino acids, useful salts and much of the water.

Tubular secretion

Tubular secretion is the movement of certain substances from the blood into the kidney tubules for removal.

Examples include hydrogen ions and some drugs.

The remaining fluid becomes urine, which passes through the collecting ducts into the renal pelvis, down the ureter and into the urinary bladder.

THE LUNGS AS EXCRETORY ORGANS

The lungs remove waste products produced during cellular respiration.

Excretory products of the lungs

  • Carbon dioxide.

  • Water vapour.

During exhalation, carbon dioxide and some water vapour leave the body.

THE SKIN AS AN EXCRETORY ORGAN

The skin removes small amounts of waste products through sweat glands.

Sweat contains mainly water, mineral salts and small amounts of urea.

Functions of the skin in excretion

  • Removes some excess water.

  • Removes some mineral salts.

  • Removes small amounts of urea.

  • Helps regulate body temperature through sweating.

THE LIVER AS AN EXCRETORY ORGAN

The liver performs several functions related to excretion.

Functions of the liver

  • Converts excess amino acids into substances that can be used for energy or other purposes.

  • Converts toxic ammonia into urea, which is carried to the kidneys for removal.

  • Breaks down old red blood cells and helps eliminate waste pigments through bile.

  • Breaks down or processes certain harmful substances, including some drugs.

EXCRETORY PRODUCTS IN HUMANS

Excretory organWaste product removed
KidneysUrea, excess water and mineral salts
LungsCarbon dioxide and water vapour
SkinWater, mineral salts and small amounts of urea
LiverWaste pigments through bile; converts ammonia into urea

EXCRETION IN PLANTS

Plants also produce waste products during their life activities, although they do not have specialised excretory organs like humans.

Methods of excretion in plants

  • Oxygen produced during photosynthesis may leave through the stomata.

  • Carbon dioxide produced during respiration may leave through the stomata.

  • Excess water is removed through transpiration.

  • Some waste products are stored in leaves, bark and fruits that may later be shed.

  • Some waste products are stored as substances such as resins, gums and latex.

HOMEOSTASIS

Homeostasis is the maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment in the body.

The excretory system helps maintain homeostasis by regulating water, mineral salts and the removal of metabolic waste products.

COMMON DISORDERS OF THE EXCRETORY SYSTEM

Kidney stones

Kidney stones are hard deposits of minerals and salts that form in the kidneys. They may cause severe pain and difficulty passing urine.

Kidney failure

Kidney failure occurs when the kidneys can no longer filter waste products effectively.

Urinary tract infection (UTI)

A urinary tract infection is an infection affecting parts of the urinary system. It may cause painful urination and frequent urination.

Nephritis

Nephritis is inflammation of the kidneys. It may interfere with their ability to filter blood properly.

WAYS OF MAINTAINING A HEALTHY EXCRETORY SYSTEM

  • Drink enough clean water.

  • Maintain good personal hygiene.

  • Avoid unnecessary use of medicines.

  • Eat a balanced diet.

  • Avoid excessive salt intake.

  • Do not regularly hold urine for long periods.

  • Seek medical attention when experiencing persistent pain or changes in urination.

CLASSWORK

Answer the following questions.

  1. Define excretion and state four examples of excretory products.

  2. State four functions of the kidneys.

  3. List the main parts of the nephron and state the function of any three.

  4. Explain ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption.

  5. State the excretory products removed by the kidneys, lungs and skin.

ASSIGNMENT

  1. Draw and label the human urinary system, showing the kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder and urethra.

  2. Explain the three main processes involved in urine formation.

  3. Differentiate between excretion and egestion.

  4. Explain the roles of the liver and lungs in excretion.

  5. State five ways of maintaining a healthy excretory system.

SS 2|First term|Biology.title: NUTRIENT CYCLING
SS 2|First term|Biology.note:
MEANING OF NUTRIENT CYCLING

Nutrient cycling is the continuous movement and reuse of nutrients between living organisms and the non-living environment.

Nutrients are substances that living organisms need for growth, energy, repair and survival.

Examples of nutrients that cycle in nature include carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and water.

IMPORTANCE OF NUTRIENT CYCLING

Nutrient cycling is important because it:

  • Makes nutrients available to plants and animals.

  • Maintains soil fertility.

  • Supports the growth of living organisms.

  • Prevents the permanent loss of important nutrients.

  • Maintains the balance of gases in the atmosphere.

  • Helps decomposers return nutrients to the environment.

THE WATER CYCLE

The water cycle is the continuous movement of water between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere.

Processes involved in the water cycle

Evaporation

Evaporation is the process by which liquid water changes into water vapour due to heat from the sun.

Transpiration

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of plants, mainly through the leaves.

Condensation

Condensation is the process by which water vapour cools and changes into tiny liquid water droplets, forming clouds.

Precipitation

Precipitation is the falling of water from clouds to the Earth's surface as rain, snow or hail.

Runoff

Runoff is the movement of water over the land into rivers, lakes and oceans.

Infiltration

Infiltration is the movement of water from the ground surface into the soil.

IMPORTANCE OF THE WATER CYCLE

  • Supplies water to plants and animals.

  • Provides water for agriculture.

  • Replenishes rivers, lakes and groundwater.

  • Helps regulate environmental temperature.

  • Supports the survival of aquatic organisms.

THE CARBON CYCLE

The carbon cycle is the continuous movement of carbon between the atmosphere, living organisms, soil and water.

Carbon is important because it forms part of carbohydrates, proteins, fats and other substances found in living organisms.

Processes involved in the carbon cycle

Photosynthesis

Green plants absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and use it to manufacture food in the presence of sunlight.

Feeding

Animals obtain carbon by feeding on plants or other animals.

Respiration

Plants and animals release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere during respiration.

Decomposition

Decomposers break down dead organisms and waste materials, returning carbon to the soil and releasing carbon dioxide through respiration.

Combustion

Combustion is the burning of wood, coal, petrol and other fuels. It releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.

IMPORTANCE OF THE CARBON CYCLE

  • Provides carbon for making food.

  • Supports the formation of organic substances in living organisms.

  • Maintains the balance of carbon dioxide in nature.

  • Helps maintain the flow of carbon through food chains.

THE NITROGEN CYCLE

The nitrogen cycle is the continuous movement of nitrogen between the atmosphere, soil and living organisms.

Nitrogen is needed for the formation of proteins, enzymes and nucleic acids.

Although the atmosphere contains about 78% nitrogen gas, most plants cannot use nitrogen directly in this form.

Processes involved in the nitrogen cycle

Nitrogen fixation

Nitrogen fixation is the conversion of atmospheric nitrogen into usable nitrogen compounds.

It occurs through nitrogen-fixing bacteria, lightning and industrial processes.

Some nitrogen-fixing bacteria live freely in the soil, while others live in the root nodules of leguminous plants such as beans and peas.

Nitrification

Nitrification is the conversion of ammonia or ammonium compounds into nitrites and then nitrates by nitrifying bacteria in the soil.

Plants can absorb nitrates through their roots.

Assimilation

Assimilation is the absorption and use of nitrogen compounds by plants to make proteins and other organic substances.

Animals obtain nitrogen by feeding on plants or other animals.

Ammonification

Ammonification is the conversion of nitrogen-containing substances in dead organisms and waste products into ammonia or ammonium compounds by decomposers.

Denitrification

Denitrification is the conversion of nitrates into nitrogen gas by denitrifying bacteria. The nitrogen gas returns to the atmosphere.

IMPORTANCE OF THE NITROGEN CYCLE

  • Makes nitrogen available to plants.

  • Helps plants manufacture proteins.

  • Supports animal growth and tissue repair.

  • Maintains the supply of nitrogen in the soil.

  • Helps maintain the balance of nitrogen in nature.

THE OXYGEN CYCLE

The oxygen cycle is the continuous movement of oxygen between the atmosphere and living organisms.

Oxygen is needed by most organisms for aerobic respiration.

Processes involved in the oxygen cycle

Photosynthesis

Green plants release oxygen into the atmosphere during photosynthesis.

Respiration

Plants and animals use oxygen during aerobic respiration and release carbon dioxide and water.

Combustion

Burning fuels uses oxygen and releases gases such as carbon dioxide.

Decomposition

Decomposers use oxygen during aerobic decomposition of dead organisms.

IMPORTANCE OF THE OXYGEN CYCLE

  • Supplies oxygen for aerobic respiration.

  • Supports the survival of many living organisms.

  • Helps maintain the balance of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere.

  • Supports the breakdown of organic matter by aerobic decomposers.

ROLE OF DECOMPOSERS IN NUTRIENT CYCLING

Decomposers are organisms that break down dead plants, dead animals and waste materials into simpler substances.

Examples include bacteria and fungi.

Importance of decomposers

  • Return nutrients to the soil.

  • Break down dead organisms.

  • Help form humus in the soil.

  • Release carbon dioxide during respiration.

  • Prevent the accumulation of large amounts of dead organic matter.

FACTORS THAT AFFECT NUTRIENT CYCLING

Temperature

Warm conditions often increase the activities of decomposers, while very low temperatures slow decomposition.

Moisture

Adequate moisture supports the activities of many decomposers. Extremely dry conditions slow decomposition.

Availability of oxygen

Oxygen affects the rate and type of decomposition that occurs.

Human activities

Deforestation, bush burning, excessive use of fertilisers and pollution can disturb nutrient cycles.

EFFECTS OF HUMAN ACTIVITIES ON NUTRIENT CYCLING

Deforestation

Cutting down trees reduces the amount of carbon dioxide absorbed through photosynthesis and may reduce the return of nutrients to the soil.

Bush burning

Bush burning destroys vegetation, kills soil organisms and releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.

Excessive use of fertilisers

Too much fertiliser can cause nutrients to enter rivers and lakes, leading to excessive growth of algae and the depletion of oxygen in water.

Burning of fossil fuels

Burning coal, petrol and natural gas releases large amounts of carbon dioxide, contributing to global warming.

WAYS OF MAINTAINING BALANCED NUTRIENT CYCLES

  • Plant more trees.

  • Avoid unnecessary bush burning.

  • Use fertilisers properly.

  • Practise composting.

  • Protect forests and wetlands.

  • Reduce pollution.

  • Use resources sustainably.

  • Protect soil organisms and natural habitats.

CLASSWORK

Answer the following questions.

  1. Define nutrient cycling and state four reasons why it is important.

  2. Explain the processes involved in the water cycle.

  3. Describe five processes involved in the carbon cycle.

  4. Explain nitrogen fixation, nitrification and denitrification.

  5. State five ways human activities affect nutrient cycling.

ASSIGNMENT

  1. Draw and label the water cycle.

  2. Draw a simple diagram showing the carbon cycle.

  3. Explain the major processes involved in the nitrogen cycle.

  4. State five functions of decomposers in nutrient cycling.

  5. Explain five ways of maintaining balanced nutrient cycles in nature.
